Ex-defence minister Fedorov’s team reveals more about his role as adviser to Italian minister: he will stay in Ukraine
Mykhailo Fedorov's press office has stated that his previous position as defence minister does not prevent him from serving as an adviser to the governments of other countries, and that he will continue to live and work in Ukraine.
Source: Fedorov's press office, commenting on his work as an adviser to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto
Quote: "Mykhailo Fedorov's previous position as defence minister does not impose any restrictions on his ability to serve as an adviser.
This [role] does not involve disclosing state secrets or specialist information required for the development, production or use of military products, or any other technical documentation or restricted-access information.
Engaging former senior officials as experts and advisers to the governments of other countries is common international practice. They are brought in precisely because of their management experience and expertise in specific fields."
Details: Fedorov's press office gave several examples, noting that former UK prime minister Rishi Sunak has been engaged by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an adviser on economic recovery; former Canadian deputy prime minister and finance minister Chrystia Freeland has become an adviser to Zelenskyy on economic development; and former UK prime minister Boris Johnson has also been involved in international advisory work since leaving government, including in the areas of international policy, security and support for Ukraine.
Fedorov's team said the role of defence innovation adviser is primarily about exchanging management and expert experience in technological warfare, and that this kind of cooperation is important for Ukraine because it "deepens cooperation with NATO countries and their defence industries and creates new opportunities for Ukrainian defence tech companies, joint development projects and investment initiatives".
The press office also noted that Fedorov has dozens of other international cooperation projects planned.
Quote: "At the same time, Mykhailo Fedorov will continue to live and work in Ukraine. His main focus remains here – helping Ukraine defeat the enemy. His international work will enable him to attract more attention, partners and investment to new projects – a think tank and an innovation fund that will invest in Ukrainian technologies and weapons that could change the course of the war."
Background
- On 28 August, Fedorov announced that he had accepted an offer from Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto to become his adviser.
- On 22 August, Fedorov said that following his dismissal from government, his future plans include working on a venture fund to attract investment in Ukrainian defence start-ups, setting up a think tank and civic initiatives aimed at a "return to democracy", and lecturing at universities.

In Ein Kerem, Israel’s most unlikely wellness retreat becomes a source of healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:39:19 UTC
02:39:19 KST

By our second morning at the Khan Ein Karem Boutique Hotel, something had already begun to shift. Roi and Tomer, the hotel’s warm and attentive hosts, understand this quiet rhythm perfectly. Their hospitality philosophy is simple: Give visitors tranquility, space, and a nourishing breakfast, then let the valley do the rest.
What Adi and I discovered over the weekend is that Ein Kerem’s deepest wellness offering isn’t the landscape alone but the remarkable concentration of people who have chosen to build their lives inside it. In a country navigating complex realities and social fractures, Ein Kerem holds an unusual number of individuals who have each developed their own philosophy of healing and chosen to share it openly with those who arrive.
“It is a capsule of this multicultural, interreligious encounter that is so special and sadly almost doesn’t exist in Israel,” Roi told us over breakfast at the hotel’s inviting dining table. “Here, when you go out and start walking, you meet. You have no choice.” Meeting, as our weekend unfolded, turned out to be the most restorative act of all.
Food for the soul: Café Itah
On Friday morning, Adi and I made our way down the stone stairs to Café Itah – meaning “woman” in Aramaic – a courtyard kitchen that operates as a model of social healing and community hospitality. Our host, Moti Levi, a local contractor who lives a minimalist lifestyle in renovated buses in nearby Givat Ye’arim, founded the café as a social enterprise under the Tirosh Association.
Its mission is to provide dignified, therapeutic employment for young women and teenage girls navigating personal crises, trauma, and institutionalization. The café also acts as a safety net for girls who age out of closed state welfare facilities at 18 and suddenly find themselves without shelter; Moti frequently steps in to give them a safe place to sleep.
Head chef Amit spent 12 years managing kitchens in high-end catering and luxury hotels, including the King David Hotel, before reshaping her career around a double purpose. Under her direction, the café delivers a genuinely high-level culinary experience – zucchini latkes, rich shakshukas, house-made pestos, and hand-preserved lemons – but the quality of the food is ultimately a vehicle for something deeper.
“I had no satisfaction in just working in a restaurant and serving food to a customer,” Amit said. “I wanted satisfaction in my heart at the end of the day – the satisfaction of doing something good for someone.” Of the kitchen itself, she added, “I am a very hyperactive person, and the kitchen is a place of creation to release that. The world of pastry and cooking is a therapeutic path.”
This approach demands a forgiving business model. Amit gives the girls time and space to process crises and anxiety attacks, noting that “in any other restaurant, they wouldn’t give you the space; they would just kick you out.” Her guiding rule: “The customer is temporary… but for her, this is her life. My girls come before the customer.”
Anchoring this support system is Avraham, a 60-year-old retired village resident who sits on a wooden bench in the courtyard each day between noon and 4 p.m. – a calm, steady figure the girls can sit beside to regulate their breathing when anxiety rises mid-shift.
The impact runs deep. One young woman told us she’d once spent an entire year shut inside her home, paralyzed by depression; another said, “I never managed to hold a job for five days a week… but here it’s like family. You aren’t treated like a robot; you are seen as a human being first.”
Sitting in the sun-kissed courtyard over this exceptional food, you understand that its therapeutic value is inseparable from the well-being of the hands that prepared it.
The scribe of lost stories: Avshalom Eshel
Between the village’s stone alleys and the ridge where the Music Center awaits, we met one of Ein Kerem’s most remarkable figures: Avshalom Eshel, who moves between the hassidic religious world and the creative world of arts as though they were never separate.
Avshalom is officially a sofer stam – a traditional Jewish scribe who writes Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzahs by hand. He playfully reinterprets the Hebrew acronym STAM as “Stories, Tricks, and Plots.” Outside his studio hangs a sign describing his daily mission: “Conductor of roads for lost stories.”
Inside, he directs theatrical plays, including an upcoming production of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov’s The Seven Beggars. His own return to religion was sparked by reading Rabbi Nachman’s stories and falling in love with a religious woman who happened to sit beside him on a bus – an encounter that led to their marriage and six children.
His calligraphy, he explained, is a spiritual remedy for the modern age. Teivah in Hebrew means both “ark” and “word.” Since a physical ark can no longer shelter a person from the flood of modern noise and anxiety, Avshalom crafts tiny “arks” out of positive words, writing them by hand on parchment to give to visitors as a portable refuge. Every person, he teaches, is like a single letter in a Torah scroll; if even one letter is cracked or missing, the whole scroll is invalid. “This is our medicine,” he said, “to return and be parts of one big story.”
That philosophy runs through his workspace: a building that houses a secular yeshiva downstairs and a joyful, “hippie” Orthodox synagogue upstairs. Before we spoke, he picked up his sitar – a stringed musical instrument – letting its resonant tones settle the room, then pressed our personalized parchment tags into our hands.
Because Avshalom lives intentionally offline and refuses a smartphone, our visit ended with him offering his wife’s WhatsApp number – a fitting close for a man whose life is devoted to genuine human connection.
Sacred soundscapes and open tables
On Friday afternoon, we visited the Eden-Tamir Music Center on the village’s upper ridge, welcomed by Prof. Rami Eden (son of co-founder Bracha), Dr. Dror Semmel, and longtime host Saleh. Founded in 1968 by the piano duo Bracha Eden and Alexander Tamir, the center has anchored Jerusalem’s classical music scene for nearly six decades.
Its intimate 120-seat hall houses a rare fortepiano – a replica of an 1819 Viennese instrument built by master craftsman Paul McNulty – whose lighter, softer sound lets us hear Beethoven and Schubert nearly as their first salon audiences did, without the volume of a modern grand piano. The center still hosts chamber concerts every Saturday morning and biweekly Friday performances for young Israeli artists.
During our Shabbat walk, we found a striking blend of art and tradition at the Jewish House, the local Chabad House run by Rabbi Shaya and Nechemi Kedelburg. Housed in a restored stone building that doubles as an art gallery and vintage boutique, it felt unlike any conventional Chabad house – artistic, localized, and rooted in Ein Kerem’s bohemian character.
Over a long Shabbat conversation, we watched secular artists, traditional residents, and international travelers share the same table, a quiet proof that belonging can be one of the most powerful forms of harmony.
The gathering table
On Thursday evening, we dined at the Ein Kerem Courtyard Restaurant, one of the village’s few kosher establishments, over baked cauliflower with tehina and cheese-stuffed phyllo.
The meal set the tone for how Ein Kerem functions as a crossroads where social boundaries dissolve. On any afternoon, its limestone alleys host Christian priests beside barefoot anthroposophical families, secular tech workers, and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) families who’ve driven in from central Jerusalem for a change of pace.
That spirit peaks every Thursday night in the courtyard of Avshalom’s building, where wooden tables go up under the open sky for 80 to 100 people – an evening of cholent, live theater, and acoustic jam sessions that bypass political and religious divides entirely. Among the regulars is a woman who drives every week from Ofakim, in the South, just to be part of it.
As the weekend closed, Adi and I sat on the Khan Hotel’s upper balcony watching the sun cast long shadows across the terraces, our Shabbat table catered by chef Eli Fadida of Beit HaKerem and the celebrated Pasha in Talpiot.
Community, it turns out, is the oldest and most effective wellness intervention. Ein Kerem doesn’t offer it packaged; it offers it in the raw, unscheduled way of a village where the streets are too narrow to walk without meeting someone. The healers, scribes, chefs, musicians, and rabbis who have built their lives here are its greatest therapeutic asset. We left rested, fed, and quietly altered, carrying what the valley gave us back into the city above – the way water carries minerals from ancient stone.

Near the Gaza border, Dream Island offers a luxury retreat built around rest and healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:39:11 UTC
02:39:11 KST

As a photojournalist, my lens is usually trained on the rugged and the raw, capturing the stories written in the dust of the road and the quiet resilience of those who call the borderlands home. But every so often, the road leads to a place that feels less like a destination and more like a collective exhale.
Just a short 20-minute drive from the city of Sderot and the Gaza border area, and a mere 45 minutes from the frantic energy of central Israel, lies Dream Island – Spa & Health Resort. It is a sprawling sanctuary that operates as a closed, secluded oasis, providing a nearby gateway for those seeking wellness and a deep physiological reset within the soft, rolling horizons of the northern Negev.
For couples and honeymooners, the resort offers 26 boutique suites that redefine the concept of an intimate getaway.
These smart-controlled sanctuaries are master classes in privacy, featuring hot tubs on balconies overlooking the open fields of the Yoav plains, or private courtyards with their own saunas and pools.
Every suite is stocked with a VIP greeting that includes a minibar filled with cocktails, sweets, and high-end treats, intended to make the transition into relaxation immediate.
The vision for the future is even more ambitious. While the current site is adding 40 new suites, the ownership’s future plans include opening flagship luxury resorts on the Ashkelon beach and on the shores of the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret) in the Migdal area.
Arrival at the oasis: a philosophy of abundance
The personal experience of arrival immediately sets the tone for a stay defined by what the resort calls “unlimited abundance.”
Upon entering the complex, guests are handed a comprehensive map of the entire 1,500-square-meter layout to ensure every corner of this paradise is accessible.
Nearby, a large digital board displays a rotating schedule for the day, allowing seamless registration for workshops ranging from meditative Pilates to the resort’s signature wine-tasting experience.
This introductory moment serves as a transition into an adults-only world where the architecture of the soul is given as much attention as the physical grounds.
This liquid paradise features a massive outdoor pool designed for ultimate comfort, perfectly suited for lounging under the unique light of the Negev sun.
Indoors, the water complex expands into four distinct pools, each offering different settings of powerful jets or waterfalls that create intimate, private spots for couples to relax together.
Oversized indoor Jacuzzis, a steaming wet sauna, a dry sauna, and a traditional Turkish hammam all contribute to the resort’s identity as a comprehensive sanctuary of healing.
The journey through the resort reveals a vibrant live kitchen experience that has evolved from the traditional food trucks of the past into permanent, high-end culinary spots. The orientation of these stands is inspired by a bustling Greek market, where specialized salads and fresh vegetables are displayed with the artistry of a boutique stall.
This marketplace vibe is complemented by an Italian station featuring personal focaccias oven-baked to order with seasonal toppings, a dedicated Asian stand where chefs prepare fresh sushi and a variety of East Asian delicacies, and a fragrant coffee stand with fresh pastries. Beside the coffee station, an artistic dessert truck features elegant “candle” cakes and fruit-designed desserts that create a fragrant, inviting atmosphere as you enter.
Everywhere you turn, from the quiet corners of the gardens overlooking the ecological lake to the sprawling pools, there is a recurring sense that you can always find a place to sit, relax, and disconnect from the world outside.
The Healing Tent and the science of the reset
Deep within the grounds, guests encounter the Healing Tent, a space dedicated to the “restart” of hot and cold water therapy.
This experience is a profound physical reset, featuring temperature-controlled ice baths and breathing exercises led by specialized guides to help guests decompress through controlled thermal cycles.
For day visitors who desire the privacy of a suite without an overnight stay, the resort offers “Premium Day capsules.”
These luxurious, smart-equipped caravans are imported specifically for the resort, providing a private living room, bedroom, shower, and a stocked minibar for a secluded rest or meal within the heart of the grounds.
The culinary heartbeat of the resort is found in the main restaurant, Armonim, which delivers a high-level experience evoking the grand theme hotels of Las Vegas. The design is elegant and fashionable, featuring a grand piano where a DJ often performs for the guests, blending classical grace with a modern rhythmic pulse.
While day guests enjoy an expansive lunch included in their visit, those staying in the suites are treated to professional dinners featuring incredible, high-level food platters.
Breakfast at the Terra restaurant is equally prestigious, with a seating area centered around a majestic olive tree that stands in the middle of the dining space, reinforcing the Mediterranean atmosphere of generosity and sophisticated display.
The spa sanctuary: Healing on a grand scale
No visit to Dream Island is complete without a journey into its Dream Spa, one of the largest and most active treatment complexes in the country.
According to the resort’s leadership, the spa performs thousands of treatments every month, utilizing approximately 20 specialized treatment rooms.
For us, celebrating a life milestone like my wife Adi’s 40th birthday, the experience was heightened by a session in one of the couple’s rooms. These rooms are designed for total intimacy and professional-grade body treatments, ranging from Swedish massage and reflexology to aromatherapy.
The suites themselves are a master class in isolated luxury, featuring remarkably high ceilings and complete privacy.
Our stay included a private pool, an outdoor Jacuzzi, and a secluded resting tent, allowing us to spend one night and two full days entirely within this “bubble.”
This sense of total seclusion and luxury is what makes the resort a premier destination for those looking to celebrate major life events in an environment that feels disconnected from the stresses of the outside world.
Fruit wine and the Byzantine legacy
A central part of the resort’s cultural experience is the wine-tasting workshop, held in a restored Byzantine-era winepress discovered during the resort’s construction.
In the modern wine room built around this ancient winepress, guests participate in workshops focusing on fruit wines produced in collaboration with the Lachish winery. These 16% alcohol, port-style wines are crafted from the pure essence of fruits like Pink Lady apples, black raspberries, peaches, and pomegranates.
The science behind these wines is fascinating. Because they are made from fruit rather than grapes, they contain no added white sugar, relying solely on the fruit’s natural sweetness. The fermentation process preserves the fruit’s natural vitamins and antioxidants, creating a boutique beverage exclusive to Dream Island and free of the industrial sulfites that often cause wine headaches.
Tasting these wines while sitting beside an archaeological treasure creates a bridge between Israel’s ancient agricultural history and its modern culinary innovation.
Resilience and a vision for the future
Beyond the luxury, there is a profound story of resilience that defines the resort’s heart.
Following the outbreak of the war, Dream Island’s ownership dedicated itself to national recovery by hosting 50 combat soldiers every single day for free.
This initiative, which lasted for months, allowed entire military teams to decompress in the resort’s quiet groves and healing waters after months of service on the front lines. This commitment also extended to the wives of reservists, who were honored with dedicated appreciation events at the resort.
In the end, Dream Island is more than just a luxury destination; it is a vital sanctuary for the spirit, proving that abundance can bloom even in a landscape that has known great hardship.
For those seeking an escape that is both physically restorative and emotionally grounding, this northern Negev oasis offers a reminder that healing is always within reach.
The writer was a guest of the resort.

Europe enters winter with its lowest gas reserves in 13 years - The Guardian
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
20:38:07 EEST
02:38:07 KST

Europe enters winter with its lowest gas reserves in 13 years - The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
EU gas storage facilities are 63% full, compared with an average of 80% at the end of August. Germany has about half of the reserves, increasing the risk of shortages.
Europe is entering winter with its lowest gas stocks in 13 years. This has caused "winter panic" among energy traders, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
According to the publication, in the last week of August, EU gas storage facilities were 63% full, significantly below the average of 80% for the end of August in recent years. This is one of the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.
According to Greg Molnar, a gas analyst and professor, given the current slow pace of filling gas storage facilities, the EU is likely to enter the winter heating season with gas stocks approximately one-fifth below the average for the past five years and at their lowest level since 2013.
Low stock levels naturally increase the risk of greater price volatility in winter
EU gas storage facilities are struggling to reach the reduced target of 80% capacity by the beginning of winter, as the US-Israeli war against Iran has caused serious disruptions to oil and gas exports from the Persian Gulf region.
Additionally
Gas supply problems are particularly acute in Western Europe, where storage levels are significantly lower than in countries such as Italy and Poland, which have managed to fill their gas storage facilities to more than 80%.
In Germany, which has the largest gas storage capacity in Europe, the facilities are approximately half full, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Storage levels in Belgium and the Netherlands, which are directly connected to the British gas market via pipelines, stand at 51% and 45%, respectively.
Recall
Gas storage levels in Germany are exceptionally low, threatening supply shortages in November. Berlin does not want to abandon the free-market doctrine, despite the risks.

NEW DELHI: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday said Hinduism believes in the unity of humanity, asserting that “If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, then he's not a Hindu.”Addressing the ‘One World One Humanity’ event in New York, Bhagwat said different religions may follow different paths, but humanity and truth remain one.“We come from a society that believes humanity is one. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, then he's not a Hindu….” the RSS chief said.“If you want call yourself hindu than you must believe that all paths are leading to the same. And every human has a dignity. There is no difference between human beings,” he added.Bhagwat said diversity must be protected while stressing the importance of unity. “Diversity has to be protected as it is the rule of nature and 'Unity is universal truth,” he said.“I am not a religious scholar, nor a religious authority like you, but I am working in a society which traditionally says that religions might be different, but humanity is one. Truth is one, and humanity is a product of that truth. So humanity is one,” Bhagwat said.He added that while truth is one, it can be described in different ways depending on how people perceive it.
“That truth is one truth, but it is described in many ways according to the describer. Because as human beings, we are prisoners of the software that has been created in our heads,” he said.“There are many religions, and in today's world, religions are largely defined by rituals. And to fit in a religious discipline, and to treat that path to divinity, this discipline of rituals is also necessary,” he added.The event was organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) and was described as a “landmark Raksha Bandhan gathering”.“The event carries a timeless and universal message: 'The world is one family'. It calls upon us to look beyond artificial divisions and differences, recognise the bonds that unite humanity, and embrace a spirit of mutual respect, harmony, and oneness,” the organisation said.The programme featured cultural presentations and keynote addresses centred on universal oneness and the Hindu philosophy of ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’, or the world is one family.Bhagwat arrived in the US earlier this week as part of the RSS's centenary-year global outreach programme, which also includes visits to Canada and the UK.During his visit, he has met members of the Indian diaspora, Indian-American business leaders and community representatives.
Ahead of his Madison Square Garden address, images of Bhagwat were projected on billboards in New York's Times Square, carrying the words “Resolve, Harmony and Dialogue”.Bhagwat also visited the Bhakti Centre and the ISKCON temple in New York. At the temple, he participated in a food distribution initiative for homeless people and spoke about the role of Krishna consciousness in addressing conflicts and divisions.Earlier, the RSS said the Madison Square Garden event was being organised in the spirit of open dialogue and invited “anyone interested” in learning more about the organisation to participate.

Music publishers sue Anthropic over 'blatant' theft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:20:46 UTC
02:20:46 KST

Some of the world’s biggest music publishers have filed a major lawsuit against artificial intelligence company Anthropic, accusing the firm of "one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history."
The lawsuit, filed late Friday, marks the beginning of what could become a yearslong legal battle over the use of music in artificial intelligence systems and the future of copyright protection in the rapidly developing technology era, according to Axios on Saturday.
Companies affiliated with Sony Music and Warner Music brought the case before a federal court in Northern California. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann were also named as defendants.
In their 48-page complaint, the plaintiffs accuse Anthropic and its founders of systematically obtaining copyrighted material without permission to develop and operate the company's artificial intelligence models.
"Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic's 'Claude' series of artificial intelligence ('AI') models," the plaintiffs said in the complaint.
The music publishers alleged that Anthropic illegally copied thousands of copyrighted musical works. They are seeking hundreds of thousands of dollars in damages for each work they claim was infringed.
The case is not the first legal challenge facing Anthropic over allegations that copyrighted material was used to train its AI models.
In September 2025, Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement with authors and publishers, described at the time as the largest copyright settlement in US history.

The draft documents will be considered on August 30 at the 21st extraordinary session of the AU Assembly of Heads of State and Government in Luanda.

'Orcas hunt these bears' — Putin says children should learn the 'food chain' to understand Russia's war
Russian President Vladimir Putin invoked orcas "tearing polar bears apart" as a new analogy for Russia's war against Ukraine while speaking to students and teachers at a Moscow university on Aug. 29, according to the Russian independent media outlet Meduza.
Putin's remarks came as near-continuous air raid alerts across Ukraine stretched into a third consecutive day, with Russia launching continued waves of attacks. The attacks killed at least 37 people in Kyiv Oblast on Aug. 28 and killed a 14-year-old girl and a 2-year-old girl in separate attacks on Aug. 29.
The exchange began when Putin asked a teacher from Russia's Belgorod region, who had visited the North Pole, whether he had seen polar bears there.
After the teacher said he had seen two "enormous" bears, Putin replied that orcas live nearby and eat those bears.
"Right nearby, orcas hunt these bears, devouring them as if they were nothing. They descend in packs — and then, boom, tear them (bears) apart," he said.
Putin then connected the example to Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Yes, that's the food chain. Children should be taught about this, so that they understand what kind of world we live in and why we are conducting the special military operation," Putin said.
The bear is a recurring metaphor in Putin's rhetoric about Russia's confrontation with the West.
In 2014, after Russia had illegally annexed Crimea, he compared Russia to a bear that the West was trying to put "on a chain," warning that its "teeth and claws" would be torn out.
"Maybe our bear should sit quietly, not chasing any piglets around, but just eating honey and berries. Maybe they should just leave him alone? They will not. They are trying to put it on a chain," Putin claimed.

Theories of Biological Development

[Revised entry by Melinda Bonnie Fagan and Jane Maienschein on August 29, 2026.
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Development is a central biological process, and ideas about its nature have been influential in biological thought. This entry surveys the history of these ideas through the lens of “epigenesis vs. preformation”. Epigenesis is, roughly, the thesis that every developing entity starts from material that is unformed, with form emerging gradually, over time, in the process of development. Preformation, in contrast, is the thesis that development begins with the entity in some way already preformed, or predelineated, or…

Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:08:43 UTC
02:08:43 KST

Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order.
Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE.
A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.
The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.
The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”
Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West.
West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper.
Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status.
At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.
He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13.
Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart.
Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk.
A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.
He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

'The police ran away': Haredi protesters block buses entering Jerusalem on Shabbat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:08:12 UTC
02:08:12 KST

Dozens of ultra-Orthodox protesters blocked buses from entering Jerusalem on Saturday in the latest demonstration against public transportation operating on Shabbat, or the Sabbath.
The protest, which began last Saturday, targeted Egged buses arriving in Jerusalem from northern Israel before the end of Shabbat. At least 13 buses were stranded and unable to enter the capital because of the blockade.
Between 30 and 50 protesters gathered on Weizmann Boulevard and completely blocked the entrance to Jerusalem from Highway 1, the main highway connecting the city with Tel Aviv and central Israel.
Several minutes passed after the blockade began before a single police vehicle arrived. It left a short time later without clearing the road. Protesters chanted, “The police ran away,” and continued blocking the entrance until they reopened it on their own after Shabbat ended Saturday evening.
The bus routes travel from northern Israel to Jerusalem every Saturday under a long-standing status quo arrangement and drop passengers off outside the city’s Central Bus Station. Public transportation on Shabbat remains a contentious issue in Israel, where most regular bus and train services do not operate during the weekly day of rest, though some routes and services operate under longstanding arrangements or local initiatives.
The protesters prevented the buses from reaching Jerusalem by placing barriers in the roadway. Private vehicles were able to maneuver around the blockade on the wide road, with protesters focusing specifically on buses operating on Shabbat.
More than an hour after the blockade began, police said reinforcements were on their way.
“Additional forces are en route to disperse those disturbing the public order and restore traffic to normal,” police said. “Police are redirecting traffic at the entrance to the city to alternative routes.”
The additional forces, however, did not arrive to remove the protesters before the blockade ended.
The Jerusalem demonstration came alongside a similar dispute in Safed, a northern city where the central Egged Square has become a flashpoint over Shabbat transportation for more than two months.
Haredi protesters, including demonstrators from outside Safed, have gathered there every Saturday to protest public transportation operating on Shabbat. Nativ Express, which runs the routes in the city, has continued transporting soldiers and civilians under an arrangement that has been in place for years.
Shabbat transportation protests have also spread to Bnei Brak, a predominantly Haredi city east of Tel Aviv.
Before Shabbat began Friday, containers were placed on a road leading to the city’s Mitcham HaSoferim neighborhood, which is also home to secular residents, blocking access to the area.
Neighborhood residents called police, saying they had effectively been trapped inside.
Police officers who arrived at the scene moved the containers and reopened the road to traffic. The truck driver who placed them was summoned for questioning on suspicion of endangering a traffic route.
The driver said he had carried out the work for the Bnei Brak municipality. The municipality denied ordering the containers to be placed on the road.

Voropayev attended a gala dinner at the hotel on the evening of August 28 for lawmakers taking part in the parliamentary session. That night, he heard sustained gunfire.
The first session of the ACS parliament is being held in Niamey from August 24 to 29. Members of the legislative assemblies of Chad and Togo were invited to attend the opening as guests. Most of the participants were accommodated at the Bravia Hotel.
The final session was scheduled for 10:00 a.m. on August 29 but was postponed following the mutiny.
According to the Niger Press Agency, citing Niger’s Minister of National Defense Salifou Modi, a group of military personnel attempted to confine their fellow servicemen to a barracks at Air Force Base 101 overnight on August 28-29 and opened fire at several strategically important facilities in Niamey.
Modi said the rapid response of security forces helped contain the uprising and gradually restore control over the affected facilities. The Defense Ministry called on residents to "remain calm and go about their business.".

'The polls are biased. The right always gets stronger': Likud’s quiet winner is suddenly hard to ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:57:59 UTC
01:57:59 KST

While much of the discussion surrounding last week's Likud primaries focused on reserved slots, political hit lists, recommended-candidate slates and speculation about party heavyweights Amir Ohana, Tally Gotliv, Yariv Levin and Shlomo Karhi, Energy Minister Eli Cohen preferred to run a campaign under the radar. It paid off.
Cohen finished first by a huge margin over the second- and third-place candidates, after also finishing near the top in the previous Likud primary. Likud members clearly like him, but to most Israelis he remains something of an enigma, with relatively little known about him. That is his weakness — and his strength.
“I’m certainly happy with the result,” Cohen said in his first interview since his primary victory. “Likud members are smart people who love the country. They chose a strong slate of people who get things done. And I want to tell you that in every ministry I’ve served in, I’ve proven myself through actions and delivered results for the public. The word ‘give up’ doesn’t exist for me.”
How does your victory square with the populist, combative rhetoric within Likud?
“Today, people want to choose someone who gets things done, not someone who only talks. And thank God, succeeding time after time speaks for itself. During the primaries, I didn’t campaign against anyone. I focused mainly on what I had done: how I managed to break the Israel Electric Corp.’s monopoly, how I ensured that the energy sector functioned flawlessly, how I reached a gas deal with Egypt and how I secured visa-free travel to the United States.”
So you cracked the formula for beating populism and shouting.
“Yes. I think actions beat populism and shouting.”
Before the primaries, no one was talking about Eli Cohen. Did that help you take the top spot?
“In the previous primaries, they predicted I would finish sixth, and I finished second. This time, they thought I would finish in the top three — and I came first. I had a feeling that this time, too, I would beat the polls. But I know one thing: I get up every morning at 7 and work all day for the good of the country.”
Finishing first in the Likud primaries is indeed an impressive political achievement and a statement of intent about the future. Moshe Kahlon, Gideon Sa’ar, Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein have all been there before.
“I’m glad that, like them, I managed to finish first.”
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also politically destroyed all four of them.
“I will continue working with Netanyahu, and I’m pleased to have his confidence. Netanyahu is the right person to lead the State of Israel for the next four years. I think he delivered unprecedented achievements during this term. From the devastation of Oct. 7, we have become the strongest power in the Middle East.”
Do you see yourself running for the Likud leadership after Netanyahu?
“That question isn’t relevant right now. We are two and a half months out from an election, and I’m focused on one thing only: ensuring that Likud, led by Netanyahu, wins.”
Why are Likud ministers afraid to say that they are worthy and capable of replacing Netanyahu one day? Are you so afraid of him that you can’t bring yourselves to say it?
“We are on the eve of an election, and what is special about Likud is that we are united around Netanyahu. Likud is the most democratic party, compared with the left, which is constantly working to eliminate its own leaders. You can see they have nothing except ‘Anyone but Bibi.’”
Why did Netanyahu demand nine reserved spots on the slate? Doesn’t he trust Likud members?
“I think the prime minister looks at other parties, where the party leader determines the entire slate however he sees fit, and that is why he wanted those reserved spots for himself as well. In the end, the prime minister determines 25% of the slate through reserved slots, while 75% is determined by party members.”
Not simply a treasurer
Cohen, 53, began the current government’s term as foreign minister before moving to the Energy Ministry as part of an internal political arrangement. He has his sights set high. The next job he is eyeing is finance minister.
“I definitely expect to hold a senior position in the next government,” he said. “The three most senior portfolios are foreign affairs, finance and defense. Since I’ve already been foreign minister, the Finance Ministry interests me. I think that in the next term, the Finance Ministry must remain in Likud’s hands, and I have the qualifications for the job: my experience in the business world, my training as an accountant and my personal background. I would want to lead a free-market economy with social sensitivity.”
What do you think of Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich?
“In my view, the finance minister should not be the treasurer who simply hands out money. A finance minister needs to grow the pie, create engines of growth, ensure that young people want to live in this country, give them the opportunity to earn a decent living and work to reduce social disparities.”
Is it a mistake to appoint a finance minister who represents a particular sector?
“As I said, the Finance Ministry must remain with the ruling party.”
Netanyahu did everything he could to bring Otzma Yehudit lawmaker Almog Cohen onto the Likud slate. Cohen himself said there are no longer any differences between Likud and the hard-right Otzma Yehudit. Is Likud no longer the party it once was?
“Likud is a governing party, a responsible party. It is the party of all the people of Israel — of the periphery and the center, Sephardim and Ashkenazim, traditional Jews, secular Jews and Haredim.”
And you aren’t offended when Likud is compared with Otzma Yehudit?
“Likud is not Otzma Yehudit. Likud is the party of the people of Israel.”
Cohen appears to recognize the potential electoral damage posed by legislation that would allow many Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, men to continue avoiding military service, as well as a measure aimed at preventing the arrest of draft evaders and deserters.
“We need to complete the conscription law,” he said. “We have to increase equality in sharing the burden, and our Haredi brothers must also enlist. Anyone for whom Torah study is not a full-time occupation — 60% of Haredim — must enlist. It is important for security, it is important for the economy and it is important for bringing unity to the people of Israel.”
You could have done that during the last term, and you didn’t.
“The government before us, the Lapid-Liberman government, which was the most anti-Haredi government since the establishment of the state, failed to bring in a single recruit. And we were occupied mainly with managing the war. Unfortunately, there are those who try to diminish the achievements, but the State of Israel’s achievements in this war are unprecedented. All those who challenged the State of Israel did not live to die of old age. Not Hassan Nasrallah, not Yahya Sinwar and not Ali Khamenei. We prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.”
You didn’t prevent it. Maybe you delayed it. Some experts argue that after two rounds against Iran, we are back where we started.
“Fine, we delayed it. But the war against Iran was a tremendous victory and an enormous achievement.”
I’m not sure the public sees it that way. Otherwise, you would be cruising to victory in the election.
“If we hadn’t attacked, Iran would have a nuclear weapon. People in the intelligence community say we delayed Iran’s nuclear program by two, three or four years. One thing is clear: If Iran tries to restart its nuclear program, we will be on our way there to strike. We have already demonstrated our capabilities.”
In other words, Israel needs to strike Iran again?
“I’ll say it again: If Iran makes the mistake of trying to restart its nuclear program or its ballistic missile program, even if there is an agreement with the United States, we will be there to strike.”
There were significant achievements in the campaign against Iran. On the other hand, we achieved none of the war’s three objectives: eliminating the nuclear program, eliminating the ballistic missile program and bringing down the regime.
“If we had not launched that campaign, Iran would already have a nuclear weapon. Look at the State of Israel’s deterrence. The fact is that until a few weeks ago, Iran attacked most of the countries in the region. Who didn’t it attack? The State of Israel, because it knows we have deterrence. To this day, Mojtaba Khamenei has not emerged from the hole where he is hiding. He knows the long arm of the State of Israel can reach anywhere.”
Does Israel have a plan to create a route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz?
“The prime minister and I are currently working with the United States to advance the creation of a route that would bypass both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. The idea is to lay pipeline infrastructure, some of which already exists in Saudi Arabia and Israel.”
What is your biggest achievement at the Energy Ministry and the Foreign Ministry?
“My most significant achievement at the Energy Ministry is that the energy sector functioned flawlessly during the war, despite all those scenarios about blackouts and generators. And, of course, breaking the Israel Electric Corp.’s monopoly is also a very significant achievement. At the Foreign Ministry, after many years, I managed to complete the effort to secure visa-free travel for Israeli citizens traveling to the United States.”
It’s who you know
As someone who came to Likud from former finance minister Moshe Kahlon’s Kulanu party, Cohen has difficulty aligning himself with the confrontational rhetoric directed at the judiciary by Justice Minister Yariv Levin or Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana. Nor is he willing to say he would defy a ruling by the High Court of Justice.
“The government is not above the law, but neither is the court above the law. There is a sense that the balance between the branches of government has been disrupted,” Cohen said. “When we see attempts to interfere with the appointment of Roman Gofman as head of the Mossad or David Zini as head of the Shin Bet, then intervention by the High Court is unnecessary.”
I’m sorry, but the High Court approved both Gofman’s appointment and Zini’s appointment.
“Yes, but I think the petitions regarding Gofman and Zini should have been dismissed outright. They should not even have reached a hearing. We need a court that acts according to the law. We need a court that enjoys the public’s trust. I want a court in Israel that represents all parts of society, like in the United States. The ‘friends appointing friends’ system in the courts has to end. I succeeded in life because of who I am, not because of friends. That is how it should be in the military, in politics and in the judicial system.”
According to media reports this week, Netanyahu is deeply concerned about polling for Likud and the broader right-wing bloc. He reportedly believes he has lost 10 Knesset seats during the current term and is uncertain whether he can win those voters back. Cohen argues that Likud is consistently underestimated in polls.
“In 2015, the polls gave Likud 21 or 22 seats. We finished with 30 seats and won. In the last election, the polls gave our bloc 57 or 58 seats, and we ended up with 64. In other words, there is a bias in the polls. In the actual results, the right always gets stronger. I believe that even those who are undecided and sometimes talk about wanting change, when they come to vote, their hand will tremble. They won’t want a government formed here with the Islamic Movement.”
Maybe their hand won’t tremble because of Oct. 7 and Netanyahu’s responsibility for the deadliest massacre in the country’s history?
“The issue of Oct. 7 needs to be investigated by a national commission of inquiry that examines everyone going back years. But today, the State of Israel is the undisputed power in the Middle East. We have achieved successes on every front. So I’m confident that this time, too, we will get far more than the polls predict.”
There is still a cloud hanging over the issuance of a diplomatic passport to Yair Netanyahu. Why did you get yourself caught up in that affair?
“This investigation should never have been opened because Yair Netanyahu’s passport had been renewed for security reasons several times by several directors-general, beginning in 2009. Diplomatic passports were also issued to mayors, as had been done in the past, because of the international activities they conduct as part of their official duties.”
Your son served in the reserves in Lebanon. You are a member of the Security Cabinet and are expected to make decisions that also concern Lebanon. Does that affect your decision-making?
“I try to make decisions based solely on what is right and best for the security of the State of Israel. Sometimes Security Cabinet decisions mean that my son is also called up for reserve duty. A month ago, he completed several months of reserve service in Lebanon. By day, I’m a Cabinet member, and on quite a few nights, I’m also a worried father. I understand the significance of the decisions we make. And yes, I can tell you that I’m proud of him and his friends.”

Most of those killed by explosions in Bucha were elderly care home residents – photos
Most of the 37 people killed as a result of a Russian UAV strike and the subsequent detonation of ammunition in the village of Myla, in the Bucha district near Kyiv, were residents of a care home for the elderly.
Source: hromadske, citing Svitlana Vodolaha, a spokesperson for Ukraine's State Emergency Service, and its own correspondents; hromadske journalist Diana Butsko on Facebook
Details: Vodolaha said the deaths of 27 people have so far been confirmed. The other 10 cases have not been confirmed, as these relate to human remains found at the site of the Russian attack. The exact number of people killed will only be known after they have been identified.
According to hromadske's correspondents, the private care home for the elderly was the worst affected, and most of the people killed were residents of the home. The State Emergency Service said at least 27 residents were killed.
The spokesperson for the State Emergency Service also said that "literally within the first few seconds" after first responders arrived, they rescued 10 people who were outside or trapped in basements and unable to get out on their own. Overall, firefighters and police officers evacuated around 400 people that night.
The State Emergency Service also said that firefighters from other regions have been brought in to deal with the aftermath of the attack. It is currently unclear when the work will be completed, as it is being hampered by further Russian attacks.
Butsko said on Facebook that the care home was called Dobryi Dim (Good Home).
"Everyone who was in the building was killed. At least 31 bodies have been found. Three people from the local area were also killed. Two died in the building opposite the care home, and one person was in a car," she reported.
According to Butsko, local residents heard two strikes, the first at 20:30 on 28 August. The explosions continued throughout the night.
Background:
- Powerful explosions were heard in the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast on the evening of 28 August. A warehouse facility caught fire, and all traffic was blocked in both directions on the M-06 Kyiv-Chop road between kilometres 15 and 32.
- As of 29 August, local authorities reported that the death toll from the Russian attack and subsequent detonation in the Bucha district has risen to 37, while another 42 people were injured.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that ammunition cannot be stored near residential buildings. He also said the first strike in Myla village hit a defence forces warehouse that "should not have been there".
- Commenting on the deaths of dozens of people after the Russian strike on Myla, Ukraine's General Staff said Russia is the root cause of the tragedy.
- The Security Service of Ukraine has launched a criminal investigation into the Russian strike on warehouses in the Bucha district.

Doctors urge kids to get vaccinated ahead of school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

With school beginning this week and COVID-19 and influenza activity at high levels, doctors at the Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy said children are at higher risk of infection and should get vaccinated as soon as a new program begins.
COVID-19 is still in the epidemic period, with weekly cases at a high level, while weekly flu cases in the past few weeks were at the highest level for the period in a decade, Centers for Disease Control (CDC) data showed.
Infection risks might increase as students return to school, the CDC said.
Photo: Lin Huei-chin, Taipei Times
Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy chairman Lee Ping-ing (李秉穎) said that young children are at high risk of severe flu complications, and with the recent high levels of flu and COVID-19, and school starting, children face a risk of contracting both.
The flu is not a common cold, he said, adding that in addition to pneumonia, children might also develop severe complications, including encephalitis, encephalopathy and myocarditis.
A US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report on flu-associated pediatric deaths in the US in the 2024-2025 flu season showed that among the documented clinical complications before death in children, 38 percent had pneumonia, while 18 percent had encephalopathy or encephalitis, the association said.
Children have a substantially higher risk of infection from outside the household than adults, but they are also the largest source of secondary transmission, often passing the disease to family members in the same household, it said, citing a study from Japan.
Taiwan Immunization Vision and Strategy executive member Huang Yu-cheng (黃玉成) said young children are often exposed to cluster infection risks at daycare centers, preschools or after-school care facilities.
The condition of children with the flu can deteriorate rapidly, so caregivers should seek immediate medical attention if warning signs of severe illness arise, including rapid breathing, altered consciousness, abnormal tiredness or clearly reduced activity levels, Huang said.
Some children might be afraid to get a vaccine shot, especially young children, so Taiwan last year introduced a nasal spray flu vaccine, he said, adding that the product is available for children and adolescents aged two through 17 years old and paid out of pocket.
The nasal spray flu vaccine is sprayed directly into the nasal cavity, inducing the nasal mucosa to produce antibodies for an immune response, Huang said.
It only takes a few seconds to provide protection, so it is a needle-free alternative for those who are unwilling to get traditional flu shots and will hopefully increase overall vaccine coverage rates, he said.
Parents should get their children vaccinated as soon as possible after the government-funded COVID-19 and flu vaccination program begins in October, Lee said.

Warning systems can learn from Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

Massive flash floods and landslides struck along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, killing hundreds and leaving more than 1,000 people missing.
The disaster is noteworthy for Taiwan, as analysts said there was no significant rainfall before it occurred. Initial assessments suggested that a high-altitude rock and ice avalanche blocked a river, forming a barrier lake that suddenly burst.
People have traditionally associated floods with torrential rains, but in an era of increasingly frequent extreme weather and complex disasters, the next deadly flood might not be preceded by heavy rain at all. For Taiwan, which is similarly home to high mountains, steep slopes and short, fast-flowing rivers, this disaster should prompt the nation to re-evaluate its disaster prevention strategies.
Taiwan’s disaster prevention system has improved significantly, but early-warning mechanisms still rely heavily on weather conditions — authorities determine whether it would issue warnings based on factors such as the amount of rainfall and how high water levels have risen. The problem is that disasters causing significant casualties are increasingly likely to involve compound risks. An earthquake could destabilize a mountainside, that landslide could block a river and the resulting upstream waterway could burst without any additional rainfall.
When disasters lack a single, straightforward cause, the government’s meteorological, water resources, geological and forestry agencies might each monitor only one part of the picture, with no single office holding all the pieces of the puzzle.
The next phase of Taiwan’s disaster prevention policy should focus on building a multi-source risk early warning system. The government already has access to satellite imagery, river water levels, rainfall data, earthquake records and slope-displacement data. Artificial intelligence could be used to quickly cross-check this information for anomalies.
For example, if satellite imagery detects a large-scale landslide in a mountainous area while river monitors detect an unusual drop in water levels downstream, that could indicate an upstream blockage. The system could automatically raise the risk level and dispatch drones for confirmation, rather than waiting for rainfall to reach a predetermined threshold before responding. In disaster prevention, one of the most important pieces of lifesaving information is knowing that something is occurring 20 minutes before the disaster strikes.
Early warning systems must also translate into effective evacuation procedures. Once a fast-moving mudslide enters a river valley, it could be too late to escape by the time it becomes visible to the naked eye. The government should establish clearer evacuation protocols for high-risk areas — who issues the alert, where residents should evacuate, how they would be notified at night and who would assist those with impaired mobility should all be determined and rehearsed in advance. Otherwise, no matter how sophisticated the integrated monitoring capability is, if all they send is a message to cellphones, the technology alone cannot save lives.
The disaster in Nepal offers a clear warning: Disaster preparedness must shift from only preparing when we see rain to acting when risks are identified, thoroughly integrating meteorological, water resources, geological and satellite monitoring. The most worthwhile investment is not post-disaster infrastructure, but in that crucial 20 minute window.
Roger Lo is a freelancer.

Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Lin attended at the invitation of Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr and toured the exhibition with Whipps, Palauan officials, and representatives from the US, Japan and Australia, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.
The exhibition detailed cooperative projects involving Taiwan, its Pacific allies and the three countries in fields including low-carbon energy, social empowerment, smart agriculture, smart healthcare, digital resilience and infrastructure, the ministry added.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Visitors viewed a presentation on the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, a regional framework aimed at addressing shared challenges and promoting sustainable development.
Lin said Taiwan has long participated in the Pacific Islands Forum as a “development partner” and supported the objectives of the 2050 strategy.
Taiwan would continue sharing its development experience and working with like-minded countries to address energy and digital transitions, climate change and marine sustainability based on the needs of Pacific countries, he said.
The event featured a joint performance by Taiwan’s Naluwan Dance Troupe and the Belias Dancers from the Palauan state of Airai, as well as Taiwanese International Youth Ambassadors assisting with exhibition tours.
The exhibition was held as Palau prepares to host the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Koror from today to Friday next week.
Although Taiwan is not a forum member, it has participated as a development partner since 1993, and usually holds dialogues and other events alongside the annual summit.
Taiwan and other non-member countries were excluded from last year’s leaders’ meeting in the Solomon Islands, whose government said the forum was reviewing its partnership arrangements.
Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu are the only three forum members that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:47:08 UTC
01:47:08 KST

Two men bought tickets to enter the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna before smashing a display case, grabbing a 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace and walking away, police said on Friday.
Austrian media said the Van Cleef and Arpels necklace, with 673 precious stones, was worth several million dollars. It is the latest in a series of high-profile heists to hit European museums.
Police said the two men did not wear masks, paid to enter the museum and were clearly seen on surveillance cameras in Thursday’s heist.
Photo: AFP
They “smashed a glass display case” with a hammer before “fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction,” a police statement said.
The MAK museum confirmed the theft, but said it would not comment while the investigation went ahead.
The necklace had been part of an exhibition devoted to the French designers Van Cleef and Arpels. About 500 pieces had been on display since June. The exhibition is scheduled to end on Sept. 27. Despite the MAK announcing the exhibition would remain closed until further notice, the wing where the theft occurred reopened hours later. The smashed display case was covered with a blue panel, but no notice on it explained the theft.
The stolen necklace was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter, Faiza, to the future Iranian shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
On its Web site, Van Cleef and Arpels called the stolen piece a “triumph of white jewelry.”
The French company did not immediately comment on the theft.
European museums have been hit by a series of spectacular thefts since thieves in October last year broke into the Louvre museum in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewelry worth US$102 million.
Thieves on Thursday raided the Treasure of Villena — one of the greatest Bronze Age gold collections — at a museum in the Spanish city of Villena, taking most of the 50-plus mainly gold bracelets, bowls, bottles and other items on display.
Four works “of extraordinary value” by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, the Italian Ministry of Culture said on Sunday last week.
Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth over US$10.4 million which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:47:06 UTC

US President Donald Trump on Friday said his administration has reached a major oil deal with Venezuela that gives the US majority control of 65 billion barrels of proven petroleum reserves.
The deal — which Trump called “the biggest oil deal in world history” — would bring about US$100 billion in private investment to Venezuela, US and Venezuelan officials said.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves. Its government has operated under intense pressure and close scrutiny from the Trump administration since the US in January abducted then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
Photo: Reuters
Washington allowed then-Venezuelan vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, to stay on and serve as interim leader so long as she toes the US line.
Trump has made no secret of his desire to secure Venezuelan oil for the US, and in his post announcing the deal on his Truth Social platform, he said it would more than double US oil reserves.
Interim leader Rodriguez confirmed what she called a “historic agreement” that would “have a significant impact on the rebirth of our nation.”
Writing on social media, she hailed potential investment of “more than US$100 billion and more than US$209 billion in tax revenue for the state.”
Trump said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had reached the deal with Rodriguez “through a partnership with private business.”
“This Transaction will greatly strengthen the already growing relationship between Venezuela and the United States!” Trump wrote.
Jorge Pinon, a senior researcher at the Energy Institute at the University of Texas at Austin, said the agreement was unconventional and many questions remained about how the oil assets would be transferred, “not to a private enterprise, but to another country.”
“We don’t know how the transfer would take place,” he said. “Is it a sale? Is it a title transfer? Is it only transferred once the reserves are actually produced?”
The news site Axios had on Thursday reported that the two countries were in talks on a dozen productive oil fields with 90 billion barrels of proven reserves — about one-third of Venezuela’s total proven reserves of 300 billion barrels.

Tarik Skubal shed tears, walking onto a field that used to be his home stadium as the team that traded him away paid tribute to the two-time Cy Young Award winner with a video before the first pitch.
“Luckily enough, I was able to make it to the tunnel before more happened,” Skubal said after allowing one run over six innings to help the LA Dodgers beat the Detroit Tigers 2-1 on Friday night. “It’s tough. This is the place I’ve known my entire career since 2018. It’s special.”
Skubal was welcomed with cheers and a smattering of boos in his return to Detroit, pitching for the first time against the middling franchise that traded him to the two-time defending World Series champions.
Photo: AFP
When the visitors’ lineup and Skubal were shown on the videoboard and his name was announced before the first pitch, most of the crowd at Comerica Park clapped for him while some jeered.
The Tigers showed highlights from his seven-season career with the team and posted a message at the end: “Thank you, Tarik.”
Skubal turned his head to the right a few times to watch the video as he walked from the bullpen beyond the left-field wall and toward the Dodgers’ dugout with a white towel draped around his neck, which he used to wipe away sweat and tears.
He extended his right arm, holding his glove, toward his former teammates and used his left hand to pat his chest.
After the game, Skubal returned to the field to catch up with former teammates.
Skubal did not appear to react to, or acknowledge, the fans before or during the game and did not get a chance to do so as he exited the game because a pitching change was made after the sixth inning in a 1-all game. He struck out seven over six innings with 83 pitches, the fewest since he threw 74 in the season-opening game in March.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the plan was to limit Skubal’s pitches after he threw 106 and 109 in his past two starts.
In a crowd that had mixed emotions about Skubal’s return, a couple young fans had fitting outfits sporting white Tigers jerseys with 29 and Skubal on the back — and a blue Dodgers hat.
When Skubal jogged to the mound to pitch for the first time as a visitor to Detroit, booing fans were heard first followed by more cheers from fans in the stands.
His first pitch was delayed because he appeared to have trouble with his communication device.
After throwing a 96-mph fastball for a ball, Gleyber Torres hit Skubal’s second pitch to center for a double and the crowd roared in unison.
Skubal settled in, striking out Lee Hao-yu and All-Star Kevin McGonigle and getting All-Star Dillon Dingler to fly out.
“It’s weird to see him on the other side,” McGonigle said before the game.
Tigers manager AJ Hinch said the team’s familiarity with Skubal might not be helpful at the plate.
“If anybody knows him, it’s us,” Hinch said. “You can know everything about a pitcher, that doesn’t make it easy to hit.”
That was evident when Skubal retired 12 straight batters, including striking out the side in the third, before Eduardo Valencia led off the fifth with a double. Max Clark followed with a two-out triple in the inning to break a scoreless tie.
Skubal was drafted by Detroit out of Seattle University in the ninth round of the 2018 draft and spent his entire career with the Tigers until they traded him earlier this month.
Skubal said last month that it was his preference to finish the season with the Tigers and to compete for a World Series championship, which has eluded the franchise since 1984. Fitbit creators unveil wearable to help track aging parents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

The co-founders of Fitbit, nearly six years after agreeing to sell their company to Alphabet Inc’s Google, are launching a new type of wearable tracker: A screen-free device aimed at continuously monitoring family members, including aging parents.
The company, called Luffu, announced its first hardware product on Tuesday, prioritizing a jewelry-like design over the clunky appearance of traditional medical devices. The news comes as wearable giants such as Whoop, Oura, Garmin and Google embrace increasingly sophisticated screenless devices that focus on serving as sensor packs that pair with smartphone apps.
Luffu co-founder James Park said in an interview that the new device, called the Luffu Link, and an accompanying app that went into beta testing earlier this year are designed to help families coordinate care for family members.
Photo: AFP
“We’ve seen location tracking, family calendars, fitness devices, emergency pendants and smart home tools. But at the end of the day, someone still has to manually piece all of these features together,” Park said. “Many artificial intelligence [AI] agents focus on consumer tasks like booking travel or restaurants, but we wanted to build an integrated ecosystem for the family that directly supports safety and care coordination.”
The US$300 (US$250 for preorders beginning on Tuesday) Luffu Link wearable, launching in blue, black and gold color options early next year, supports location sharing, health sensing — such as activity, sleep and heart rate — the ability to get help from family members, and voice logging for medications, meals, mood, doctor visit updates and reminders. It offers up to five days of battery life and connects to cellular networks to allow for the sending of voice messages or health data to trusted contacts without a phone nearby.
The device syncs its data with the app, which uses AI to organize information, identify long-term patterns and surface insights for families. The system is designed to help caregivers understand in real time what has changed, what requires attention and what steps to take next, Park said. The app is to launch broadly in the US later in the year. It works with a US$19 per month subscription, which includes access for four family members.
Park and Luffu co-founder Eric Friedman, another member of the Fitbit founding team, sold their prior company for US$2.1 billion. Google used the deal to update its wearables and health device strategy, including by launching the popular Fitbit Air.
“The background for me is deeply personal,” Park said. “My parents live in Cleveland while I live in San Francisco, so I have to manage their care from afar. I would often learn about a condition only after a critical doctor visit, getting only part of the story, and I didn’t want to constantly call them for updates.”
Friedman faced a similar challenge while managing care for his children. “It’s not just us,” Park said. “There is a massive need. One in four American adults acts as a caregiver, whether for aging parents or children with chronic health needs.”
Luffu was built on many of the key principles from their Fitbit days, Park said. “Fitbit was always designed to be accessible, from the user interface to the app,” he said. “A lot of that design philosophy comes over, alongside fostering user trust. When Fitbit launched in 2007, we established clear privacy controls ensuring data was not shared with third-party providers without user content, and that commitment carries over to Luffu.”
The company plans to eventually expand into the home with a dedicated device designed to assist multiple families across separate households. It did not share timing or pricing details for that product.

Critters bugging CWA weather stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:58 UTC
01:46:58 KST

Squirrels, spiders and snakes are among the unexpected culprits disrupting Taiwan’s automated weather station network, Central Weather Administration (CWA) maintenance workers said at a seminar for intern meteorologists.
Observation division head Chen Yen-lin (陳燕玲) said that the CWA operates 1,337 weather stations to monitor weather conditions for public safety, agriculture and transportation infrastructure management.
The enormous amount of raw data generated by the stations must be sorted and analyzed by a mixture of algorithms and human experts, but plenty can go wrong before the information can be passed up the network, Chen said.
Photo courtesy of the Yushan Weather Station
In May, one of the sub-survey sites of a weather station in a mountainous area went dark and all data from it vanished during heavy rain, when the CWA most needed the information, she said.
Maintenance technicians dispatched to the site reported soon after arrival that they identified the problem: A squirrel sheltering from the rain in the junction box had chewed on the Internet cable, she said.
“Almost anything can happen out in the wild,” Chen said, adding that squirrels are not the only critters that can interfere with the CWA’s work.
A weather station near a branch facility of the Forestry Research Institute in Nantou County reported an abnormally small amount of rainfall amid a downpour in the region, prompting a call for a repair team, she said.
The engineers found that thick cobwebs had tied the tipper of the rain gauge in place, preventing rainwater from flowing into the bucket, she said.
Other animal-related service disruptions included a 265cm-long piece of shed snake skin interfering with a weather station near Bamboo Lake (竹子湖) on Yamingshan in Taipei’s Beitou District (北投), as well as a report of mole activities damaging equipment, she said.
“These anecdotes might be amusing, but each piece of compromised data that we do not catch would go on to compromise every calculation we make,” she said.
To help ensure that CWA predictions are based on accurate information, the agency needs dedicated personnel to monitor the data for abnormalities, Chen said.
“Working in the field not only requires an understanding of meteorology, but also skills to determine from the data whether equipment might have been affected,” she said, adding that “the integrity of CWA’s analyses depend upon it.”
