EDITORIAL: Airing dirty laundry in public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:58 UTC
01:46:58 KST

Former Hsinchu deputy mayor Andy Chiu (邱臣遠) is the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) nominee for the Jhubei City (竹北市) mayoral seat in November’s local elections. TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) nominated Chiu after reaching an agreement with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) that the latter could field Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩) for the position of Hsinchu County commissioner unchallenged by the TPP, while the KMT would not field a candidate for the Jhubei race.
That was until Hsu and her party colleague Hsinchu County councilor Wu Hsu-chih (吳旭智) pushed back, and Wu picked up a registration form for the Jhubei mayoral race on Thursday morning, the first day the forms were available.
When her party’s change of mind came to light, all KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) could do was say she was unable to resolve the issue, and thank Huang and Chiu for their understanding.
Chiu responded, saying: “I’m not sure exactly what there is to understand.”
On Hsu’s call for all those concerned to “look at the bigger picture,” he said: “I’m not sure whose ‘bigger picture’ we’re supposed to be looking at.”
That tells you all you need to know about the power dynamics within the blue-white alliance of the KMT and the TPP; about how the former views the relationship and how that has become painfully apparent to the latter.
Reports said KMT figures feel that Chiu is a weak candidate in a strategically important seat that it needs to keep out of the hands of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). Jhubei is a county-administered city within Hsinchu County. Popular Jhubei Mayor Cheng Chao-fang (鄭朝方) of the DPP is vacating the position to stand for Hsinchu County commissioner, which leaves the Jhubei mayoralty up for grabs and the position of Hsinchu County commissioner in contention. The KMT knows that it is important to win both, and is apparently willing to renege on promises to make that happen.
This is what Hsu means by the “bigger picture.” Chiu was accurate in his assessment of who the main beneficiary is. The DPP looks to benefit, too, from the potential fallout of the emerging divisions.
In a news conference in Taipei on Friday morning, Huang criticized the KMT for reneging on its promise and said that he would continue to throw the TPP’s resources behind Chiu’s candidacy.
He added that he no longer had faith that rewards promised to the TPP in return for staying out of the Hsinchu County race — namely seats on the council — would be forthcoming, suggesting that, like Chiu, he was not sure what it was he was supposed to “understand.”
After the KMT cleared its path to the Hsinchu County election unchallenged by the TPP, it suggested changing the mechanism for selecting nominees to a popular vote, Huang said, adding that he rejected the move.
The disagreement over using the polling method to select nominees brings to mind talks for a KMT-TPP joint ticket during the 2024 presidential election, which would have put forward the KMT’s candidate, New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), and then-TPP chairman Ko Wen-je (柯文哲). Those talks fell apart over differences in the methods each side insisted upon and their inability to compromise, in full view of prospective voters.
As then, so it is now: a failure to compromise and the parties’ inability to refrain from airing their dirty laundry in public. It is a messy situation, unseemly and politically myopic.
That Cheng, in her capacity as KMT chair, says that she cannot resolve the issue is astounding: It makes her look impotent or disingenuous and insincere. Chiu looks wounded and frustrated. Huang is projecting an image of occupying the moral high ground, but in this scenario, Cheng is not his adversary, and in fact, the party she leads is the only reason either he or the post-Ko TPP that he chairs has any political relevance in today’s politics.
We are witnessing the emergence of cracks in the blue-white alliance, which have been apparent several times before, as structural fatigue causes the ediface to give way under stress from a domineering partner increasingly dismissive of a junior appendage that is losing its way.
If the two parties do not find a way to resolve their differences privately, the damage would go beyond November’s local elections and impact their chances in 2028.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Nepal and China flood missing toll nears 3,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:56 UTC
01:46:56 KST

Rescuers in Nepal and China were battling yesterday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages.
Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
Rescue worker Kawan Koirala, from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they were struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud.
Photo: AFP
“People want their family member’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them... You can see the mud,” he said, exhausted after an 18-hour shift. “It is very traumatic for me too. It is my first time seeing these types of things. Everywhere is mud. We faced flood in Nepal before, but not like this.”
The US Geological Survey said the disaster on Wednesday on the Tibet-Nepal border was caused by a glacial collapse that created a torrent of debris downstream.
While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of such disasters.
Survivors face an agonizing wait to learn the fate of missing relatives, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol said in Nuwakot, Nepal. “There is nothing left.”
At Bidur’s army base, a key rescue hub in the same district, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall.
“I have come here looking for my son,” Kalka Sharda said, scanning the list in desperation. “He was a laborer at the hydropower plant, but I can’t find his name, and the authorities are not saying anything.”
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, along with 517 foreigners, including trekkers and Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous,” and as many as 93,000 people might have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Nepal’s reconstruction bill after devastating floods could run into “billions of dollars,” Nepalese Minister of Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal said on Saturday.
“The urgency is on rescue and saving lives as much as we can,” he added, appealing for specialized assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.
He also called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them, saying bodies which have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.
“Our own healthcare capacity is very limited to put these bodies in a frozen state for a long time,” he said.
Emergency teams worked flat-out to find survivors as widespread devastation left communities short of food and water.
Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods.
In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing had paused its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding.
On the Nepali side, soldiers were yesterday trying desperately to drill through to 100 people trapped in tunnels, including at the Trishuli 3A and 3B hydropower projects.
The Nepalese prime minister’s office said teams had begun “clearing mud and debris” to open the entrance, while a specialized Indian tunnel rescue unit had arrived to help.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Nepal yesterday reported a death toll of 626 people.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in the country.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, the state Xinhua news agency said yesterday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, officials said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.

The coast guard warned of an increasingly severe situation, as analysts say the increased activity is part of China’s bid to map the region for submarine warfare. The number of Chinese ships detected around Taiwan proper soared to a record 244 last month — an average of nearly eight every day, official data showed. FDA orders recall of heart drug tablets over impurities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has ordered the recall of 586,000 tablets of a heart medication because of impurities that could potentially affect its efficacy.
The recall of Biocor Film-Coated Tablets 5 mg, supplied by Anxo Pharmaceutical Co and bearing batch number BCLA91, was announced by the FDA on Wednesday.
FDA official Liu Chia-ping (劉佳萍) said yesterday the recall was ordered after the agency was notified by the supplier that impurity levels had reached the upper limit of specifications during recent stability testing, potentially affecting the drug’s quality and efficacy.
Photo: CNA
Liu said the company was ordered to complete the recall by Aug. 31 and submit a recall report, along with corrective and preventive measures to avoid similar problems in the future.
The drug contains bisoprolol fumarate and is approved for the treatment of hypertension, angina and stable, moderate-to-severe chronic heart failure.
According to data from the National Health Insurance Administration, 750,151 tablets were dispensed through the National Health Insurance program in 2025.
Pharmaceutical companies that fail to conduct recalls as required by law can face fines ranging from NT$200,000 (US$6,317) to NT$5 million under the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act (藥事法).
Liu said more than 10 other drugs with the same active ingredient, dosage form and strength are licensed in Taiwan, meaning there is no concern about a shortage.
People with concerns about their medication should consult their doctors as soon as possible about switching to an appropriate alternative, she added.

Cabinet to support drone bill: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:54 UTC
01:46:54 KST

The premier is to countersign a Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-led bill on defense self-reliance and the uncrewed vehicle industry, and include funding for it in this year’s supplemental budget, sources said yesterday.
The Legislative Yuan on Thursday passed the Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例), providing for NT$240 billion (US$7.59 billion) over six years in principle, while allowing additional funding subject to legislative approval.
The act directs the Ministry of National Defense to prioritize the procurement of domestically produced “low-cost, high-performance” uncrewed systems. It requires the central government to, in principle, earmark NT$40 billion annually for six consecutive years, using its general budget to procure uncrewed vehicles, to reinforce national defense and drive industrial growth.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The Cabinet’s proposal, which requested NT$210 billion in a special budget over six years, failed to win approval. The bill, backed by the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus, was rejected by the KMT and the smaller opposition Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), which together hold a legislative majority.
The legislature only passed this year’s central government budget on Aug. 14.
The Cabinet had originally planned to approve the supplemental budget on Thursday, but decided to delay the move by a week, because the legislature was scheduled to vote on the uncrewed vehicle bill that day, sources said.
The Cabinet also planned to adjust the supplemental budget depending on the outcome of the vote, they said.
The Executive Yuan wants to accelerate defense buildup and is preparing to co-sign the uncrewed vehicle bill, they said, adding that therefore, following the passage of the opposition-led version on Thursday, it refrained from harsh criticism and instead expressed deep regret and said it would “expedite the allocation of the necessary funding.”
The ministry has confirmed that all items cut from the Cabinet’s NT$1.25 trillion defense special bill would be included in this year’s supplemental budget, which means funding for uncrewed vehicles would also be included, the source said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) is expected to make the final decision on the amount of the supplemental budget after receiving a report from the ministry this week, sources said.
The Cabinet initially planned to fund uncrewed vehicles through a special budget, so no funding for the program was included in next year’s central government budget. As the budget proposal must be submitted to the legislature tomorrow, there is not enough time to revise it beforehand, sources said.
Waiting until next year’s budget is passed before seeking additional funding could be too slow, they said.
The Executive Yuan is expected to submit amendments to the budget at an appropriate time, so it can be reviewed alongside the main budget proposal by the legislature, they said.

To survivors of the Srebrenica massacre, the death of former Bosnian Serb military leader and war criminal Ratko Mladic changes little about his legacy.
Mejra Djogaz, whose three sons, husband and grandson were killed by forces led by Mladic, lives at the edge of the memorial center in Potocari, Bosnia and Herzegovina, where thousands of marble gravestones mark the victims of the 1995 massacre.
“It’s because of him that I was left alone, and I’m not the only one who was left alone: All the mothers in Srebrenica, and many others across Bosnia and Herzegovina, suffered the same fate,” the 77-year-old said.
Photo: Reuters
Mladic died on Thursday while serving a life sentence in The Hague for war crimes committed during the 1990s Bosnian war; his conviction led international media to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia.”
Decades on from the conflict, Djogaz said she remains too afraid to return home to her village on the outskirts of the town, which has been left almost emptied by the wartime killings.
Instead, she stays with friends within walking distance of the memorial site, where she can visit the graves of her family.
“I would have liked him to live even longer, so that he could suffer more, as we mothers suffer,” she said of Mladic.
Mladic experienced several strokes in the past few months before his death in hospital, as he served a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the Bosnian War.
He became infamous for his role in the Srebrenica massacre, where more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed and their bodies dumped in mass graves, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
Sehida Abdurahmanovic, a member of the main association of mothers in Srebrenica, said knowing he died suffering was some solace to victims’ families, but his conviction was more enduring.
“For us, the main thing is that he was convicted and that he was serving his sentence,” said Abdurahmanovic, whose brother went missing during the massacre and has never been found. “With this sentence, his life was already over.”
Fadila Efendic, whose son and her husband were killed in July 1995, said Mladic’s death brought “neither a joy nor a particular sadness.”
“What is particularly difficult for me to accept is that his ideas are not dead,” the 74-year-old said. “If they had disappeared, then I could be happy about it. Unfortunately, they continue to exist. This ideology is not dead.”
In parts of Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb statelet, Republika Srpska, Mladic is still lauded as a hero, and his death was greeted with vigils and memorials overnight.
In Zvornik, on the border with Serbia, hundreds marched through the streets chanting his name, waving Serbian and Republika Srpska army flags and carrying banners bearing his portrait.
In Visegrad, where thousands of Bosnian Muslims, or Bosniaks, were brutally killed in 1992, a group of young people unfurled a banner honoring Mladic from a bridge and lit flares.
In Serbia’s capital of Belgrade, footage aired by a pro-government private television channel, Informer, which had rolling coverage in tribute to Mladic, showed dozens of men holding flares on the city’s main bridge.
Serbian officials have remained largely restrained in their reactions, with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic telling media on Friday that it was “not the day for song or for a celebration” after supporters greeted him with chants at an unrelated event in a western Serbian town.
“We tried and did everything we could to ensure that General Mladic would spend the end of his life in Serbia,” Vucic said.
The court rejected requests for Mladic’s release on health grounds, a move the populist leader labeled “unprecedented and unjustifiable behaviour.”
Serbian Minister of Justice Nenad Vujic said Mladic “will receive all the military and state honors to which he is entitled,” but Vucic did not confirm whether plans were under way for a state funeral.
“Should the family wish for him to be buried on the territory of Serbia, we will help ensure that this is done in a dignified and proper manner,” he said.
Serbian officials were awaiting details on when authorities in The Hague would release the body, he added.
Regardless of reactions from his supporters, Abdurahmanovic said attempts to revise his legacy were in vain.
“History will undoubtedly remember him as one of its great negatives, a war criminal,” she said.

The world’s mountains are ticking time bombs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:52 UTC
01:46:52 KST

From the Apostle Paul to Ira Gershwin, mountains have for millennia been a symbol of immovable stability. A warming planet is undermining that, leaving landslides, floods and avalanches in its wake.
The apocalyptic scenes after Wednesday’s flash floods on the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region are the latest example of the devastation that can result. At least 157 people have been confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a wall of mud and rock swept through valleys in the Himalayas, causing the Trishuli River to rise 9m in half an hour.
Preliminary investigations suggest that a slide of ice and rock unleashed a surge of water, debris and boulders downstream. Researchers must work fast: The initial disaster might have left behind a fresh dam of material, which could prompt further flash flooding if it crumbles.
Illustration: Constance Chou
You might be tempted to dismiss the significance of climate change in all this. Individual heatwaves, cold snaps and extreme rainfall events can be linked to global warming with high confidence these days using weather-attribution science. The same influence can be traced in droughts and wildfires, although with less certainty.
However, landslides and their associated floods can result from such complex chains of failure in once-stable ground that the signal of global warming gets lost amid the noise.
That might be the case for individual events, but the broad backdrop is exceptionally clear, because the crucial component that holds together many high-altitude landscapes is not granite, schist or limestone: It is ice.
Nearly one-quarter of the land area of our planet lies beneath ice sheets or within permafrost regions — places at high latitudes or altitudes where the earth remains frozen from one year to the next and ice acts as a kind of glue binding soil and rock together. As temperatures rise that frozen structure weakens, threatening a sudden collapse like snow sliding off a ski chalet roof in spring.
This is now happening to mountain terrain on four continents. When permanent ice disappears, steep slopes can give way under their own weight. Repeated cycles of freezing and thawing make the process more destructive. Water penetrates deep into cracks before crystallizing, gradually wedging the rock apart and driving deeper with each seasonal cycle.
Glaciers themselves can act as buttresses, propping cliffs upright. As the atmosphere warms, they retreat up the valley, stripping away supports that have stabilized the landscape for millennia. When water falls as rain rather than snow, it is more likely to erode the surface and carve deep channels, further undermining the soil.
The evidence of accelerating instability is mounting. In records dating back to 1950, eight of the 10 worst years for glacier ice losses have occurred since 2016. Above 3,000m in the eastern Himalayas, landslides are now displacing five times more material than they were in the 1980s. The frequency of glacial lake outburst floods, a particularly damaging disaster where the dam impounding melted water from a glacier gives way suddenly, grew almost three-fold between the 1990s and the 2010s.
Despite the horrifying footage, this week’s tragedy might not even be the worst instance. More than 6,000 people were killed around the Indian pilgrimage town of Kedarnath in 2013, when torrential monsoon rain, snowmelt and an overflowing glacial lake combined to produce catastrophic floods. Another 200 were marked dead or missing in 2021 when water and rock swept through two hydropower plant construction sites in Chamoli, southeast of the town.
Summer in the Himalayas is rapidly becoming a time when such events are a recurrent feature rather than a freak occurrence.
The damage is not confined to Asia, either. Glacial outburst floods have become an annual threat to Alaska’s capital, Juneau, with the last surging through just weeks ago. At the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Zermatt, a new US$630 million hydropower dam has been designed in part to shield the town as the Gorner glacier melts.
Worldwide, about 15 million people live in regions at risk of glacial lake floods.
There is no sign that the world is working to curb our emissions with anything like the urgency required to avert this calamity. In Europe, where summer heatwaves have caused more than 30,000 excess deaths, politicians are now treating climate as a toxic issue, while companies abandon net zero targets. India, home to the largest population at risk from mountain flooding, is likely to add more emissions to the atmosphere than any other country over the coming decade. The US is dismantling policies intended to shrink its own carbon footprint.
Unlike the disintegration of highland slopes, these political acts are choices, not forces of nature. Mountains might be moving beneath our feet. That is no excuse for those in power to stand still.
David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy. Previously, he worked for Bloomberg News, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. An Ecuadoran court on Friday sentenced former Ecuadoran president Lenin Moreno to five years in prison for accepting bribes from a Chinese company that built the country’s biggest hydroelectric dam.
The prosecution said on social media that Moreno, who governed from 2017 to 2021, was among 20 people convicted in the case involving the construction of the Coca Codo Sinclair dam by China’s Sinohydro.
Moreno was vice-president under socialist former Ecuadoran president Rafael Correa at the time of the alleged corruption, between 2007 and 2013.
Photo: AFP
He succeeded Correa, with the latter’s backing, but later fell out with his mentor by shifting to the right and aligning himself more closely with the US.
Moreno has already announced plans to appeal the court’s ruling, which also saw his wife and other relatives sentenced to about three years in prison for complicity.
Prosecutors had sought a six-and-a-half-year prison term for Moreno.
The 73-year-old paraplegic, who served as the UN special envoy on disability issues, insisted on Friday after the ruling that he had never received “a single cent” from Sinohydro.
He blamed the case on “the Correa regime,” saying his former backer-turned-rival, who has also been convicted of corruption but lives in Belgium, “promised to take revenge on me.”
Prosecutors said Sinohydro paid bribes totaling US$76 million, about 4 percent of the cost of the hydroelectric project.

Cabinet outlines demography strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:52 UTC
01:46:52 KST

The Cabinet has launched a new national strategy to address Taiwan’s demographic challenges, with plans to implement measures covering family support, elderly people, talent development across all age groups and global talent recruitment to improve the country’s resilience in responding to demographic changes, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said on Friday.
The National Development Council earlier in the day released its population projection that showed Taiwan’s population could nearly halve by 2075, while births are projected to drop below 100,000 this year.
On May 27, President William Lai (賴清德) instructed the Executive Yuan to launch the family support chapter of the New Response Strategy for Taiwan’s Population Challenges, elevating population and family policies to the level of national strategy, Lee said.
In the face of demographic shifts such as declining birthrates and an aging population, the government’s responsibility goes beyond increasing birth subsidies to reducing the costs and risks families face in raising children, including childcare, education, employment and housing, she said.
The family support chapter focuses on increasing subsidies, reducing burdens, increasing flexibility and expanding public care, proposing 18 measures to establish a public childcare system under which costs would be shared by the government, families and society, she said.
The proposed 0-to-18 Child Development Subsidy would provide financial support for children as they grow up, Lee said, adding that the NT$5,000 monthly subsidy has been included in the budget for fiscal 2027, she said.
Eligible children and adolescents would begin receiving the subsidy next year, she added.
The policy would allow children to accumulate at least NT$1.08 million (US$34,147) from birth until their 18th birthday, Lee said. In addition, there are development accounts for disadvantaged children and adolescents.
The government is also working to balance work and family needs by amending laws to allow both parents to take an additional three months of subsidized parental leave on top of the six months already legislated, she said.
The government also plans to extend marriage leave to 14 days, increase maternity leave to 12 weeks from eight weeks and double the leave for a husband to accompany his wife to prenatal examinations to 14 days, she said.
Lee added that the Executive Yuan would introduce other policies in theme-based chapters, including an “elderly generation” chapter, an “all-age talent development” chapter and a “global talent attraction” chapter, to increase Taiwan’s resilience to demographic change.

Deep-ocean carbon trails tracked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:52 UTC
01:46:52 KST

“Blue carbon” produced by coastal ecosystems might “ride” ocean currents for more than 1,000km to fuel deep-ocean carbon sinks, National Sun Yat-sen University researchers said on Thursday.
The university’s Carbon Research Lab, led by Hung Chin-chang (洪慶章), a professor of oceanography, conducted oceanographic observations in the low-latitude warm pool of the northwestern Pacific, an area often called an “ocean desert” due to low biological productivity and a lack of nutrients.
Researchers detected biosignals of algae, mangroves and seaweed at depths of 500m to 1,000m in the area, Hung said.
Photo courtesy of National Sun Yat-sen University
The results showed that organic matter produced in coastal systems can be carried by ocean circulation systems into the deep sea far from land, the university said in a statement.
The research is primarily funded by the “sailing to the blue sea” project of the the National Science and Technology Council, it said.
The research team on the research vessel Legend in 2023 visited five oceanographic stations in the northwestern Pacific, where they conducted observations, it said.
Drifting sediment traps were deployed in waters at depths of 150m, 500m and 1,000m around the stations to collect sinking organic particles, the statement said.
Stable carbon isotopes from the samples were used to distinguish between land-derived and ocean-derived sources, while environmental DNA (eDNA) was used to identify the organisms from which the carbon originated, it said.
The results showed that eDNA signals of large algae, mangroves and seaweed were detected at depths of 500m and 1,000m, it said.
The five oceanographic stations spanned four degrees of latitude, with some of them about 900km from the Philippines and more than 1,200km from Indonesia, the university said.
However, eDNA and isotope evidence is insufficient to determine whether the blue carbon originated from Palau, the Philippines or Indonesia, it said.
Mangroves, seaweed beds and algae are important coastal blue carbon ecosystems that can absorb carbon dioxide and store it in their biomass and surrounding environment, the university said.
While previous studies mostly focused on marine biological carbon’s downward flux from the ocean surface, the university’s research showed that carbon can travel via currents to the open ocean — a carbon transport pathway that has not received much research attention, it said.
The research is significant, as it provides evidence showing that carbon sequestrated by coastal systems can reach the deep ocean, it said.
Surface currents, submarine currents and mesoscale eddies all contribute to the transportation processes, it added.
The research showed that carbon in the ocean can float a long way out to sea before sinking, the university said.
The particulate organic carbon flux measured at 1,000m were 2.7 to 4.2 times higher than the values predicted with the Martin Curve carbon attenuation model, it said.
That shows that the conventional vertical sinking model might not fully explain the carbon flux mechanism in the deep ocean, the university added.

Hsinchu prosecutors clear former officials in four-year stadium probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:50 UTC
01:46:50 KST

The Hsinchu District Prosecutors’ Office on Friday closed its four-year criminal investigation into former Hsinchu mayor Lin Chih-chien’s (林智堅) municipal baseball stadium project, saying there was insufficient evidence to bring charges.
In a news release, the office said no charges would be filed against any former city officials. Four people employed by the construction company and the construction inspection service involved in the project, however, were granted deferred prosecution.
Ju Jia Construction Engineering Co was contracted to build the Hsinchu Baseball Stadium between 2019 and 2022.
Photo: Hung Mei-hsiu, Taipei Times
The stadium hosted only two games, both of which resulted in player injuries that critics attributed to substandard construction.
Prosecutors examined communications records, financial transactions and account books, and conducted multiple searches related to the stadium project, the office said.
They found no evidence that Lin or other city officials had accepted bribes, violated government procurement laws or otherwise obtained illegal benefits from the project, it said.
Investigators also found no evidence supporting allegations by the Kao administration that the contractor had buried construction waste beneath the stadium’s foundation or sold soil excavated from the site for profit, the office said.
Although small quantities of materials and foreign objects not authorized under the contract were found at the site, they accounted for less than 0.75 percent of the foundation’s volume, it said.
Surveillance camera footage also showed no evidence that contractors had dumped waste at the construction site, the office said.
The investigation also examined numerous modifications to the stadium’s construction contract under the Lin administration that increased the project’s budget from an initial NT$350 million to NT$1.15 billion.
However, each modification had a verifiable legitimate purpose, and none of the individual increases exceeded the 50 percent threshold stipulated by the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法), the office said.
Prosecutors reached deferred-prosecution agreements with four people who were believed to have falsified progress reports related to the construction project without the knowledge of city officials, it said.
Prosecutors assigned to the case did not consider the alleged mismanagement of the project serious enough to constitute a crime and referred the matter to the Control Yuan for further review, the office said.
In response, a Hsinchu City Government spokesperson said yesterday the city government respects the prosecutors’ authority and judicial procedures, but added that some factual findings and legal assessments still require clarification.
The city government will seek a review of the decision in accordance with the law and pursue the relevant contractors’ civil and contractual liabilities, the spokesperson added.

China goes rural in quest to power AI data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:46 UTC
01:46:46 KST

In China’s hilly Guizhou Province, a cluster of European-style buildings complete with clock tower and multi-arched bridge emits a low, permanent hum — a clue to its unexpected identity as tech giant Huawei’s largest data center.
The town-like complex is unique in design, but not in its placement. Dozens of data centers have been constructed in the southwestern province in the past few years.
They are part of a government strategy that has seen much of the digital infrastructure for breakneck artificial intelligence (AI) development across China’s eastern seaboard established in the country’s less populated, rural west.
Photo: Bloomberg
The build-out is ongoing. China is on course to nearly double its data center capacity within the next five years, as a tech race with the US intensifies and countries everywhere try to swerve a computing crunch that could stymie AI expansion.
The projects have transformed some places — such as Guian New Area, where the Huawei data center and others are located.
“It used to be a barren mountain, but since the area has developed, transportation has become more convenient, trade has picked up, business opportunities have emerged,” local shopkeeper Shu Peihua said.
When AFP visited last month, street vendors were catering to data center workers on their lunch break near a roadside banner calling for “promoting high-quality development,” a government tech policy catchphrase.
In Europe and the US, data center construction has often been met with resistance from local communities citing concerns around energy prices, as well as environmental issues such as water usage and noise.
However, dissent in China is tightly controlled, especially around central government policy.
Still, Guian residents who spoke to AFP were positive about the changes to their area.
A vendor selling savory pancakes, who did not give his name, said two universities had been established since the facilities were built.
Another local, Li Xixiu, said that the main road had been developed because of the centers, which in general had “really boosted the economy of this entire area.”
“All the villagers in our neighborhood now find jobs nearby, unlike before, when they had to go to other places,” Li said.
In 2021, the government gave its strategy a name: Eastern Data Western Computing.
The logic of construction in Guizhou, with its cooler climate, abundant renewable energy and empty space, is multifaceted. AI processing is extremely energy intensive, and China has demanded that data centers draw 80 percent of their power from renewable sources by the end of this decade.
That makes regions such as Guizhou and Inner Mongolia, which have massively expanded renewable capacity such as solar and wind, ideal for operators looking to meet those commitments, Rystad Energy senior analyst Simeng Deng said.
Energy-guzzling server farms could also help solve renewables’ issue of curtailment, or the over-production of energy.
The data centers “can be an engine to digest or absorb the surplus of renewable power generation,” Deng said.
Developing previously neglected parts of the countryside is another potential benefit.
Despite the enthusiasm of the locals, some researchers question the overall economic gains to host regions.
Data centers do not necessarily create a “huge spillover effect” on local jobs, said Andrew Stokols from Singapore Management University.
“The hope is that you can use data centers as an engine for broader digital development... bringing in industries that will come in around data centers,” he said.
However, in China and elsewhere, “immediate benefits have been elusive.”
Guizhou has averaged an annual GDP growth rate of 7.4 percent over the past decade, but its wage growth over the same period was second to last nationwide, the Taiwan-based Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology (DSET) said.
“This contrast suggests that while data centers drive heavy investment in land and equipment, their impact on boosting local per capita income remains limited,” DSET researchers Cartus Bo-Xiang You and Angela Glowacki said.
Massive investment in infrastructure, coupled with policy incentives to attract data center builders, have earned Guizhou one of the highest debt burdens in the country.
In 2024, Guizhou ranked 30th among Chinese provinces for its debt-to-revenue ratio, a DSET report showed, and 27th for its debt-to-GDP ratio.
However, the demand for data processing capacity as countries scramble for technological supremacy means the building would continue.
Even before ChatGPT heralded the beginning of the AI boom, Chinese policy documents were “talking about the idea that computing power is correlated with national power,” Stokols said.
“It’s essential for national competitiveness in the age of digital technology... the AI competition has accelerated that,” he added.

The Panama Canal’s real challenge is water, not geopolitics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

Almost two years after US President Donald Trump first threatened to take over the Panama Canal, the storied watershed is thriving.
The upheaval in global trade, driven by the Strait of Hormuz crisis and US tariff uncertainty, has boosted demand for the interoceanic shipping route, pushing the canal’s revenue and profits to records. Traffic rose more than 6 percent to 10,623 ship crossings in the 10 months through last month, underscoring its amplified importance to global commerce. Shippers have been willing to pay millions of dollars at auctions this month to secure one of the scarce slots allowing unscheduled vessels to pass through the congested waterway.
Trump also seems to have forgotten about Panama these days, much to the relief of locals. In fact, the greatest challenge looming over the canal has little to do with White House’s obsessions, the US-China rivalry or the security of its strategic infrastructure.
It is water.
In the coming decades, climate change and shifting rainfall patterns will have a growing impact on the canal’s traditional business, but they also present an opportunity for the iconic waterway to reinvent itself from a route for ships to a hub where everything from cargo to energy can move from west to east and vice versa through different links, taking advantage of Panama’s privileged location and narrow geography.
Ricaurte Vasquez Morales, the charming technocrat whose seven-year mandate as the canal’s administrator ends next month, sees the challenge as shifting the focus from ships to cargo.
“You need to diversify how you’re going to move the cargo,” Vasquez Morales told me this week during an interview at the historic Panama Canal Administration Building. “The country must evolve in that direction, anchored in the fact that it has the canal. It must be a crossing point for all kinds of things.”
It is an ambitious, complex strategy with a potentially huge payoff.
The return of the El Nino is threatening to bring severe drought to Central America, so much so that the Canal Authority, the autonomous operator of the waterway known as ACP, has announced restrictions on daily transit slots beginning next month. The goal is to conserve as much water as possible as the dry season approaches, typically starting in December.
Panamanians have fresh memories of the severe drought of 2023-2024, which forced the canal to slash daily traffic, slowing global trade and hurting the country’s economy. That was not a one-off. If there is one place where the impact of climate variations can be tracked in real time, it is Panama.
Vasquez Morales, 73, says the past 25 years have exposed “a clear trend” toward lower rainfall combined with greater volatility in rain cycles, making water availability an existential risk to the canal’s future.
“Unlike other canals in the world, this canal is constrained by these rainwater issues,” he told me. “Water remains the critical factor.”
While Panama enjoys abundant hydrologic resources, the combination of human consumption and cargo transit, together with new rainfall patterns, is taking a toll. Each ship crossing the 80.5km canal uses almost 200 million liters of fresh water drawn from the country’s artificial reservoirs. The water lifts and lowers vessels through a system of locks before flowing out to the ocean.
However, the same lakes must also meet the local population’s drinking-water needs — and Panamanians are thirsty. By some measures, Panama has among the highest per-capita water consumption in Latin America.That creates a growing tension between the needs of human consumption, and those of the canal and other businesses, one that will ultimately be addressed through infrastructure investments, not geopolitics.
ACP, and Panama more broadly, will need to accelerate investments in reservoirs and water-treatment plants while introducing conservation measures to prepare for a future with less water.
The canal’s long-term response is the US$1.5 billion Rio Indio reservoir project, which it bills as the “most viable option” to guarantee water for more than 50 percent of Panama’s population and economic activity, including canal operations, for the next 50 years. Once completed, potentially around 2031 or 2032, the reservoir will significantly increase the canal’s water-storage capacity, providing insurance against droughts. Still, project managers will need to proceed with extreme caution: The social cost of relocating about 500 families could be high. It would be the first major project the canal undertakes outside its property and its reputation with Panamanians is on the line.
In any case, Rio Indio will be a key tool for water management, but it will not make it rain more over Panama. That helps explain why Vasquez Morales has pushed other diversification efforts, including an energy corridor with a pipeline that would allow fuels and petroleum liquids to move faster from coast to coast, freeing up vessel capacity.
The ACP is also moving ahead with plans for two new container-transshipment terminals, Corozal on the Pacific and Telfers on the Atlantic, while working to extend a land corridor for containers to cross the isthmus.
The projects undergird a broader transformation plan that could make the canal less dependent on ships and on rainfall.
Vasquez Morales says they could lift ACP revenue to about US$10 billion by 2032 or 2033, from almost US$6 billion last year.
The canal is an extraordinarily profitable and client-focused business, with a profit margin of about 65 percent, but Vasquez Morales, a former minister of economy and finance, and an economist by training, has an important caveat: That figure does not account for the value of the water it consumes.
Including that implicit cost, he estimates that the margin would fall to 38 to 40 percent.
That profitability translates into larger annual transfers to the Panamanian state, as required by law. Since the expansion to include a third set of locks in 2016, the canal’s annual contributions to the Panamanian National Treasury have tripled and its target is to deliver a record US$3.2 billion in fiscal 2026. That track record offers reason to believe the diversification strategy, years in the making, could continue underpinning the country’s economy in the long run or, as the administrator puts it, to leverage Panama’s geographical position “so that it captures its true value.”
In his final days as administrator, Vasquez Morales goes further, arguing that the canal should also control the disputed Balboa and Cristobal port terminals, which sit at the two entrances to the waterway. The terminals are at the center of a bitter legal fight after Panama’s Supreme Court in January invalidated their operation contracts of Panama Ports Co, a subsidiary of CK Hutchison Holdings Ltd. The Hong Kong-based company is now seeking more than US$1.5 billion from Panama in international arbitration.
In Vasquez Morales’ view, the terminals have historically been part of the canal’s property, and the government should sell its interest in them to the ACP, which could then select their operators.
“Cristobal and Balboa and everything in the waters of the canal must be managed by the canal,” he said. “It’s important because whoever has some degree of control over the terminals can affect the volume of traffic through the canal.”
The hectic pace of running the canal over the span of the COVID-19 pandemic, droughts and trade wars has taught Vasquez Morales a few lessons: the importance of putting a value on water and listening carefully to clients’ needs, and of training and guiding the canal’s staff.
He also emphasizes the need for consistency and transparency in dealing with stakeholders.
Resurgent great-power pressures have highlighted the value of the canal’s neutrality treaty, which requires the waterway to remain open to vessels of all nations without discrimination in times of peace and war. “Neutrality is the main guarantee this country has and one must know how to handle it, how to understand it,” he said. “There will always be pressures, but consistency in handling neutrality is critical.”
For all the grandstanding, threats and geopolitical fascination that the canal generates, that might be the bigger lesson of Vasquez Morales’ tenure. Panama’s strategic advantage depends precisely on treating everyone fairly. In that respect, it cannot control climate any more than geopolitics.
However, it can control how it responds to both.
J.P. Spinetto is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Latin American business, economic affairs and politics. FEATURE:Penghu troops prepare for strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:44 UTC
01:46:44 KST

In the pre-dawn darkness on an island in the Taiwan Strait, Taiwanese troops earlier this month pulled long, gleaming 105mm shells from their green plastic canisters. After all the ammunition had been checked and safely loaded through hatches on four tanks, troops waited silently for the order to fire.
The soldiers are among the thousands of troops who form a garrison in Penghu County and they were training for war with China.
A popular tourist destination known for its pristine beaches and coral reefs, the strategically crucial cluster of 90 islands and islets about 50km off the southwest coast of Taiwan proper would be hit in the first wave of an attempted Chinese invasion, senior Taiwanese security officials and military experts said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
For Taiwan, holding Penghu would allow its forces to resist a Chinese invasion fleet heading toward Taiwan proper, they said.
If Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Navy ships tried to attack Taiwan while bypassing Penghu, they “could be struck by missiles from Penghu,” Institute for National Defense and Security Research research fellow Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) said.
“That forces the PLA to attack Penghu before it can attack Taiwan,” he said.
By deploying longer-range weapons such as Hsiung Feng III (雄風, “Brave Wind”) missiles on Penghu, Taiwan could also make it harder for the PLA to assemble its forces along the Chinese coast for an invasion, a senior Taiwanese official said on condition of anonymity.
Chinese forces could be targeted even before they set out across the Strait.
If Penghu were taken, the entire Taiwan Strait would effectively fall into China’s hands, they said.
Taipei has been investing in Penghu’s defense, including running programs to beef up the resilience of the 110,000 people who live on the islands in the event of war.
Chinese Ministry of National Defense spokesman Jiang Bin (蔣斌) has said that Taiwan’s plans to fortify the islands were “increasingly absurd and delusional.”
For the troops waiting in the dark during the Aug. 10 drill on the main island of the Penghu group, the quiet was shattered when artillery guns nestled under camouflage netting fired illumination rounds out to sea.
The shells burst with a crump in the distance, casting brilliant light over the ocean approaches.
In a series of maneuvers, the four tanks, along with armored personnel carriers, wheeled forward through clouds of dust, exhaust fumes and explosive gases, blasting away at “invaders” attempting to land.
As sunlight crept across the sea, artillery, mortars and infantry poured fire down over the ocean below. Orange-red tracers from machine guns arched into the sky.
The live-fire drill during the annual Han Kuang exercises was part of rehearsals across Taiwan to resist landings by air and sea.
In the same week, the navy’s Coastal Operations Command were deployed to Penghu for the first time, sending Hsiung Feng missile launch vehicles to beachfront positions in anti-ship and anti-landing operations, military officials said.
Penghu’s strategic location, along with the presence of such weapons, makes the islands a prime target for the PLA, Su said.
Taiwan’s two other major outlying counties, Kinmen and Lienchiang, are too close to China to be a useful part of a defensive network, he said.
However, Taiwanese forces could catch invading Chinese ships in a crossfire of missiles between the Penghu islands and Taiwan proper, Su said.
Missiles on the islands could also launch “counterstrikes” further into China’s hinterland, he added.
The defense ministry is pushing the use of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to defend Penghu.
The military established the first drone force on the islands last month and UAVs were deployed during the Han Kuang exercises.
Beijing tightly restricts public discussion of military plans related to Taiwan, although Chinese strategists have previously identified the importance of Penghu.
Retired Chinese lieutenant general Wang Hongguang (王洪光) in 2019 suggested that the PLA “strategically suppress” Taiwan by occupying the Penghu Islands.
During a war game attended by retired Taiwanese, US and Japanese military officials last year, Penghu fell just a day after China began surprise long-range attacks on military and infrastructure targets across Taiwan.
The quick capitulation to the PLA startled Taiwanese participants, a report of the activity said.
Asked about that war game, the ministry referred to Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo’s (顧立雄) statement last year that the government takes such exercises into account when making adjustments to its defensive plans.
While the Taiwanese military trains to repel a Chinese landing, Penghu officials and residents are preparing to play their part.
Yen Min-ching is one of about 1,200 people on Penghu who have been certified by the government’s Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Program. Volunteers are trained to provide support, including first aid, in the event of emergencies such as earthquakes and invasions.
Yen, a retired police officer who is a neighborhood warden, is acutely aware of Penghu’s exposed position between the Chinese coast and Taiwan proper, and has encouraged residents to sign up for the program.
By the end of the year, about 200,000 Taiwanese are expected to have completed the training.
“We absolutely need to have a sense of crisis,” said Husi (湖西) Township Mayor Chen Chen-chung (陳振中), whose district hosts key infrastructure, including cargo transport docks, an airport used for civil and military purposes, and Penghu’s main power plant.
Penghu County “would definitely be one of the first places attacked,” said Chen, who leads about 100 people in a civil defense group that is tasked with wartime support missions.
Those might include distributing rations, setting up defensive fortifications and countering enemy propaganda.
Local businesspeople such as auto workshop owner Ho Chi-hua have signed agreements to cooperate with Taiwanese authorities.
During a drill this month that simulated a scenario in which military logistics facilities were damaged, rifle-carrying troops joined Ho’s staff as they practiced emergency repairs on military vehicles.
Penghu is also preparing for Chinese coercion that stops short of a military attack: Beijing could impose a blockade on Taiwan, which could quickly choke Taipei’s trade-dependent economy and leave outlying islands isolated.
Locals starved of supplies might quickly capitulate, said Kao Yu-jou, a 15-year-old student in Penghu. “People might think: Let’s surrender first, get something to eat, and after I’m full, then we’ll see.”
However, taxi driver William Chen said he would resist.
“If my homeland were invaded, there’s no way I could just stand by,” he said.
Magong (馬公), Penghu’s urban center, has rehearsed its response, holding drills that simulate a blockade and all-out combat, Mayor Huang Jian-zhong (黃健忠) said.
Municipal authorities have signed agreements with grocery stores, pharmacies and construction companies to safeguard emergency supplies and repair capabilities if a crisis occurs, government documents show.
The islands have been a springboard for invasions of Taiwan over the centuries. When Taiwan was a Japanese colony during World War II, the harbor was the target of Allied bombing attacks late in the conflict.
Some analysts think Penghu would provide stiff resistance.
The prospect of heavy losses during WWII had prompted US war planners to cancel a planned offensive on the islands as part of a wider invasion of Taiwan, US Naval War College associate professor Ian Easton said.
“My guess is that if the terrible crunch ever comes, the PLA will find these islands a tough nut to crack,” he said.

Shein’s IPO has only  one winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:41 UTC
01:46:41 KST

Shein Group Ltd spent years trying to distance itself from China, only to discover that the supply chain underpinning its success was the one thing it could not leave behind. That very ecosystem appears to be the main beneficiary of a long, tortuous listing.
For everyone else, the journey has been costly — starting with the company itself. The Singapore-based online retailer priced the Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO) at HK$48.56 (US$6.19) per share on Thursday, valuing it at just more than US$26 billion. That is about a quarter of the US$100 billion it was worth at its private-market peak four years ago.
Some existing shareholders are being cushioned from the collapse in value, but that hardly makes them winners. Shein had agreed to pay as much as US$3.5 billion to pre-IPO investors. Their purchases included protections against a steep markdown. As a result, the hefty payout could amount to about double the US$1.7 billion raised in the IPO.
Photo: Bloomberg
However, there is one group with reason to celebrate: The vast network of suppliers in southern China that powers the retail juggernaut. Concentrated in the southern part of Guangzhou, thousands of small factories, making mostly clothing, are the muscle behind the ultra-fast-fashion model. A close-knit, tightly integrated supply chain located in a compact area allows Shein to identify trends, place tiny initial orders and get them ready for delivery within two weeks.
The irony is that this is the network that the fashion giant had once tried to play down by moving to Singapore and rebranding as a global company to appeal to Western investors. That strategy failed due to fierce US opposition, as well as an inability to reproduce in countries such as Brazil and Turkey the speed, flexibility and low costs of its production base.
The IPO should bind those suppliers even more closely to Shein. The company plans to devote 40 percent of the proceeds to technology, including investments designed to improve the manufacturing network at the heart of the business.
Shein’s next act would only deepen the relationship. With growth in the US and Europe, two of its biggest regions, slowing due to greater protectionism and competition, the company is telling investors that future expansion would come from offering the Guangzhou supplier network to other brands. The approach calls for acquiring labels and plugging them into the same group of factories or providing those services to other firms.
However, turning its manufacturing prowess into someone else’s growth engine might be harder than it sounds. The retailer launched a fashion incubator for budding designers in 2021. Two years later, it evolved into the Xcelerator program, which offers product fulfillment, production support and access to the sales platform. The results have been modest, accounting for no more than 1 percent of sales last year. It is hard to see how the scheme could move the needle.
Buying brands might be a better bet. An established label comes with something that Shein’s factories cannot make: recognition and a ready-made customer base. But this strategy also comes with caveats. The deal to purchase US millennial clothing brand Everlane, announced in May and subject to a US security review, looks like an awkward fit.
The US label built its fanbase on supply-chain transparency and sustainable production, attributes that clash with an ultra-fast-fashion ethos. Plugging it into the same manufacturing machine risks eroding the very qualities that made the brand worth buying in the first place.
The subdued response to the IPO suggests investors are not totally convinced that Shein has found its next growth engine. At this price, the company trades a 13 times trailing earnings, a considerable discount to Zara owner Inditex SA, Swedish retailer Hennes & Mauritz AB and Japan’s Fast Retailing Co. The retailer has the difficult task of proving that the manufacturing system that transformed fashion can do so again.
The listing has already delivered one verdict. Shein spent years recasting itself as a global company, only to discover that its greatest strength remains unmistakably Chinese. Its valuation might have shrunk, but the value of the manufacturing ecosystem behind it has never been clearer.
Juliana Liu is a columnist for Bloomberg Opinion’s Asia team, covering corporate strategy and management in the region. She was previously CNN’s senior business editor for Asia, and a correspondent at BBC News and Reuters. Indonesia steps up wildfire fight as haze spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Indonesia has intensified efforts to fight wildfires with cloud seeding and water bombing as thousands of people countrywide battle to breathe in the smoke and haze, officials said on Friday.
More than 5 million people on Borneo and Sumatra islands were directly exposed to the risks of a putrid haze coming off dozens of fires across the vast archipelago, Indonesian Deputy Minister of Health Dante Saksono Harbuwono said.
About 13,500 people were treated for respiratory infections last month and this month, Dante said.
Photo: Reuters
Several schools had been closed intermittently, and the haze has also made people in Singapore and Malaysia unwell.
“Vulnerable groups that must be evaluated are children, the elderly, pregnant women with asthma and outdoor workers,” Dante said.
Nongovernmental organizations have set up two shelters in Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan on Borneo island, for babies and children affected by the haze, with more planned.
The shelters, which can accommodate only five children at a time, were equipped with baby formula and oxygen tanks, medicines, and a playground.
Katharina Abi, 30, brought her two small children, aged one and five, to one of the shelters on Friday as thick smoke blanketed their home.
“There’s a lot of smoke at my house. In the morning it’s not too bad, but in the afternoon and evening, there’s so much dust, like there’s a fire nearby. It really bothers my breathing,” she said. “My children often have coughs and colds, maybe because there is a lot of smoke.”
Dante said prolonged exposure to toxic air can cause serious longer-term health complications.
He said the ministry has distributed more than 5 million masks across Indonesia — a country of 289 million people dealing with the effects of a super-charged El Nino weather event dubbed “Godzilla.”
Disaster agency BNPB on Friday said the government has intensified efforts to battle wildfires, with some success.
“Cloud seeding remains one of the measures to support efforts to tackle forest and land fires. Its implementation depends heavily on atmospheric conditions and the presence of rain-bearing clouds in the target areas,” BNPB spokesman Berton Suar Pelita Panjaitan said.
“However, cloud seeding is not the only effort, because the ground and air task forces continue working in the field to carry out extinguishing and cooling operations,” he said.
The agency said it has poured more than 4 million liters of water on burning areas in the past few weeks, and on Wednesday alone it scattered more than 8 tonnes of salt onto clouds.
Cloud seeding involves sprinkling silver iodide, salts or other particles into clouds to trigger precipitation.
Such operations this week succeeded in prompting light to moderate rains over east and south Sumatra and west Kalimantan, Berton said.
Fires from July to last month burned more than 200,000 hectares of land — an area three times the size of the capital Jakarta, the Indonesian government said last week. That is more than during previous El Nino seasons in 2019 and 2023.
El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns — typically experienced as drought in Indonesia.
Many wildfires in Indonesia are blamed on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices for agriculture.
“We hope the government will immediately address the root causes behind the haze that returns every year,” Indra Syahnanda of the WALHI environmental advocacy group said.
“The people of West Kalimantan remain haunted by the haze and have to breathe unhealthy air,” Syahnanda added.

KMT lawmaker says birthrate measures have failed
Unknown

16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmaker yesterday criticized the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government over the nation’s declining population, calling it Taiwan’s top national security threat.
The National Development Council on Friday said that Taiwan’s population would fall below 20 million by 2045.
The prospect of a declining population is immediate and real, threatening Taiwan’s economy, finances, healthcare, social welfare and national security, KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said yesterday.
Photo: CNA
The decreasing workforce would come under increasing pressure to support the National Health Insurance program, pay taxes, provide people to defend the nation and care for a growing population of elderly people, Hsu said.
The DPP government is not truly aware of the pressures facing the younger generation, she said, citing real-estate prices, stagnant wages, surging commodity prices and low savings.
The Executive Yuan’s decision not to countersign the Taiwan Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例) passed by the Legislative Yuan earlier this month is evidence that the DPP government is oblivious to the issue, she said.
President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration is calling on people to marry and have children, but fails to understand that doing so involves costs ranging from housing and childbirth to child-rearing, daycare and education, Hsu said, adding that education is an expense for more than two decades for most people.
Many couples spend every waking minute weighing decisions against the pressure of rent, mortgage, baby formula and daycare expenses, she said.
Lai has failed to fulfill campaign pledges to build more social housing, she said.
When the prospect of a stable life is constantly assaulted by fresh waves of anxiety, it is difficult to muster the courage to bring another life into this world, Hsu said.
KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said the DPP government over the past eight years has allocated nearly NT$600 billion (US$18.97 billion) to address the low birthrate, but has failed to reverse the trend.
Young adults cite high housing prices, the cost of raising children and an unwillingness to change their lifestyles as the top three reasons for not having children, Lee said, adding that their collective decision is bringing Taiwan closer to a population crisis.
The number of births in 2012 was 230,000, but fell to 108,000 last year and is expected to be below 100,000 this year, she said.
The government should convene a national affairs meeting on the birthrate issue, she said.
If the trend cannot be reversed, Taiwan risks going from a thriving and prosperous technological place to somewhere devoid of people, she added.

Taiwan in Time: The once-bustling temple atop 1,200 steps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Aug. 31 to Sept. 6
More than 3 million people visited Taipei’s Zhinan Temple (指南宮) in 1973, making it Taiwan’s second-most visited scenic area that year.
Built in 1891, the temple had been a tourist destination since the Japanese colonial period, when visitors had to initially take a ferry across the Jingmei River before climbing a winding trail up Houshan (猴山).
Photo courtesy of Academia Historica
Its popularity was reflected in popular media. The 1932 tune New Song of the Black Cat and Black Dog (新烏貓烏狗歌) depicted two lovers who prayed at the temple for their marriage. The man couldn’t afford to hire a sedan chair, so they made the arduous journey on foot. They later committed suicide after the man was unable to pay the bride price demanded by the woman’s family.
The 1959 movie Brother Wang and Brother Liu Tour Taiwan (王哥柳哥遊台灣) featured the titular duo huffing and puffing their way up the temple’s stairs on their first stop.
Although visitor numbers have declined from their historic peak, Zhinan Temple remains a destination for many, with the Maokong Gondola making a stop there. Its Lingxiao Hall, completed in 1966, was seriously damaged in a fire on Monday. Officials say the rest of the complex will remain open.
Photo courtesy of National Museum of Taiwan History via Open Museum
DISPUTED ORIGINS
The principal deity of Zhinan Temple is the Taoist immortal Lu Tung-pin (呂洞賓). According to the temple, sacred incense representing Lu Tung-pin’s spiritual presence was brought from China in 1882 by Wang Pin-lin (王斌林), who had been appointed magistrate of Tamsui County. The deity was initially housed in Wanhua District (萬華), but locals later invited it to Jingmei District (景美) during an epidemic. After the sickness passed, local gentry built a small thatched-roof shrine on Muzha District’s (木柵) Houshan in 1890 to honor the deity.
But this account is disputed. The National Taiwan University database of Qing officials lists Wang as a county deputy in Bangka (today’s Wanhua), rather than as Tamsui magistrate. Taiwan Daily News reports suggest that he was already in Taiwan by 1878.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Examining Japanese-era sources, historian Paul Katz traces Zhinan Temple to a spirit-writing temple in Wanhua dedicated to Lu. After hearing of the deity’s powers, Jingmei residents had Wanhua artisans carve an identical statue and established their own temple. Worshippers from nearby Muzha later joined them, and helped establish Zhinan Temple in 1891.
Ethnologist Wu Tsung-ming (吳宗明) argues that Wang was already established on Houshan in the 1880s, where spirit writing may also have taken place. Wang’s son, Wang Yu-ching (王毓卿), later worked with worshippers from Jingmei and Muzha to establish Zhinan Temple and served on its first board.
The temple no longer offers spirit-writing services, having shifted its focus to Taoism, with Buddhist and Confucian characteristics.
At first, visitors had to cross the Jingmei River from Muzha to reach the temple. They could make the crossing on foot when the water was low, writes Hsu Chung-chieh (徐仲杰) in “The formation of the religious attraction of Muzha Zhinan Temple” (宗教景點木柵宮的形成), but taking a ferry was the safer option. Around 1900, as the temple’s popularity grew, Muzha District head Chang Te-ming (張德明) and eight others purchased local farmland and used the collected rent to fund a free ferry service.
A Taiwan Daily News article in 1909 attributed the temple’s popularity not only to the efficacy of its principal deity, but also to the cool mountain air and superb views of Taipei. Lu Tung-pin was said to cure illnesses and provide worshippers with dreams that predict the future.
EXPANDING FACILITIES
Photo courtesy of Lienyuan Lee
The journey to the temple from Muzha’s main street took 30 to 40 minutes, painter Kinichiro Ishikawa wrote in the Taiwan Daily News in 1926, adding that “visiting once was enough.” The “thousand stone steps” leading to the temple already existed by then, and sources show beggars waiting along the route for visitors, Hsu writes.
By the 1920s, visitors could take a train to Jingmei and continue to Muzha by bus or pushcart. The crowds persisted into the intensified Japanization period of the late 1930s, when extra Lunar New Year buses were reportedly required despite government promotion of State Shinto. A 1938 report showed 700,000 to 800,000 visitors per year.
The temple began large-scale renovations and expansion in 1920, a project that took seven years to complete. A temporary wooden bridge was built in 1928 for the opening ceremony, but it survived only a few years before being damaged by torrential rains. The steel Daonan Bridge (道南橋) was completed in 1934, with a ceremony held in October. Although it was conducted by Shinto priests per government policy, it still featured the temple’s deities crossing the river and other Taoist elements.
Visitors continued to use the ferry afterward, although ridership gradually declined.
The stone steps were rebuilt in 1936, with stone lanterns and benches added along the way. Palm and pine trees were planted on either side for shade. Tourist photographers and vendors selling food, drinks and worship supplies set up shop outside the temple.
The temple remained popular after the war. A 1955 report recorded tens of thousands of people visiting during Lunar New Year, prompting bus companies to add more than 100 extra trips to Muzha.
MOTORIZED ERA
Although a road for motorized vehicles was built to the temple in 1955, general Hsu Yung-chang (徐永昌) recalled still hiring a sedan chair to traverse the steps in 1956. The government restricted the number of vehicles during Lunar New Year, and a 1980 United Daily News report described people waiting up to four hours to catch the bus down the mountain.
The grandiose Lingxiao Hall was completed in 1966. The structure was featured in the 1969 Hollywood thriller The Chairman starring Gregory Peck, where it served as a stand-in for Mao Tse-tung’s (毛澤東) residence in Beijing.
That same year, an amusement park and zoo were added to the temple complex, greatly boosting visitor numbers. The park closed in the 1980s, and the temple saw a decline in visitors during the 1990s. Bus routes were reduced, making the remote temple even less accessible.
The idea of building a cable car up to the temple dates back to the Japanese era. A 1932 Taiwan Daily News article briefly pondered the feasibility, and plans were repeatedly floated through the 1950s and 1960s. The gondola finally became a reality in 2007, and the rise of Maokong as a tourist destination brought the temple renewed attention.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore. The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year
During the Martial Law era, newspapers and magazines were strictly controlled by the government. But from 1985 to 1990 — a period that straddled the lifting of martial law in 1987 — a free monthly expat magazine emerged as one of the first published and edited by foreigners. It was also perhaps the first to express a uniquely local expatriate voice. Taiwan Grapevine’s articles were irreverent, politically incorrect and plagued by typos. Neither editors nor writers were named in the magazine, and those bylines that appeared were obvious pseudonyms like Archibald Hellbender. Yet the magazine achieved nationwide distribution. And while

Taiwan’s rivers are significantly cleaner today than they were a few decades ago. The country’s rapid industrialization left many waterways polluted by untreated factory discharge, domestic sewage and runoff from livestock operations. Since the 1990s, expansion of municipal sewerage infrastructure and stricter enforcement of environmental standards have turned the situation around. However, freshwater ecosystems now face a very different threat — one that’s far less obvious to people living nearby. “Southern Taiwan — Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung — is facing a particularly critical crisis regarding freshwater biological invasions,” says Lin Yen-ting (林晏廷), an assistant professor in the Master’s Program in Biodiversity
