James English: one of many men with far-right ties accused of domestic violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:31 UTC
01:00:31 KST

In many ways, the case heard this week at Glasgow sheriff court was, unfortunately, not out of the ordinary. It was one of thousands of domestic violence trials to have passed through the Scottish courts since new legislation was introduced in 2019 to clamp down on a grimly persistent problem.
A woman had testified that her former partner had waged a campaign of terror against her, and that she suffered abuse while she was pregnant with his child. The court heard that her partner had grabbed her by the throat, pinned her to a door, kicked her off a bed and sent her abusive texts, sometimes calling her a “fat slag” and a “little bitch”.
What caught the eye of onlookers, however, was the identity of the man convicted.
James English may not be a household name, but in the online world he is a star, a podcaster with millions of followers across several social media platforms for his interview show, Anything Goes.
English has won plaudits for securing high profile guests, such as the footballer Paul Gascoigne and Rebecca Loos, who allegedly had an affair with David Beckham.
However, he has also attracted controversy for his ties to figures from the far right, particularly the English Defence League founder Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, more commonly known as Tommy Robinson. Last September, English appeared at Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally, describing the event as “legendary” and praising Robinson for organising it.
During the course of his podcasting, English has also platformed personalities from what has become known as the manosphere.
Other guests on English’s podcast have included men accused of serious sexual offences, such as Andrew Tate, the internet personality recently charged with rape and sex trafficking, and the footballer David Goodwillie.
Goodwillie and his former teammate, David Robertson, were ordered to pay £100,000 in damages to Denise Clair after a judge in a civil case ruled they had raped her after a night out in 2011.
English, a 42-year-old father of three from Larkhall, Lanarkshire, reinvented himself as an independent journalist after appearing on Glow, a failed reality television show billed as a Glaswegian Towie.
Although he says he does not necessarily share the views of his guests, he has given a range of far-right activists a sympathetic platform. As well as hosting Robinson several times, he has interviewed the commentator Katie Hopkins and the Raise the Colours founder Ryan Bridge.
The Unite the Kingdom march was “beautiful” and “very patriotic”, English said. “The people that have been on stage speaking, Katie Hopkins, Tommy Robinson, it’s been unbelievable,” he said, on a clip posted on Robinson’s X account. “It’s been great to see so many people getting behind each other and uniting for a better future.”
English is one of many men with ties to the far right who have found themselves accused of intimate partner violence.
Project Starlight, a 2021 study commissioned by Counter Terrorism Policing, found that about a third of people referred to the government’s Prevent programme had links to a domestic abuse incident, either as an offender, victim, witness or a combination of all three. In 18% of these cases, extreme rightwing ideology was present.
Deniz Ugur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said police data had “consistently shown that a significant proportion of men arrested during far-right riots are already known to the police for domestic abuse”.
The Guardian previously revealed that 41% of those arrested in the 2024 riots, prompted by the murders of three young girls in Southport, had been reported to the police for alleged domestic abuse. After the riots, 21% were accused of similar offences.
English had already been charged with abusing the woman, a model he met on Instagram, by the time he travelled to London for the Unite the Kingdom protest. One of its central themes was the threat supposedly posed by migrant men to British women and girls. “It’s all about saving the children,” English said.
Some speakers promoted conspiracies about migration, including the “great replacement theory – the suggestion that there is a plot to replace white Europeans with people from other races. While English described the march as “peaceful”, the Metropolitan police said its officers faced “unacceptable violence” from some demonstrators, more than 20 of whom were arrested.
This week, Sheriff David Hall, who heard English’s case without a jury, convicted him of engaging in a course of abusive conduct towards his former partner between July 2022 and November 2023. The single charge included 19 allegations, six of which Hall judged to have been proved. He described the woman as “credible and reliable”.
Alice Russell Harris, public affairs lead at the domestic abuse charity Refuge, said: “The manosphere, which significantly overlaps with far-right communities, has helped amplify misogynistic narratives that objectify and seek to control women, casting women as subordinate to men and suggesting that those who reject male expectations deserve punishment. These ideas can directly promote abuse – both online and offline – by encouraging men to engage in coercion, control and related harms.”
English, who will be sentenced next month, was not in court to hear Hall’s verdict on Tuesday. However, the next day, he used his social media platforms to issue a rallying cry to his followers, sharing misinformation about the legal basis for his conviction.
“Men need to be worried, especially in Scotland,” he said. “Ladies, if you have a brother or a son, you should also be worried, because women can say anything and it’s a man’s job to prove his innocence.” He added that, in Scotland, “accusations are enough to get the man charged”.
In fact, Scottish law is underpinned by the principle of corroboration, where two independent sources of evidence are required to prove a criminal accusation. Defendants are innocent until proved guilty and the testimony of a single witness – no matter how compelling – is not enough to secure a conviction.
Neither English nor any of the nine people he claimed could support his version of events took the stand. English said this was because he was “so confident” he would be cleared. “I should never have been charged, never mind convicted,” he said.
Ugur said: “It is no surprise to see a convicted perpetrator of domestic abuse and prominent figure in the far right promote deeply harmful misinformation about violence against women and girls.
“Most victims do not report to the police, and those who do, know how many hurdles there are to seeing a conviction due to institutional cultures of victim blaming and failures to treat violence against women and girls with the seriousness it warrants.”
Despite the headlines his case has generated, English has remained defiant, criticising the mainstream media for covering it. “People need to be wary, because if they want you, they’ll find something to get you on,” he said, adding that he was “tired of men getting fucked over”.
He did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian, but vowed on his social media channels to continue broadcasting. “I’m still going to keep doing what I’m doing,” he said. “If anything, it’s just fuelled me to keep raising the bar.”

Andrey Belousov: NATO nuclear expansion leaves Russia no choice but to respond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:18 UTC
01:00:18 KST

Andrey Belousov: NATO nuclear expansion leaves Russia no choice but to respond
RT: It is well known that the United States has stationed nuclear weapons in NATO countries in Europe since the 1950s as part of a nuclear‑exchange programme. Why has the issue of removing US nuclear weapons from the region become a matter of fundamental importance at this moment?
Andrey Belousov: First and foremost, it must be noted that the problem of US nuclear weapons on the territory of European states and Turkiye has long been the subject of bilateral meetings on strategic stability, including at the beginning of the mid‑1990s. For the record, under presidential initiatives in the early 1990s, Russia reduced its non‑strategic nuclear arsenal four‑fold and kept the remainder at central storage bases.
We could reasonably expect symmetrical moves from the United States. Yet the actions taken by the US in the early 2000s – such as the withdrawal of nuclear weapons from Greece and the United Kingdom, and partially from Italy and Germany – seemed more like a tactical concession or a trick, without changing the military‑political context in Europe. After all, the US nuclear weapons withdrawal from Greece was fully compensated by their presence in Turkiye, and those withdrawn from the UK were replaced by its own nuclear arsenal of the United Kingdom – which is the main and most important ally, strategic ally of the United States.
In contrast, the measures taken to remove and reduce US nuclear weapons in Italy and Germany did not significantly enhance security, trust, or predictability, because the practice of US nuclear weapons in Europe and joint NATO nuclear missions continued unchanged. In short, if we keep talking about this, we must remember that at that time the United States consistently followed a line to enhance its strategic capabilities, primarily through the implementation of plans and programmes not directly related to strengthening its nuclear potential, most of which was under the arms‑control bans at the time – Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty and Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty.
By the mid‑1990s, the US began implementing its Global Missile Defence configuration, which envisaged deploying one of its segments – the third positional sector – in Europe. At the same time, the concept of a global lightning‑strike was being implemented, under which the US could use non‑nuclear strategic carriers to strike any target anywhere on Earth.
We should also mention the development of new nuclear delivery systems and, finally, a programme to create laser anti‑satellite air‑based systems. This also included the development of heavy strike UAVs that, by their technical characteristics, fell under the criteria of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, but were not covered by it. It was also a key element of enhancing US strategic capacity.
Accordingly, during that period of reshaping strategic stability from a military‑security view, Russia’s priority was to mitigate the risks and threats that could arise from the execution of the projects and programmes I mentioned. It does not mean that the issue of US non‑strategic nuclear weapons in Europe fell out of Russian diplomatic focus, let alone the Russian military, which could not ignore this problem in its defensive planning.
As tensions with the United States and its satellites increased, Russia sharpened the issue of removing American nuclear weapons from Europe, and the complete withdrawal of that armament from European territory to national territory.
Today, however, we live in entirely different, more complex and dangerous conditions. The United States, with the support of its closest partners and allies, has disintegrated the system of arms‑control agreements on nuclear disarmament. The very important treaty on missile defence, essential for strategic stability, has been discarded. The removal of political and international‑law restrictions on the unchecked buildup of nuclear arsenals, together with Washington’s steps to create a missile‑defence system for the country combining land, sea, air and space segments – now all under the “Golden Dome for America” programme – coupled with the deep modernisation of U.S. nuclear potential, upgrading nuclear warheads and creating new carrier systems for intermediate‑ and shorter‑range missiles, has led to a radical deterioration of the military‑political situation both regionally and globally.
Naturally, this has had a profoundly negative impact on the strategic environment.In fact, the negative factors are not limitк ed to the present situation. Factors that must be considered in analysing the current modern context also include NATO’s provocative positioning as a nuclear alliance and the continuous attempts of member states to expand that alliance eastward. Moreover, plans for advanced and extended deterrence, and the expansion and deepening of NATO’s joint nuclear missions, are increasingly being implemented. All of this must be considered together to understand the environment in which we live now.
And, undoubtedly, these aspects compel us to give enhanced attention, during this historical period, to the non‑strategic US nuclear weapons deployed in Europe, as well as those of US allies in NATO – France and the United Kingdom. As a result, in the current conditions the factor of the total nuclear arsenal or the combined nuclear potential in the region takes on special importance in Russia’s military‑security context. The involvement of new states, NATO’s schemes for practising nuclear usage and discussing the possibility of deploying such weapons on their territory, and the introduction of new multifunctional aircraft platforms as delivery systems, increase the threat to Russia. The reason is that nuclear warheads can be moved quickly and covertly from permanent locations to points from which their use could have the greatest effect, including an attack on strategically important targets in the European part of Russia.
To summarise, I would like to note that all of this confirms that the European component of US nuclear forces, as well as the nuclear weapons of its allies, is designated for carrying out strategic objectives specifically, which poses critical risks for our country. This compels us to a corresponding military‑technical response. On the diplomatic front, our current efforts are focused on sparking an international discussion on the extremely destabilising nature of NATO’s joint nuclear mission practice, and on encouraging the United States to take steps toward removing its nuclear weapons from Europe.
RT: Andrey Ivanovich, what arguments, in your view, could persuade the American side and European countries alike to agree to remove this weapon?
Andrey Belousov: Here we can offer an entire battery of arguments – political, diplomatic, military, economic, international‑law and even historical in nature – grounded in the present state of inter‑state relations and the overall military‑political environment in the world.
The core of our arguments is, in principle, well known, because it is based on our doctrinal documents, our foreign‑policy concept, the fundamentals of national‑security strategy and military doctrine. Most of them relate to the fact that the international community is essentially faced with a choice: will inter‑state relations continue to develop in a confrontational paradigm that threatens a direct armed conflict between nuclear powers and the use of nuclear weapons, or will prudence prevail among our opponents, allowing the leading powers to reach an agreement on concrete joint measures to prevent escalation and avert a catastrophic scenario for the entire world?
Obviously, unlike our opponents and most Western countries, Russia does not stand at a crossroads. We have repeatedly expressed, at various levels and on different international platforms – including the UN – our readiness to cooperate with all interested states to maintain peace, strengthen regional security, and ensure strategic stability. Moreover, our statements are regularly reinforced by concrete initiatives. Recall that one of the founding principles of Russia’s foreign‑policy course in international and regional security remains the principle of equal and indivisible security. A key part of that principle is the non‑acceptance of a situation in which one state or a group of states creates comfortable conditions for itself – or a privileged status – at the expense of lowering the security level or damaging the security of other states.
From that widely recognised principle, which is set out in a host of international multilateral documents, Russia has recently put forward a whole set of key initiatives. These include proposals for the United States and its NATO allies to introduce a mutual moratorium on the deployment of intermediate and shorter range missiles. Another initiative, launched in late 2021 and early 2022, was the establishment of a security guarantee on the western front in the form of an agreement with the United States and NATO allies. Yet another initiative was a proposal, unfortunately still unrealised, to convene a summit of heads of state, the United Nations Security Council’s permanent members, to discuss urgent problems in international security. Among the latest proposals is the one put forward by Russian President Vladimir Putin on September twenty second of last year to preserve the legacy of the START Treaty through voluntary limits.
It is obvious that if these initiatives were implemented they would act as deterrents, contributing to the prevention of a new arms race and creating favourable conditions for the renewal of strategic dialogue between Russia and the United States, with the prospect of involving other nuclear powers. Unfortunately, most of our ideas were either rejected, received no adequate response, or were simply ignored. The only exception, perhaps, was the initiative to have leaders of the nuclear powers sign a joint declaration on preventing nuclear war and halting the nuclear arms race, which was carried out on January third 2022. Yet even this document is not clearly worded. In terms of practical implementation and compliance with its provisions by Western states, the matter largely remains at the level of empty declarations, which raises serious concerns and deep disappointment.
In short, our opponents – primarily in Europe – must decide where we are headed next. In that context, it is far more important to bring forward arguments that are conditioned by the course of the historical process associated with establishing a new multipolar world order in which the imperative is the abandonment of global dominance by any one state or bloc of states. The new system of geopolitical coordinates, in whose formation Russia actively participates, does not allow perpetual escalation, the accumulation of unresolved contradictions critical to international security, or the further erosion of trust between the emerging centres of power, whose dangerous balance risks armed conflict. Furthermore, this system of coordinates does not allow continuous fuelling of a conflict‑generating potential in international relations and an uncontrolled arms race. It is also unacceptable, in a new world order, to create security systems aimed at a single state or predicated on bloc‑based confrontation. Rather, the new order dictates the necessity for mutually beneficial cooperation and constructive collaboration between states.
The quest, above all, is for political‑diplomatic solutions to the most urgent regional and global problems, strict adherence to the fundamental principles of the UN, the goals and tasks of the global community, respect for international law, and the recognition by every member of the international community of its responsibility for the fate of the world and international security.
RT: how could these negotiations – and the withdrawal of the weapons themselves – be organized if, in an optimistic scenario, the US side agreed with this position?
Andrey Belousov: That’s a very interesting question. At this point the organizational aspects of such negotiations, or even the procedure for removing US weapons from Europe, are secondary. The key issue now is Washington’s unwillingness to find a principled agreement to discuss this problem with a view of reaching any real agreement on the matter. What is needed is an openness to start and conduct negotiations without tying them to the question of Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons, which, unlike US weapons of this class that can be used operationally against our country, do not pose a direct strategic threat to US territory.
It is obvious that Washington’s attempts to initiate a dialogue on our non‑strategic nuclear arsenal serve a single purpose – shifting the international community’s focus away from the danger posed by US nuclear weapons in Europe, and more broadly, from the missile‑nuclear programs and plans that Washington is implementing. Speaking of that danger, it cannot be overlooked that Washington’s persistence in trying to launch discussions about Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons – those that do not threaten US territory – at various multilateral disarmament forums repeatedly suggests that US military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons on the European theater of operations. In fact, Europe is being viewed as a probable military theater.
Obtaining, through negotiations or discussions on strategic stability, objective data on Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons via the implementation of some intrusive transparency practices – or reducing or even completely eliminating them – would increase the likelihood of a scenario in which the US and its European allies use nuclear weapons. I hope Europe will recognize the danger of such a strictly operational‑planning approach that Washington adopts toward the territory of its allies.
In a principled sense, regarding the conditions for launching any substantive US dialogue, there are three points that must be understood. First, what must precede such negotiations? Our country’s leadership – and the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs – has repeatedly stated their position on this issue. Our delegations have mentioned it both in the First Committee of the UN General Assembly and at the recently held 11th Conference on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. To create a favorable climate for starting US negotiations, it is essential that they first, not in words but in action – declaratively and through concrete steps – demonstrate that they are ready to irreversibly abandon an anti‑Russian course and to resolve the most critical issues in international security together with us, starting with the elimination of fundamental contradictions and the root causes of the current crisis in interstate relations, and ending with questions of arms control, disarmament, and non‑proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
Second, it is important to understand what the nature of the negotiations should be. We have always and continue to insist on a mutually respectful dialogue built on trust and the consideration of all participants’ interests. It is unacceptable for Russia to be subjected to fabricated claims and unsubstantiated demands, or for the discussion to be conducted in the style of an ultimatum. The conversation must be substantive and equal, with both sides fully aware of the danger of rising tension, loss of trust, the degradation of bilateral relations, and of their individual and collective responsibility for humanity’s future.
Third, the content of the negotiations and their ultimate goal. Russia rejects mere performative speeches that, under the pretext of making the world safer, drag us into another propaganda campaign aimed at enhancing the US image or maintaining its reputation at our expense or that of our close partners and allies.
In the strategic sphere, for us a constructive dialogue aimed at achieving long‑term and indisputable agreements on the entire complex of factors affecting strategic stability is crucial. Removing some specific, extremely technical issues from the interdependent framework of the sector will not help move forward or achieve the required agreements and understandings.
Another important point I would like to emphasize concerns the nature and content of the dialogue: we will never, under any circumstances, start a serious conversation on US terms only to make an effort to address American security issues. The starting point of any strategic‑stability negotiations must be a clear recognition of the inviolability of the principle of equal and indivisible security, and no exceptions can be made from strict adherence to this principle.
RT: Nevertheless, American media outlets are reporting a potential expansion of the number of participants in the program. What risks and threats could such plans create, given that among European countries Poland – and the Baltic states as well – have expressed interest in hosting U.S. weapons?
Andrey Belousov: It is a very important issue from the standpoint of our country’s security, and essentially it concerns maintaining strategic balance and strategic stability. In answering the first question, I already partially addressed your question, which touches on this issue.
The involvement of an ever‑growing number of NATO member states in schemes that envisage the practical use of nuclear weapons against Russia primarily is fully in line with NATO’s nuclear status and the logic of the trans‑Atlantic linkage, whose key element today is precisely nuclear dimension. Securing a nuclear status for NATO is not merely a declaration or a sign lacking substance or implying any action. On the contrary, one must clearly understand that such a status is concrete. It means that nuclear weapons, their possible use, and the concept of nuclear deterrence – as understood by the military‑political establishment of NATO and the European Union states – have become a fundamental means by which westerners ensure their security.
It is important to note that the security views of Europe’s current elites differ sharply from the narratives and concepts we tried to align with the West and jointly implement at the end of the last century and at the beginning of this one. The main distinction lies in our opponents refusal to create a security architecture in Europe together with Russia in favor of attempts to build a regional security system aimed at our country. The results of this radical shift – so to speak – are now evident.
Currently, the minds of our Western opponents, under significant influence, are shaped by a new view of how regional and international security should be ensured, induced by pressure from the United States. The concept of “peace through force,” which seems long out of date and paradoxical at its core but is actively promoted by Washington, has been adopted.
Returning to the question of involving ever more states in joint nuclear missions and expanded, now even advanced, deterrence schemes, we again note that this process fully fits within the logic of the aforementioned approach. More importantly, the “peace through force” concept is in sharp contradiction with the rapidly accelerating and now irreversible process of the emergence of a multipolar world order. Western states collectively, fearing the loss of their leadership and dominant position in the world, strive to preserve it by any means. When political and economic measures fail, they repeatedly resort to the tried‑and‑true method of creating a real military threat to their global competitors, backed by continuous modernization and unrestricted buildup of military potential, developing new means and methods of warfare.
Thus they bet on overwhelming military superiority, which requires mastering and implementing the most advanced scientific‑technical achievements. This is precisely what the United States and its closest allies are doing now. After all, the practice of joint nuclear missions, and indeed the rehearsal of any other combat systems, is no longer carried out with outdated technology or the old algorithms and tactics developed in the 1950s and 60s. It is executed at a completely new technological level that would guarantee indisputable advantages both on the local theater of operations and in large‑scale conflicts.
The drive to obtain overwhelming military advantage largely through the modernization and scaling of nuclear potential – in which NATO states are involved – leads to a breach of strategic balance and creates risks and threats to our country’s defense and security. Accelerated Western implementation of such nuclear plans, with active assistance from allies, will bring about the most severe consequences in the military‑political and strategic spheres. One such consequence could be a new arms race, not limited to nuclear weapons.
RT: What could Russia’s potential response to such actions look like?
Andrey Belousov: Regarding countermeasures, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s statement on the expiry of the New START Treaty on February fourth unambiguously notes that the parties to the treaty are free to decide on subsequent steps. Yet, our country intends to act responsibly and prudently, charting its line on strategic offensive arms based on a thorough analysis of the overall situation – the analysis of US military policy and the overall strategic environment – which, among other things, includes the actions of American allies.
We are talking about a combination of political‑diplomatic and military‑technical compensatory measures aimed at maintaining strategic balance and mitigating potential additional threats to Russia’s military security.

Moroccan lawyers refuse to call off strike over reforms
Moroccan lawyers announced Friday no let-up in a long-running strike over judicial reforms that have left many litigants without legal representation in court.
Members of Morocco's Association of Bar Associations went on strike on June 15 in protest at the changes, which they say undermine the independence of lawyers.
The reforms, championed by Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi, who is also a lawyer, envisage a thorough overhaul of the profession, including training, financial management and internal governance.
The associations said after a marathon meeting held on Thursday that they would keep up the strike action to force the law to be annulled "in order to defend the independence of the profession, the immunity of the defence, and its organisational autonomy".
As a result, it would "continue the total suspension of the provision of professional services", it added.
Moroccan lawyers staged an intermittent strike and a national protest in February.
Tensions eased after the government decided to set up a joint commission to look at the reform proposals but the adoption of the text in a parliamentary committee in mid-May reignited tensions.
The law was eventually passed by parliament.

'I am sure of myself': A look back at Dolly Parton's unspoken feminist legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:57:29 UTC
00:57:29 KST

'I am sure of myself': A look back at Dolly Parton's unspoken feminist legacy
Beloved country star Dolly Parton was many things to her fans, including an actor, singer, philanthropist and entrepreneur. But after her death on Tuesday at the age of 80, some admirers are remembering her as something she never overtly claimed: feminist icon.
Twelve "Women of the Year" are pictured smiling on the January 1987 cover of "Ms." magazine, co-founded by feminist pioneer Gloria Steinem. They include a US senator, a renowned novelist, a former nun who helped Central American refugees and, smiling brightest of all, Dolly Parton.
The beloved country superstar, who died this week at 80, never embraced the feminist label. She eschewed it when asked, just as she carefully avoided political labels.
But when Parton was building her groundbreaking career in music, more telling were Parton’s life choices, social alliances and especially her lyrics – words that made clear how fiercely independent the woman beneath the wig and rhinestones truly was, and what she believed in.
“People who haven’t listened to Dolly Parton or to feminism may be surprised to learn that they go together,” Steinem wrote in that 1987 magazine issue. “She has used her business sense to bring other women and poor people along with her. And her flamboyant style has turned all the devalued symbols of women to her own ends.”
“If feminism means each of us finding our unique power, and helping other women to do the same,” Steinem wrote, “Dolly Parton certainly has done both.”
Parton may not have claimed to be a feminist, but her female fans claim her as an icon with pride and affection.
“She didn’t tell us she was a feminist,” says Lynn Melnick, author of “I’ve Had to Think Up a Way to Survive: On Trauma, Persistence, and Dolly Parton”.
“She showed us – in her actions and her words and in her songs. And I think that’s why people loved her so much.”
At the Newport Folk Festival in 2019, a cheeky Parton, then in her early 70s, drew delighted cheers when she sang lyrics skewering double standards: “My mistakes are no worse than yours just because I’m a woman.”
Parton had just explained to the crowd that the song was a reference to a frank conversation she’d had with her husband soon after marriage, when he asked if she’d been with other men.
“When you boys get married you want us to be just as pure as snow – well, sometimes we’re not!” she told the crowd. “This is for you, gals, and your boys just gotta take it, OK?”
The remarks were vintage Parton, making a point without alienating anyone. She was, after all, about relatability.
“One thing about Dolly is that no matter what side of the political spectrum you’re on, you think she’s with you,” Melnick says.
“Everyone claims her. And so as a feminist I always thought, well, obviously she’s a feminist, and the more I read about her and wrote about her, it was just undeniable – first of all because of how she lived her life completely on her own terms.”
She and Carl Dean met in 1964 and were married for nearly 60 years. But they both gave each other a lot of space and freedom to live their own lives. After she convinced Dean to attend an awards show early on in her career, they both quickly realized it was just not his thing.
"He said, 'Look, now I want you to do everything you want to do and I wish you the best, but don't ever ask me to go to another one of these damn things 'cause I ain't going,'" Parton recalled.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Read moreEmbraced across divides, Dolly Parton leaves a lasting legacy
To music writer Evelyn McDonnell, Parton’s looks – the eyelashes, the big hair, the curves – served as an invisible cloak, helping her freely express progressive feminist views while leaning into the ultra-feminine.
“She took the objectification of being a pop star and embraced it,” says McDonnell, editor of the music anthology “Women Who Rock” and a professor at Loyola Marymount University. “It was like her magic cloak – she could be saying feminist things and doing feminist things and modelling a life and a voice that was outspoken, progressive, political. But you saw the package and you’re like, ‘Oh, okay.’ It made it safe.”
“She knew she was blonde and pretty, and that it was always going to work against her,” says music writer Caryn Rose. “So she figured out how to make it work FOR her. There's not anything more feminist than that.”
McDonnell says Parton’s values are clear from songs like “9 to 5”, which she wrote for the movie in which she starred with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda about a tyrannical boss who made a sport out of sexual harassment.
“It’s all about feminism, right? About women in the workplace, economic empowerment, pushing back against the male supervisor, uniting women’s voices,” she says.
Equal pay was just one of the issues Parton wrote about. She also, Melnick notes, addressed reproductive justice, teen pregnancy and "all of these very feminist issues ... she was just doing the work quietly, in her songs”.
One such song was “The Bargain Store", from 1975. “I may have just what you’re looking for, if you don’t mind the fact that all the merchandise is used," Parton wrote. “But with a little mending, it could be as good as new.”
Parton said later that country radio shunned the song because they took it to be about prostitution, when it was really about healing after a relationship.
Then there was “Down from Dover,” about a teenage single mother. “I wrote that back during a time when people didn’t talk about unwed mothers,” Parton told Vulture in 2023. “They wouldn’t play that on the radio.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Melnick posits that Parton exemplified so-called third-wave feminism, which gained currency in the ’90s with a focus on individual choice. A feminism where one could wear big heels, big hair and sparkly rhinestones.
And that’s exactly how Parton framed her looks in a 1977 interview with Barbara Walters: “It's certainly a choice.”
Parton said later that people had warned her against talking to Walters, who they said would chew her up and spit her out.
But a 31-year-old Parton, with quiet confidence and a generous smile, emerged looking far better than her interlocutor, who relied largely on sexist assumptions.
Walters asked if she was faithful to her husband, and why she was even married if she was constantly travelling. She even asked Parton if her famous breasts were real – saying an assistant wanted to know.
Walters then asked Parton to stand up and display her body. She did so, politely.
"But do you ever feel that you're a joke?" Walters asked.
Parton easily explained why she was comfortable with the jokes about her – because she was, in fact, in on them.
"Oh, I know they make fun of me, but actually, all these years, the people have thought that the joke was on me, but it's actually been on the public," she said.
“I know exactly what I am doing and I can change it at any time,” Parton added.
“I make more jokes about myself than anybody ... I am sure of myself as a person and I am sure of my talent. I am very content. So I can afford to diddle around with makeup and clothes and stuff because I am secure with myself.”
And what could be more feminist than that?
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

The pace of forest fires in Algeria slowed Saturday as firefighting operations continued in several provinces and major solidarity convoys headed toward affected areas, particularly the eastern province of Jijel.
The Civil Protection Authority said in a statement that 123 fires were recorded between Aug. 28 and 29 as of 7 a.m. local time (0600GMT), of which 118 had been extinguished while five remained active.
Two of the ongoing fires were in Jijel, two in Setif and one in Tebessa, according to the statement.
In Jijel, civil protection teams continued efforts to extinguish a forest fire in the Mechta El-Maissa area of Texenna municipality.
Several families were evacuated from their homes as a precaution before the flames were brought under control and residents were allowed to return, while firefighting operations remained underway.
The authority deployed two AT-802 aircraft to support firefighting crews in Jijel.
Local media reported that the authority mobilized 19,000 personnel to battle the fires across Algeria’s eastern provinces.
Funerals for wildfire victims began Friday in Jijel, with a collective burial held at Dar al-Baqaa cemetery in Beni Habibi municipality. Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb and several government ministers attended the ceremony.
Authorities also launched a search Friday for missing people in the Djemaa Beni Habibi municipality, according to the provincial civil protection authority.
As firefighting and search efforts continued, Algerians organized large solidarity convoys to deliver assistance to fire-hit areas, particularly Jijel, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
The convoys departed from several provinces carrying food, bedding and other essential supplies for affected residents.
Jijel authorities, meanwhile, began assessing material damage caused by the fires ahead of compensation for those affected.
Algerian Interior Minister Said Sayoud said Wednesday that 12 people had been killed in the wave of fires across several eastern provinces, according to local media.

Russia extends diesel export ban after record strikes on oil refineries
The Russian government has extended until 30 September a ban preventing direct producers from exporting diesel, marine fuel and gasoil amid record numbers of Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries.
Source: the Russian government, as reported by Bloomberg
Details: The government said the measure is necessary to maintain stability in the domestic fuel market.
Ukraine has attacked Russian oil refineries at least 21 times since the beginning of August. This is the highest number of strikes in a single month since the start of the full-scale war. The attacks have triggered a new wave of petrol shortages across Russian regions.
Before the escalation in strikes, Russia accounted for around 10% of global diesel supplies. Extending the ban will further squeeze global supply, which is already strained by the war in the Middle East.
US diesel inventories have fallen to their lowest seasonal level on record. Faced with fuel shortages, Europe has begun importing diesel from Mexico for the first time in seven years.
Russia introduced the restrictions in early July as a temporary measure and subsequently extended them until the end of August. The ban does not apply to supplies under intergovernmental agreements or humanitarian aid.
Background:
- At the end of August, petrol production in Russia fell to 70% of the usual summer consumption levels.
- Ukrainian strikes have knocked out over 30% of Russia's actual oil refining capacity.

Israeli settlers stage new attack on home in West Bank's Qusra, witnesses say
QUSRA, West Bank, Aug 29 - Dozens of masked Israeli settler militants attacked homes surrounding the occupied West Bank village of Qusra on Saturday, the first major attack since a siege by settlers in the area earlier this month drew an international outcry.
The settlers surrounded a Palestinian home, throwing stones while seven Palestinians were trapped inside, according to witnesses who spoke to Reuters.
Saddam Oday, one of those trapped, said the Israeli military fired tear gas into the home and detained the residents inside while letting him go. He said the Israeli military had not detained any of the settlers and had allowed them to leave.
The owner of the house, Luay Bayruti, said when the military arrived they handcuffed, blindfolded and beat those inside, before later releasing them.
The Israeli military said in a statement that troops and border police forces had arrived on the scene to remove "rioters" and protect the residents inside the house.
The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why they had reportedly fired tear gas at the house and detained and beaten the residents.
In his first public statement on Qusra, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence in Qusra and blamed a "handful of rioters".
"I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud," said Netanyahu, referring to a separate incident in a neighbouring village.
The United States had previously pressured Netanyahu to publicly condemn the militant settlers who had besieged Palestinians in their homes, U.S. and Israeli officials told Reuters around two weeks ago.
The Israeli government has previously blamed a "fringe minority" for settler violence, a characterisation disputed by findings from rights groups.
A U.N. inquiry in June found that Israeli authorities are directly involved in settler attacks that have killed, injured and displaced Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. The Israeli mission in Geneva rejected the report's findings.
RESIDENT REPORTS NEAR-DAILY ENCROACHMENTS
Bayruti said that after calling the Israeli military for help, he and six others were trapped inside the home for more than an hour as settlers threw stones.
Bayruti showed a Reuters reporter his bandaged arm, which he said had been injured by a stone during the attack.
Oday, a medic, said four of those trapped had suffered injuries due to the tear gas, and two had suffered injuries from the stones thrown by settlers.
The attack occurred a few hundred yards away from three homes to which settlers laid siege this month, drawing international condemnation and a massive Israeli military deployment that residents say has kept them effectively trapped in their homes.
"They spotted the residents working on their house, which is still under construction and they started throwing rocks," said Loui Ridi, a Palestinian-American whose home was one of the three under siege this month. He said he watched Saturday's attack occur from his home.
Ridi said he had seen near-daily encroachments of Israeli settlers into the area surrounding his home, despite the heavy Israeli military presence in the area.
SETTLER VIOLENCE ON THE RISE
Rights groups say the increasing settler presence on the edge of Palestinian villages, like Qusra, is part of a wider effort by settlers to seize more land from Palestinians, further eating into territory where Palestinians aim to establish a state.
Violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank has increased, with some emboldened by the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a massive settlement expansion in the territory.
U.N. bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the area as disputed rather than occupied. REUTERS

Following the withdrawal of international technology corporations like Apple, Samsung, Intel, and Asus during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, DNS became a primary channel for supplying gray-market and parallel-import goods from China into the Russian market.
On August 24, 2026, Ukrainian strike drones targeted three major Ozon logistics centers across southern Russia, igniting large fires at facilities with a combined warehouse area of over 314,000 square meters.
The strikes formed part of a broader overnight operation in which Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces engaged 66 Russian military targets deep behind enemy lines, including a MiG-29 fighter jet in the Rostov region, four radar systems, and two shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea.
Among the targeted marketplace hubs were large distribution centers in Dagestan, Stavropol, and Adygea, which serve as critical nodes in Russia's e-commerce supply network.

At least 37 killed after Russian strike hits an ammunition depot near Kyiv, triggering massive explosions. Many of the victims were residents of a nearby care home.
The Russian army struck the village of Myla on the outskirts of Kyiv on the evening of August 28, setting fire to a warehouse where ammunition was being stored. The fire triggered a series of detonations, sending flames into nearby private homes. The explosions were powerful enough that authorities shut down traffic entirely on the Zhytomyr highway between the 15th and 32nd kilometer markers. Nearly 400 people were evacuated from the area affected by the strike.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said Saturday morning that at least 27 people had been killed in the Russian strike on Myla, in Kyiv region’s Bucha district. Another 42 people, including four children, were injured to varying degrees. Among the dead was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community in the Kyiv region, who had been helping rescue people from the fire.
Update. As of 2:00 p.m. Saturday, 37 people are known to have died in the Russian strike, Tymur Tkachenko wrote.
About 50 residential buildings were damaged. The heaviest damage was to a nearby care home for elderly and disabled residents, where 20 people died, according to local social media pages.
Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the care home had been damaged. “Those who allowed this must certainly bear responsibility for their decisions. Investigators from the National Police and the Security Service of Ukraine are conducting a pretrial investigation, and a criminal case has been opened over official negligence. There are rules: ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential buildings. There will definitely be appropriate conclusions,” the president of Ukraine said.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi called what happened in the Bucha district the result of “criminal negligence,” recalling the “terrible tragedy in Vyshneve,” which he said “did not serve as a lesson.” Russian forces struck a Ukroboronprom warehouse in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July. The resulting detonation damaged 300 residential buildings and killed nine people.
The Kyiv region declared August 30 a day of mourning for those killed in the Russian strike.
Russia’s Defense Ministry stated that its drones struck an ammunition warehouse belonging to the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point in the village of Myla, where components for FP-1/FP-2 UAVs were stored. The ministry also claimed that overnight on August 29, Russian troops struck logistics centers in the villages of Chaiky and Kalynivka near Kyiv, where components for Ukrainian “Flamingo” cruise missiles were stored as well, among other things.

Late on August 4, a UAV carrying an improvised explosive device was found on the grounds of Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft. The device’s detonator failed to activate. That same night, a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane.
Ten days later, investigators reportedly found a third UAV, along with traces of a powerful explosive believed to be approximately 50 grams of hexogen. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incidents as a "hybrid attack scenario" and did not rule out the involvement of "foreign states." 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries invited to youth festival in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:38:56 UTC
00:38:56 KST

10,000 young leaders from 191 countries invited to youth festival in Russia
Organizers of the International Youth Festival have completed the selection process for participants in this year’s event, which will take place in Yekaterinburg, Russia, from September 11 to 17, 2026.
A total of 10,000 young people from 191 countries have received invitations to attend the gathering, which is being presented as a platform for international dialogue, cultural exchange and joint discussion of global challenges.
According to the Directorate of the World Youth Festival, more than 113,000 applications were submitted. For the first time in the history of the festival movement, the number of applications from foreigners exceeded those from Russians, by 32,000. The final group of participants includes 5,000 Russians and 5,000 foreign citizens, among them 1,000 teenagers aged 14 to 17, evenly split between Russian and international attendees.
“Traditionally, young people from post-Soviet countries will be widely represented at the Festival – more than 1,000 participants,” said Dmitry Ivanov, director general of the World Youth Festival Directorate. “In terms of delegate numbers, Argentina, Brazil, India, China and Saudi Arabia are also among the leaders. Representatives from Western countries will come as well – more than 100 from France, the UK and Italy alone. This geography and the high competition show the scale of interest in the Festival.”
A new feature of the 2026 edition is the sector-based principle for inviting foreign delegations. Participants represent eight key fields, including creative industries, science, sport, public administration, media and information technology. Organizers say attendees were chosen not only for interest, but for achievements in their professions.
Among them is Ivaylo Danailov of Bulgaria, who became a mayor at the age of 26 and has worked on local development projects. “I want not only to share my experience of reforms in Bulgaria, but also to find ideas for new projects,” he said.
Another participant, Christian Bahati of the Republic of the Congo, runs a major mining company and founded a charitable organization in 2019 to support poor communities in neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. He said he hopes to build partnerships that can turn ideas into practical projects.
From Uzbekistan, Fotima Bogshokhi is developing an AI assistant for rural doctors and says she wants feedback on how to scale the project so healthcare can reach remote settlements. Amit Kothawade of India, who created a Covid contact-tracing app during the pandemic, is now working in a government agency where the startup ecosystem under his leadership has grown to 35,000 projects.
The event will also include bloggers and social media creators. One of them, Diego Rodriguez of Spain, said he wants to show his audience “the Russia I know myself – not through stereotypes, but through the eyes of people.”
Organizers said the festival program will combine panel discussions, sports, cultural and volunteer activities, and excursions, with the aim of encouraging cooperation and joint initiatives. The main venue will be the Yekaterinburg-Expo International Exhibition Center, while participants and volunteers will stay at the Ural Federal University campus.
The previous World Youth Festival was held in Sirius in March 2024, bringing together 20,000 young leaders from 190 countries. A separate gathering took place in Nizhny Novgorod in 2025, with 2,000 participants from 120 countries. Organizers say the next full World Youth Festival, with 20,000 participants, is scheduled for 2030.

Modi lands in Uzbekistan en route to Russia-Asia summit
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted pictures of himself and Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to social media on Saturday, thanking his political counterpart for the warm welcome and writing on X: "Landed in Tashkent to a warm welcome by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Kolkata Police file First Information Report against former West Bengal Chief Minister Banerjee
Kolkata Police on Saturday registered a First Information Report (FIR) against former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee for allegedly violating a Calcutta High Court order on a students' wing rally held on Friday.
A FIR is written document informing police of a crime and gives the authorities necessary information to launch an investigation.
Several Indian media outlets reported on the FIR. A Hindustan Times report said that the city's high court had permitted Banerjee to celebrate the foundation day of her party's youth wing on Cathedral Road in central Kolkata but had directed that one side of the road be kept operational.
Local police said that the flank was not left open and the court-specified time-limit was exceeded.
The FIR was filed against Banerjee and organizers of the rally, officers quoted by news agency Press Trust of India said.
"The FIR has been registered for the alleged violation of the court's order. The role of all those involved in the violation will be examined during the course of the investigation," the officer said.
The police also claimed the student wing supporters "breached barricades and jostled with police personnel deployed for maintaining law and order," PTI reported.
Banerjee is the leader of the Trinamool Congress Party, a major regional party in the eastern state of West Bengal. She is the former chief minister of the state and was unseated earlier this year by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party — after 15 years in power.
Incidentally, at the rally, Banerjee had claimed that the police had turned into a "monstrous entity" under BJP rule and pledged to stop "police atrocities" on her supporters.
WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute
The fight over basmati rice has become one of the most complex disputes in the global food trade.
Both India and Pakistan claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and both are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.
But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the EU has yet to decide how the name should be protected and by whom.
Basmati is among the world's most valuable rice varieties, generating significant export revenues and carrying strong historical ties to the Punjab region, which spans both countries.
Meanwhile, experts warn that widespread misuse of the name on international markets could undermine future protection altogether. As Brussels weighs its options, the outcome could have far-reaching consequences.
Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir
Leaders of India's largest opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), alleged that publishing house Penguin India was pressured to back out of publishing veteran politician Sonia Gandhi's memoir due to portions related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist group, and China's alleged occupation of Indian territory under Modi's rule.
Sonia Gandhi has been a leading figure in Indian politics for decades. She was the president of the INC from 1998 to 2017 and is the party's longest-serving chief.
Earlier this month, Alfred A. Knopf announced that Gandhi's "Belonging: A Journey of Love" will be published on November 10. Knopf is a publishing imprint under Penguin Random House.
"Suppressing the book of Sonia Gandhi, a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former Leader of the Opposition, under pressure is tantamount to the murder of freedom of Expression," senior INC leader Ashok gehlot said in a post on X.
"The real issue is that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Modi, the RSS, and the occupation of Indian territory by China during Modi's rule. This is the murder of democracy," he said.
In another post, Gehlot said "there's some kind of pressure. It could be from the PMO [Prime Minister's Office] or someone else — that time will tell."
This comes a day after Penguin India released a statement of clarification: "Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish 'Belonging' because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances."
The statement was referring to a report by The Indian Express which said the publishing house would not publish the book in India because "editorial changes and deletions" were turned down by the author.
"As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in best interests of their books," Penguin India said in its statement, adding that it "remained willing and keen to publish the book."
India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster
Days after deadly flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through the Tibet-Nepal border, India stepped up monitoring of the glaciers in its Himalayan region bordering Nepal and China.
Although the exact cause of the collapse remains unclear, global warming has increased the likelihood of such disasters.
"Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbor, and also have a similar geographic situation... we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region," said Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India's Himalayan state of Uttarakhand.
"We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state," he added.
Kaushik's state is one of India's most ecologically sensitive regions with over 1,266 glacial lakes.
Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC
Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of a controversial right-wing Hindu nationalist group in India closely associated with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is set to address about 5,000 members of Indian American groups in New York City on Saturday.
The event titled "Universal Oneness Celebration" is being held at the Infosys Theater in Madison Square Garden and is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.
It is being met with protests, a denunciation from the city's mayor Zohran Mamdani and a call for sanctions by a US panel on religious freedom.
Bhagwat's link with Modi
Bhagwat is the chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for "National Volunteer Organization."
The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus. It disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.
The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.
Why is the RSS controversial?
In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.
However, several interfaith and civil rights groups — including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York — have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history.
The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a government advisory body, has called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."
Recently, it called for the US government to impose targeted sanctions on RSS members, including Bhagwat, and Indian officials who support the group.
The Ministry of External Affairs in India quickly rejected the commission’s remarks, calling the body biased and lacking in credibility.
United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.
WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud
DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports from a village in Nepal's Nuwakot district that was buried in mud after severe flooding.
Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods
At least 320 Indian nationals were still unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet floods as of Friday evening, according to the latest update from India's foreign ministry.
A glacier collapse on Wednesday unleashed a huge torrentof rock, ice, mud and debris through Himalayan mountain river systems, killing more than 600 people in Nepal and China's Tibet. Over 2,000 people are missing.
Here's the latest update on Indian nationals:
- 84 Indian nationals have been rescued so far, including 21 from Tamil Nadu who have returned to India and 63 who were working at the Trishuli-I power project in Nepal
- 149 crossed over into Nepal from China
- Around 400 are safe in China, the Indian Embassy in Beijing is working on their evacuation
- 320 are missing or unreachable
Meanwhile, India dispatched a third flight carrying relief supplies to Nepal on Friday evening. The flight also carried an 11-member medical and tunnel rescue team, who are now working on the ground, according to India's Foreign Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.
Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi left for a state visit to Uzbekistan, where he is set to discuss ways of deepening cooperation with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
Ahead of departure, Modi said he looked forward to his discussions with the Uzbek president to "further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan."
"Viksit Bharat" roughly translates to "Developed India" and is a commonly used term by Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. "Yangi Uzbekistan" translates to "New Uzbekistan" and is a political slogan used by Mirziyoyev.
On Saturday, Modi will attend a dinner hosted by Mirziyoyev, followed by bilateral engagements with him on Sunday at the Presidential Palace.
After his two-day state visit to Uzbekistan, Modi will travel to the Kyrgyz Republic to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, where he is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with the Russian President, Vladimir Putin.

Leaders of Russia, China, Iran to attend summit in Kyrgyzstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:30:43 UTC
00:30:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Leaders of Russia, China, Iran to attend summit in Kyrgyzstan
Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia's Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran's and India's leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West.
Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow's Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India's Narendra Modi and Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran's Pezeshkian and China's Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran -- among the most sanctioned states in the world -- have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin's meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA's director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in recent years under Moscow's and Beijing's leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 "dialogue partners", including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO's founding declaration says the group is "not an alliance directed against other states".
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year's gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced "acts of intimidation", referring to US-Chinese tensions.
Real and trade wars
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars -- the Ukraine and Iran conflicts -- or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation, and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran's allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will "firmly defend" its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces "economic difficulties".
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran "believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions".
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as "in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties".
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world's population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia -- a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia -- while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Song Yadong scored the biggest win of his UFC career with a stunning second-round knockout of former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov in Shanghai on Saturday, while compatriot Yan Xiaonan suffered a first-round stoppage defeat to Brazil's Denise Gomes in the co-main event.
Sixth-ranked bantamweight Song (23-9-1, 1 NC) entered the fight as a sizeable underdog against No. 3 Nurmagomedov, whose only previous defeat came against then-champion Merab Dvalishvili.
In the first round, both men began cautiously, looking to launch their offense behind lead kicks. The tentative opening stanza changed when Nurmagomedov shot for a takedown and got Song's legs faster than the Chinese could sprawl.
However, Song was able to get back to his feet - no easy task against Nurmagomedov, after being taken down in the middle of the cage without spending much time on the ground, and without being in any danger.
The round ended with both men on their feet and remained relatively even, with Song perhaps landing the cleaner strikes.
In the second, Song successfully defended an early takedown attempt, much to the delight of the sold-out Oriental Sports Center. The pair began exchanging more freely on the feet, and Song started to shift the momentum in his favor.
Nurmagomedov shot again midway through the round, but Song was ready, stuffing the attempt before landing a hard right hand to the neck that dropped the Dagestani. Song then swarmed with a series of hammer fists to secure the knockout 1:48 into the round.
The victory puts Song firmly into bantamweight title contention and underlined the 28-year-old's development from a primarily striking-based fighter into a more complete mixed martial artist capable of dealing with Nurmagomedov's highly regarded wrestling.
In the co-main event, fourth-ranked Yan suffered a major setback to her hopes of another strawweight title challenge after being stopped by 14th-ranked Gomes.
Yan initially used her movement and side kicks to maintain distance, while both fighters landed hard shots. But Gomes found her way inside late in the opening round, dropping Yan with a sharp elbow before following up with punches that forced referee Herb Dean to stop the contest.
The victory is the biggest of the 26-year-old Brazilian's career and should propel her toward the top of the division, while leaving 37-year-old Yan with a difficult route back to title contention.
Former RIZIN bantamweight champion Kai Asakura continued his resurgence since moving back up from flyweight with a second-round stoppage of China's Aoriqileng.
After a measured opening round, Asakura increased the variety and pace of his striking in the second, rocking Aoriqileng with a head kick before finishing the fight with punches.
China's Sumudaerji earned a unanimous decision over 11th-ranked Alex Perez in their flyweight rematch after their first meeting in Macao, China, in May ended in a no contest.
Perez found repeated success with his wrestling through the opening two rounds, but Sumudaerji's takedown defense improved sharply in the third as he landed the cleaner strikes from range and attacked with knees and elbows in the clinch to secure a 29-28 verdict from all three judges.
Chinese light heavyweight Liu Ce made an explosive UFC debut with a first-round knockout of Brazil's Levi Rodrigues Jr.
The former K-1 kickboxing champion traded heavy shots with Rodrigues before gradually taking control of the exchanges, eventually landing a devastating overhand right late in the round to end the contest.
In the main-card opener, Indonesia's Bilal Hasan remained unbeaten with a second-round knockout of Peru's Nilson Rojas. Rojas showed resilience after a difficult opening round, but Hasan's superior speed ultimately told, with a perfectly timed straight right ending the fight in the second. Alongside Song, Hasan was awarded a Performance of the Night bonus.
On the preliminary card, China's Ding Meng dropped a 29-28 decision to Canada's Cameron Nelson after being controlled on the ground for much of the opening two rounds, despite rallying with improved takedown defense and cleaner striking in the third.
Xiong Jingnan suffered a first-round head-kick knockout loss to Brazil's Julia Polastri, while Lawrence Lui and China's Xiao Long were both stopped by strikes.
Sean Woodson edged Jack Jenkins by split decision before Japan's Rei Tsuruya dominated Kevin Borjas on the ground to secure a first-round rear-naked choke.
In the featured prelim, Andre Lima submitted Namsrai Batbayar with a guillotine after countering a takedown attempt. ■

China Focus: Rescuers still combing mudslide-stricken Gyirong Port for survivors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:26:33 CST
00:26:33 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- "Is anyone there?" Rescuers crouched down together and called out in unison every few meters, as they picked their way through mud, boulders and chunks of rock.
Since Saturday morning, the members of the Sichuan provincial fire and rescue corps of the China Search and Rescue team have been carrying out a sweeping search in key areas at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The team has been searching the heart of the disaster zone, with torrents of muddy water still surging in the nearby waterway. They sifted through piles of rocks and picked through what appeared to be the wreckage of a vehicle, as seen in Xinhua video footage.
A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, has left seven people dead and 554 others missing at Gyirong Port in Xizang on the China-Nepal border.
RELENTLESS SEARCH, ROAD RESTORATION
China immediately sent professional rescuers, firefighters and military forces to the site to search for survivors. A total of 2,141 rescuers have joined the mission, according to the update by the region's emergency management department on early Saturday morning.
Fire and rescue personnel approached the hard-hit border gate on three fronts: by rubber boats on waterways; on foot through mountainous terrain; and conducting aerial reconnaissance and supply drops via drones.
Rescuers at the site are conducting the search while guarding against falling rocks and potential breaches of a barrier lake formed after the mudslide. Excavators were busy repairing a key road to facilitate entry into the port. A total length of 2.6 km of road section had been restored, leaving 1.7 kilometers to go before reaching Gyirong Port by around 1 p.m. Saturday.
Earlier on Saturday, drones were seen delivering supplies to rescuers already stationed in the core disaster area, launched from a supply zone three kilometers away from the mudslide-hit port.
Huo Jianxin, a member of the advance group from the China Search and Rescue team, told Xinhua on Friday night that the team would deploy drones, search dogs and life-sign detectors in search operations. The team reached the core disaster zone on Friday afternoon.
"After we saw the situation here upon arrival, my team and I had just one hope: as long as there is even the slightest chance of finding survivors, we will never give up," Huo said.
Rescuers say operations remain challenging due to the harsh terrain, the risk of secondary disasters, damaged roads and disrupted communications.
Local authorities have warned that a barrier lake, formed upstream of the port, sits in an unstable geological setting and could breach, endangering rescue operations downstream.
The mudslide has destroyed a section of the G216, a national highway leading to the port, seriously hampering emergency response and rescue efforts.
China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, deployed 60 technical and skilled personnel and mobilized 14 pieces of engineering rescue equipment, including excavators and loaders, to try to reopen the damaged section of G216.
As an important channel for China-Nepal border trade and a national first-class land port, Gyirong Port normally sees bustling commercial activity, a dense population and extensive infrastructure.
The disaster struck during daytime working hours, when crowds of people were present at the port, a factor rescuers said might have contributed to the heavy casualties.
"COMPLETELY DESTROYED"
Rescuers who reached the border gate area described the sight as devastating, as the mudslide that crushed down at terrifying speed from a high-altitude glacier left barely any structure standing.
"When we arrived, all we could see at first was mud. The ground was so soft that it was impossible to walk on," said Yin Wei, a firefighter from Gyirong County.
Yin said the border gate area was completely destroyed. The river was littered with vehicle wreckage and clothing washed down probably from upstream settlements, he recalled.
Lai Jun, another firefighter from Gyirong County, said the severity of the disaster went beyond their expectation.
"Images sent back by our drone show there was nothing left standing, not a single building. It was devastating. We kept searching for the border gate we hoped to reach, but it was gone," he said.
On Thursday morning, when a Xinhua reporting team reached a hilltop overlooking the barrier lake, a low, steady rumble filled the air.
"That's not the sound of water," a rescue expert explained. "It's rocks falling from both sides of the barrier lake and crashing down the slopes."
Xinhua video reporter Huang Zhiqi then began a live broadcast from a relatively flat ground on the hilltop. Two hours into the broadcast, just as it ended, a rescuer suddenly shouted, "Pull back! Pull back now! The landslide across the valley is intensifying."
"Abandon the vehicle! Head for the ridge!" another rescuer yelled, grabbing Huang and running uphill.
Dust billowed across the slope, thick and gray, shrouding the mountain. "That's when it really hit me that I was on the front line," Huang said. ■
