EU enters ‘winter panic’ mode as gas storage hits record low – Guardian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:26:04 UTC
00:26:04 KST

EU enters ‘winter panic’ mode as gas storage hits record low – Guardian
EU gas storage is now at one of the lowest seasonal levels on record, with the shortfall feeding a “winter panic” among traders amid the Iran war and Brussels’s continued push to phase out Russian energy, according to The Guardian.
EU gas stocks are at around 64% as of Friday, far below the 80% average maintained during this season over the past several years, according to the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
For comparison, EU stocks were at about 66% on August 29, 2021, and around 72% on the same date in 2013, although the fill level typically drops much lower in winter months when consumption is high.
As for the country breakdown, German gas storage is only slightly above 50% capacity, while the Netherlands is at around 45% and Belgium around 50%, according to recent GIE readings.
Officials in the Netherlands in particular have complained that they expect to miss their planned winter targets, and are blaming sluggish injections and poor commercial incentives for traders to buy gas now and store it for winter.
Meanwhile, the UK’s facilities are only at around 30% capacity, although the country has historically relied more on continuous imports than storage.
Amid the crunch, natural gas prices have risen above €66 ($76) per megawatt-hour, more than double from levels earlier in the year, according to the Trading Economics website.
Speaking to The Guardian, Bjarne Schieldrop, chief commodities analyst at SEB, remarked that the market had “stayed relatively calm” this summer, hoping that the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will normalize.
However, now “no one expects it to happen any time soon,” he said, adding: “As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week.”
The weak storage position leaves the market more exposed to cold weather, low wind generation and unforeseen supply disruptions. Gas analyst Greg Molnar told the paper that “low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility.”
The immediate pressure comes from the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz that disrupted Qatari LNG exports. While Qatar supplied only 6.6% of LNG to the EU in the first quarter of 2026 – compared to the 57% supplied by the US – the Middle East conflict has intensified competition between European and Asian buyers for energy, prompting a rally in gas prices.
The shortfall also comes as the EU maintains sweeping sanctions on Moscow and has vowed to wean itself of Russian energy. While Russia provided around 45% of EU gas imports in 2021, its share had dropped to only about 12% by 2025.
After the EU imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia in 2022, it endured one of the worst energy crises in decades. Gas prices exploded to more than €300 per megawatt-hour, hitting industry and consumers alike, with EU countries reeling from soaring inflation and costs of living.
When the EU began cutting its dependence on oil and gas from Russia following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova suggested that the bloc was on a “suicidal” course and was “shooting itself in the head.”

It added that between 2,500 and 3,000 people may have been subjected to forced disappearance in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war.
The centre’s estimate is based on an analytical study of a sample of 317 cases, and it said the findings showed indicators warranting an investigation into the possibility of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances.
Of the 317 cases examined, 302, or 95.27 percent, were male and 15 were female. The sample included 41 children and 17 people aged 60 or older.
Since Israel’s war began in October 2023, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and more than 174,000 injured, most of them women and children.

James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.
The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.
The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead the Conservatives to Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”
He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success in London,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”
Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.
According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.
Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.
Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028. Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.
If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.
Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.
“Sadiq has been trying to get out of that job for quite a while. He went in with the intention of doing what Boris [Johnson] did, using it as a high-profile platform to get him his next big job in government. There has been lots of posturing, very little delivery. Lots of picking rows with the president of America, less focus on bringing down street crime. It wouldn’t surprise me if he bows out for 2028. He’s lost the passion for the job.”
Days before Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister, he handed Khan a peerage, potentially opening the door to him joining Andy Burnham’s cabinet in future. However, while Burnham and Khan have worked closely together over the years and have a shared understanding of the challenges of devolution, it is understood Khan has told the former Manchester mayor that he has no wish to be a minister in his government.

Iceland's EU referendum sees high preliminary voter turnout in expected close race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:24:35 UTC
00:24:35 KST

In Reykjavík, voter turnout was higher by noon than at the same time during the 2024 parliamentary election, local media reported.
Iceland's capital Reykjavík recorded a higher voter turnout in the high-stakes EU referendum by noon than at the same time during the country's parliamentary elections in 2024, preliminary figures showed on Saturday.
In the hours after voters began casting their ballots in the referendum that will determine whether to reopen EU accession talks, 13.7% had voted by noon in the Reykjavík North constituency, compared to just over 10% in the 2024 election.
In Reykjavík South, just over 14% had voted by noon, compared to just over 11% for the parliamentary election.
More than 20% of voters cast early ballots in advance of election day, Iceland’s national broadcaster RÚV said.
A close race is expected, with a final poll on Friday indicating 50.4% of voters plan to vote yes and 49.6% no.
Backers of EU membership say it’s best for Iceland to get closer to its European neighbours to combat issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change. They also say the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna currency.
Opponents say the current setup is just right and that Iceland already enjoys all the benefits of European integration without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They cite trade deals, such as one with China, that are more favourable.
"I think that we should be a part of a bigger unity. I think it's worth looking into it," Unnur Jokulsdottir, a 71-year-old retiree, said after casting her ballot in Reykjavík's City Hall.
In contrast, Olafur Thorsson, a 53-year-old fish trader, said he was sceptical.
"I used to like the European Union back when it was a good thing. But today it's become a sort of big economic prison," he said.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
A yes vote would trigger renewed negotiations with the European Commission covering 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.
The issue of fisheries — a pillar of Iceland's economy and over which Reykjavík wants to retain exclusive control — would have to be hammered out with Brussels, which this time around appears more willing to compromise.
On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.
Trump's unpredictability and his threats to take over neighbouring Greenland — which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions — have added to Icelanders' concerns.
Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.
The result of the vote will be followed closely by the EU, which has not welcomed a wealthy, net contributor to its budget since 1995.

Germany's Merz plans to blame Russia for drone incident in Leipzig
Politico has learned that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is preparing to hold Russia responsible for a recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and respond with sanctions.
Source: Politico, a Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation, citing its sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Politico notes that Merz plans to blame Russia for the appearance of a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig airport and respond with sanctions, in parallel with the EU's preparations for its next sanctions package.
The announcement is reportedly planned for the beginning of next week to coincide with a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council in Ireland, although it could come earlier if the chancellor decides.
Two of the sources cited by Politico compared Berlin's upcoming announcements to Zeitenwende 2.0 – the major change in Germany's defence policy announced by former Chancellor Olaf Scholz in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to one source, the German government believes that expelling individual Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power in Berlin would no longer be an adequate response to the Leipzig drone incident. Berlin believes the response should involve significantly tougher sanctions or further increases in military assistance to Ukraine.
Merz said on 25 August that there would be serious consequences for the incident in Leipzig, but he did not name those responsible.
In response to an official request for comment on these plans, the German government said it "does not engage in speculation".
"The only thing that matters is the official attribution made by the federal government at its own discretion and after weighing all the results of the investigation," the spokesperson said.
Background:
- On 4 August, a drone fitted with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft that was being used to transport military equipment.
- According to media reports, the German security authorities have almost no doubt that Moscow was behind the incident.
- US intelligence has linked the incident to Russia. The Russian Embassy in Berlin called the Leipzig incident a fabricated provocation.

Lessons from Bhutan’s pursuit of happiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:13:15 UTC
00:13:15 KST

There are destinations that specialize in scenery, while others are all about culture and history. Few places offer all of these together, with a touch of something deeper. These are places that cause the traveler to step outside the familiar, to observe the world and life from a different angle, and to return home with new thoughts, wonderings, and questions. Bhutan is exactly such a place.
Bhutan is a small kingdom in the heart of the Himalayan mountains, sandwiched between India and China, and one of the most unique countries I have ever visited.
Getting there from Israel requires a bit of planning, as there are no direct flights. Israeli travelers typically fly to a major Asian hub – most commonly New Delhi or Bangkok – and connect to one of Bhutan’s two official airlines, Drukair or Bhutan Airlines, which fly directly into Paro.
The experience begins in the moments before landing in Paro, as the plane maneuvers between the high mountains surrounding the valley. Paro Airport is considered one of the most challenging in the world for landing, and pilots require special training and deep familiarity with the terrain. Landing takes place under restricted conditions and hours, and in recent years, the number of pilots certified to operate at the field remains very limited.
And then you land and discover a place where life moves at a different pace.
'High Value, Low Volume' tourism model
Bhutan opened to international tourism in the mid-1970s, and unlike conventional tourist destinations, it chose a model that does not prioritize quantity. Instead of mass tourism, it promotes the principle of “High Value, Low Volume” tourism on a limited scale, designed to preserve the local culture, nature, and lifestyle. Part of this model is a government fee imposed on tourists, aimed, among other things, at supporting sustainable development and preserving the kingdom’s character.
While many believe that an organized group tour is the only way to visit, Bhutan’s tourism policy has evolved. You can visit either by joining a pre-packaged organized group tour or as an independent traveler using a licensed local agency to customize your itinerary.
Whichever route you choose, you cannot simply backpack on your own: all tourists must pay Bhutan’s mandatory Sustainable Development Fee of $100 per night, possess an officially approved visa clearance letter before arrival, and be accompanied by a licensed Bhutanese guide throughout the journey.
But what made Bhutan famous worldwide is not just its tourism model, but the concept of happiness.
In the 1970s, the fourth king of Bhutan conceived a unique principle known as gross national happiness (GNH), as opposed to gross national product (GNP). Instead of evaluating the country’s success solely through economic activity, Bhutan seeks to look at a broader question: how to improve the quality of life while preserving nature, culture, community, and spiritual heritage.
This view encompasses areas such as education, psychological well-being, environmental quality, health, culture, community, governance, and standard of living. The message is simple but profound: money is important, but it is not everything. The model recognizes the importance of basic material wealth and its contribution to quality of life, but argues that other metrics – such as community life, cultural heritage, nature, and inner peace – are equally important.
Happiness comes from impermanence
During the visit, I decided to ask a local person a simple question: “What is your secret?” How is it possible that a small country, relatively undeveloped and not wealthy by the standards we are used to, became so closely identified with happiness?
His answer was short. One word: “Impermanence.”
This word stayed with me, perhaps because it recalls a fact that the modern world tends to forget. Things change, nothing is permanent, and a significant part of the ability to be happy probably lies in the ability to accept life as it is, appreciate what you have, and moderate the urge to attain what you lack.
In the 19th century, Bhutan became a kingdom with the crowning of its first king. In 2008, during the reign of the fourth king, the country transitioned to a democratic constitutional monarchy, with elections and an elected government.
The royal family are still “present” almost everywhere – in conversations, decisions, billboards, and especially in the attitude of the Bhutanese toward them. King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck is highly respected by many residents and is perceived not only as a monarch but also as a unifying figure who is relatively close to the people.
One of the things that caught my attention in Thimphu, Bhutan’s largest city and capital, was actually something that does not exist there: traffic lights.
At the most central intersection in the city center, there is a small traffic island with a policeman directing traffic with elegant and precise hand movements. There was something charming and calming about this sight, standing in contrast to the modernity and automation found almost everywhere in the familiar Western world.
At the same time, Bhutan lacks the culture of giant mega-malls and international brands that characterizes many cities worldwide. Shopping centers consist of local markets, small arcades, shops, and stalls, in a style of commerce that reminded me in some ways of Israel in the 1950s and 60s.
Bhutan food culture
And then comes the food – and here, too, everything is a bit different.
In a traditional restaurant, we sat on the floor as part of the local custom. Tea was served even before the food – a local tea called Suja, which combines tea with salted yak butter. For someone used to tea with milk and sugar, or morning coffee, the taste was surprising. But for the Bhutanese, it is much more than a beverage: it is part of the hospitality culture and daily life, especially in the mountainous regions.
Among the other characteristic products I tasted were dried Bhutanese cheese, which has an intense flavor and a texture very different from the cheeses we know in Israel, as well as a salad where the main ingredient was hot chili peppers.
The traditional dress also tells the country’s story. Men wear a robe called a gho, and women wear a long, embroidered dress called a kira, featuring colors and patterns that blend seamlessly with the traditional architecture and the prominent presence of local Buddhism.
Buddhism in Bhutan is practically everywhere, not just in temples. It is present through monasteries, colorful prayer flags fluttering in the wind, art, architecture, and people’s relationship to nature and community.
In sacred places, visitors are asked to remove their shoes, refrain from photography, behave modestly and respectfully, speak softly, and even pay attention to how they sit. In the local culture, it is disrespectful to point the soles of your feet toward a holy statue, a person, or a monk. These are small gestures that together say a lot about a society where respect for tradition and others is part of daily life.
The colors in Bhutan are also not just a matter of aesthetics. The prayer flags flying everywhere come in five colors – blue, white, red, green, and yellow – which are linked to five elements and different dimensions of existence. Prayers and mantras are written on the flags, out of the belief that the wind will carry them forward.
Various symbols also express mythology and meaning, including the lotus flower and the Dharma wheel. You can encounter them in temples, buildings, traditional art, and various objects. They are not merely decorations, but a way to bring spirituality into everyday life.
Trail to the “Tiger’s Nest” monastery
One of the most meaningful personal moments for me in Bhutan was the climb to the “Tiger’s Nest” monastery (Paro Taktsang), arguably the site most identified with the country. The monastery hangs on a cliffside high above the Paro Valley, at 3,100 meters above sea level.
The trail to it is an integral part of the experience, featuring a mountain path, steep ascents, stairs, forests, and sections where you have no choice but to stop and catch your breath. The altitude, the continuous climb, and the stairs make the trek a true challenge.
I also set out on the climb, reaching an altitude of 2,900 meters, where I decided to stop and not go any further. This was another lesson I received from Bhutan. We are used to setting goals and pushing ourselves to reach the summit, but sometimes you also need to know when to stop, listen to your body, recognize limits, let go, and enjoy what you have already achieved or the journey itself. Perhaps this ability is also a type of success.
Bhutan offers much more beyond the iconic Tiger’s Nest. One of the most impressive locations is the Punakha Dzong, a magnificent fortress-monastery situated at the confluence of two rivers and considered one of the most beautiful buildings in the country. The road to it from Thimphu passes through the Dochula Pass, a mountain pass at an altitude of 3,100 meters, where 108 impressive Buddhist stupa monuments stand. On clear days, views of the Himalayas unfold from there.
Another place not to be missed is the Phobjikha Valley, a wide, green valley offering pastoral hiking trails and scenery completely different from urban areas. The valley is also famous for the black-necked cranes that migrate from Tibet and arrive during the winter.
Thimphu also offers a series of attractions, including a giant seated Buddha statue overlooking the valley, the weekend market selling local vegetables, fruits, grains, and incense, as well as monasteries, museums, and cultural centers.
In Paro, it is worth visiting the Paro Dzong, the National Museum, and the ancient Kyichu Lhakhang temple.
Bhutan is also an excellent destination for trekking enthusiasts, with trails of various difficulty levels – from relatively short hikes to journeys lasting days and weeks in the Himalayas. For those seeking a true challenge, the Snowman Trek awaits, which is considered one of the hardest treks in the world, featuring a long and demanding route through northern Bhutan and mountain passes at altitudes of up to 5,000 meters.
One of the most special moments for me was actually quite simple: a hot bath with local medicinal herbs, heated by scorching stones. After grueling days of driving through the mountains, visiting temples, landscapes, and sites, I had the opportunity to rest in the warm water with local plants, minerals, and scents – an experience that beautifully illustrated the Bhutanese connection between nature, tradition, and humanity.
Gelephu Mindfulness City seeks to combine economic development with traditional Bhutanese values
As if all this weren’t enough, Bhutan is currently promoting one of the most intriguing projects in the world: Gelephu Mindfulness City – in the Gelephu region in the south. This is a Special Administrative Region whose vision seeks to combine economic development with traditional Bhutanese values, promoting sectors like health and wellness, education, technology, innovation, and spirituality. The project is being advanced under the auspices of the king and aims to create a new urban model influenced by Bhutanese culture and the principles of Gross National Happiness.
This is perhaps one of the most interesting paradoxes in Bhutan: a country identified worldwide with tradition, quiet, and a different pace of life, while simultaneously trying to plan its future through an ambitious urban project.
A quick note on accommodation in Bhutan: during my visit, I found that three-to-four-star hotels can be of a very good, pleasant, and organized standard. Those looking for five-star hotels will, of course, find luxury options, but the price matches. And as a reminder, the meaningful experiences are those outside the hotel, including the culture, the people, and the landscape.
The Himalayan mountains accompany the visit almost everywhere, from landing to takeoff. Between and along the slopes of the mountains lie green valleys, forests, rivers, fortresses, villages, fields, and monasteries built onto cliff faces, alongside hundreds and thousands of colorful prayer flags.
All of these add up to the feeling of being inside a postcard or a fairy tale. To the landscape, another special component is added – the welcome. Our hosts received us with genuine warmth, heartfelt patience, and a desire to share their culture with us.
When I said goodbye to Bhutan, one thought remained with me. We live in a world that measures success through money, houses, cars, titles, achievements, or our number of followers on social networks. In the face of all this, Bhutan offers a different touchstone. It proposes adding health, time, community, nature, culture, relationships, and a sense of meaning to the equation.
I was left mostly with that same word I heard during the journey: Impermanence. Perhaps not the absolute secret to happiness, but a thought worth taking home: to appreciate what we have a little more, to be a little less preoccupied with what is missing – and to moderate our constant craving for more.
And sometimes, just like on the path to the Tiger’s Nest, knowing when to stop is also part of the journey.
Special thanks to Dr. Nimrod Sheinman for his help, advice, and assistance in editing this report.

A time for flight renewals: Delta’s and United’s return puts stamp on Israeli victory - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:12:47 UTC
00:12:47 KST

The recent announcements that Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are officially returning to Israeli skies this September aren’t just fantastic news all-around: I’m declaring it Victory Day.
After witnessing the horrors of October 7 and the ensuing and still ongoing wars against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran, it’s hard to claim a victory in the Middle East.
But when judging an era’s normality, one has to judge according to that time period. As such, the conflicts will continue, and there will unfortunately be more flare-ups and escalations.
But when the heavens open up, and the giants of the aviation world return, there will be a sense of rebirth.
When tourists fill the streets of ancient and new cities alike, there will be a feeling that the curse is over.
When residents can fly abroad with ease, sharing a mundane conversation with a visitor heading home, there is an epiphany of shared humanity.
And that shared humanity has been desperately missing not only from Ben-Gurion Airport, but from the country as a whole. It may seem like the airport has been busy and the city centers have been packed, but, alas, it’s only us Israelis getting used to the reality of the past three years.
By flying, airline global gatekeeper declares skies all clear
Which is why the return of Delta and United is crucial, much more so than the return of the European carriers: For when the American giants “put their stamps” on our skies, it means the global gatekeepers have officially declared the crisis contained.
The US airlines should first and foremost reopen the floodgates to Israel for Diaspora families and Christian pilgrims traveling for the Tishrei holidays.
But they aren’t just bringing much-needed foreign currency; they are bringing a message of solidarity. Every packed flight represents a bridge rebuilt, signaling to the world that Israel is safe, vibrant, and ready to welcome the world back.
Let this be the beginning of the beginning.
For the hard-working Israeli, this message of solidarity also translates to financial relief. With thousands of new seats being injected into the market right before the holidays, the local monopoly is on its way out, and a new-old sense of normality is making its way back in.
But even if these scenarios play out that way, is this enough to declare Victory Day?
For skeptics like myself, my hesitation is still outweighing my optimism. Not only because of the never-ending regional conflict we find ourselves in, but also because we have to take a leap of faith in foreign carriers.
I was one of the many stranded in Europe during the first round of the Iran war in 2025. And earlier this year, I narrowly escaped being stuck abroad a second time. Using local Israeli airlines is our psychological safety net because we know they will fly through almost anything to get us home.
So why should United’s and Delta’s announcements change anything? To add to Solomon’s grounded words of wisdom: There’s a time for war and a time for peace; a time for cancellations and a time for flight renewals.
We have done this before. Since October 7, Delta, United, and dozens of other carriers have been playing musical runways – announcing their return only to cancel shortly after they don’t like the way a news headline looks.
Why this time is different
Why, then, should this September be crowned Victory Day when we know a single drone or a harsh news item could send them fleeing back across the Atlantic by October?
How will we know if this aviation Victory Day is truly the beginning of a lasting normality, or just another false start?
Industry experts will tell us if the renewed flights were a success story based on their own risk-assessment protocols, insurance premiums, and logistical mileposts; individuals such as myself may need some more time before venturing off to see the prices that foreign carriers are offering.
To this I say, what an embarrassment of riches to have. It may be that I never feel comfortable again flying with a foreign carrier, or, to be a half-glass-full person, I’d rather fly with the secure state of mind that the Israeli airlines offer me.
But whether you find yourself in the same situation as I am or if you can’t wait to fly via Delta or United, the return of these American aviation giants is an undeniable triumph for the average citizen. It puts the stamp on an Israeli victory.
It proves that our skies are resilient, our economy is vital, and our connection to the world at large is on the mend.
To return to the Book of Ecclesiastes, this is the way of life. And now it’s our time to laugh, it’s our time to dance, it’s our time for peace.
How long will that last? Who knows. But let’s enjoy it while we can.
This September, as those massive jets touch down once again at Ben-Gurion Airport, it won’t just be an arrival of passengers. It will be the arrival of our global connection, allowing Israelis to finally look upward with renewed freedom, relief, and hope. To feel that, even for a moment, to me is Victory Day.
The writer is the editor of The Jerusalem Post’s Travel Page.

Delhi auto, taxi unions oppose latest hike
NEW DELHI: Auto-rickshaw and taxi unions in Delhi have opposed the latest CNG price hike, saying drivers are already grappling with rising operating costs and do not want to pass the additional burden on to commuters.Rajendra Soni, general secretary of the Auto Rickshaw Association and Delhi Pradesh Taxi Union, said CNG prices had risen by Rs 10-12 over the past two-and-a-half to three months, while repeated requests for a meeting with the government had received no response."We do not want to burden the people of Delhi. Over the past two and a half to three months, CNG prices have increased by Rs 10-12. We have written several letters to the government requesting a meeting to discuss the problems faced by auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers. It has been one and a half years since the government came to power, but nothing has been done," Soni said.This comes as Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) has raised CNG prices in Delhi-NCR by Rs 3.89 per kg, citing higher import costs of liquefied natural gas (LNG). The revised price took effect on Saturday, taking CNG to Rs 86.98 per kg in Delhi.
This is the fifth CNG price increase in the region this year and the first since May, when IGL raised prices by a total of Rs 6 per kg in four phases over 10 days amid a global rise in energy prices during the West Asia conflict.
CNG now costs Rs 95.59 per kg in Noida and Ghaziabad, Rs 95.47 per kg in Meerut and Rs 92.01 per kg in Gurugram. Prices vary across states because of differences in value-added tax (VAT) rates.The latest increase is expected to add to pressure on passenger and freight fares across Delhi-NCR, where auto-rickshaws, taxis and a large number of goods carriers rely on CNG.

Four migrants arrested in Spain’s Ceuta enclave for throwing stones at soldiers

AI generated
MADRID - Four Moroccan migrants in Spain’s enclave of Ceuta were arrested on Aug 29 for throwing stones at a patrol of Spanish soldiers, one of whom fell and injured himself while pursuing the assailants, a police spokesman told AFP.
It was the second such incident to occur in recent days in the tiny territory located in North Africa, following the arrests on Aug 27 of 12 Moroccan migrants who threw stones at a Spanish military vehicle, injuring one of its four occupants.
Eleven of those 12 were deported to Morocco, according to local reports.
Ceuta remains a source of tension, politically and security-wise, for Spain since tens of thousands of migrants crossed over into it from Morocco on July 30 and 31, triggering alarm among Madrid’s EU partners.
Most of those migrants left in subsequent days, but thousands remain in Ceuta, wandering the streets and sleeping on beaches of the territory whose population is 80,000.
Ceuta residents protesting against the presence of the remaining migrants clashed with police on Aug 27, prompting Spain’s government to appeal for calm.
Madrid is seeking ways to reduce the number of remaining migrants in Ceuta without breaching EU and international asylum and migration laws.
The EU’s commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on X on Aug 29 that Spain had asked for help from the European Union’s border control agency Frontex, the police cooperation agency Europol and the EU Agency for Asylum.
“We are already working on the request and will take a swift decision,” Brunner said, calling the situation in Ceuta “challenging”.
“The priority remains to ensure the swift return of all those who remain illegally in Ceuta,” he said. AFP

Study finds media coverage of the 2024 presidential race favored political spectacle over substantive policy debates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:00:14 UTC
00:00:14 KST

New research provides evidence that mainstream newspaper coverage of the 2024 United States presidential election focused heavily on political strategy and legal controversies rather than policy issues. The findings indicate that while coverage of Donald Trump was persistently negative, Kamala Harris received a temporary positive boost following her sudden nomination. The study was published in the Journal of Political Marketing.
The contemporary political environment in the United States is highly polarized, which shapes both how journalists report the news and how the public interprets it. During election years, readers flock to political news to inform their voting decisions. However, journalists face a choice in how they present this information. A 2011 review of political communication explained that news outlets often frame elections around campaign tactics, momentum, and horse-race polling—focusing on who is winning or losing—rather than substantive policy debates. When this strategy-based framing dominates, the news tends to emphasize political spectacle over practical governance.
Alongside this focus on campaign tactics, political news often carries a heavy dose of negativity. Journalists and readers alike tend to display greater sensitivity to conflict and scandal than to routine achievements. This negativity bias has become particularly pronounced in recent years. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that negative language use among U.S. politicians surged starting in 2015 alongside Donald Trump’s initial primary campaign and remained elevated throughout his presidency.
The 2024 presidential election presented an unusually chaotic cycle, featuring an assassination attempt, a late-stage withdrawal by Joe Biden, and the rapid nomination of a new candidate, Kamala Harris. The authors of the new study set out to document how these unprecedented political shocks altered the narratives and the emotional tone presented in mainstream print journalism.
The research, led by Ayse D. Lokmanoglu of Boston University, analyzed tens of thousands of articles from five major high-circulation newspapers. The team focused on USA Today, The Washington Post, The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, and The Boston Globe, collecting articles published between January 1, 2024, and January 31, 2025. After initially gathering over 500,000 articles, the researchers applied keyword filters to identify stories that specifically mentioned Joe Biden, Donald Trump, or Kamala Harris in the headline or opening excerpt. This process resulted in a final dataset of 37,321 full-text articles.
To make sense of this massive amount of text, the scientists used automated computer programs to conduct topic modeling and sentiment analysis. Topic modeling is a technique that identifies clusters of words that frequently appear together, allowing researchers to see what overarching themes are present in a set of documents without having to read each one manually. Sentiment analysis involves using a specialized dictionary to count the number of positive and negative words in an article, providing an overall score for the emotional tone of the text.
The researchers identified five major themes in the news coverage: elections and campaign frames, Trump family legal issues, domestic policy and regulation, foreign policy and ideology, and government and legislation. As the election cycle progressed, the share of articles dedicated to elections and campaign frames surged sharply. This spike was particularly prominent around major political events, such as Biden dropping out of the race and the Democratic National Convention.
Meanwhile, coverage of Trump’s legal issues grew steadily, peaking in late December and early January during developments in his various court cases. In contrast, discussions of domestic policy and regulation steadily declined in volume as the election approached. This pattern indicates a displacement effect, where campaign drama and legal scandals squeezed out substantive discussions of policy.
When looking at the emotional tone of the coverage, the researchers noted that the five newspapers converged on broadly similar patterns. Overall, the median sentiment of the coverage hovered slightly below neutral. However, distinct differences emerged depending on which candidate the article covered. Articles mentioning Trump were consistently negative throughout most of the pre-election period.
Articles mentioning Harris, or both Biden and Harris, trended in a slightly positive direction. Harris received a noticeable positive bump in coverage following the Democratic National Convention and the vice-presidential debate. This temporary boost aligns with the concept of a post-nomination honeymoon effect, where newly introduced or barrier-breaking candidates receive more favorable, optimistic coverage in their early days on the national ticket.
Interestingly, articles that mentioned both Democratic and Republican candidates were persistently negative, suggesting that when journalists write about both sides in the same article, they usually focus on partisan conflict and adversarial attacks.
The findings offer a detailed look at mainstream media narratives, but the researchers noted a few limitations to their work. The analysis focused exclusively on five major newspapers that generally lean toward the political center or center-left. Because the study excluded right-leaning outlets, the results might not capture the full spectrum of the American media diet.
Additionally, the automated tool used to measure sentiment relies on counting specific words, which means it can miss complex rhetorical devices like sarcasm, subtext, or strategic ambiguity. The researchers also filtered their articles by searching for specific candidate names. Articles that discussed broad political platforms or policies without naming Biden, Harris, or Trump directly were excluded, which could have artificially lowered the amount of policy coverage detected in the dataset. Future research could expand on this work by using advanced language models capable of understanding context and nuance, or by linking news publication data with social media metrics to see how readers amplify different types of political stories.
The study, “An Overview of Media Coverage Shifts Before and After the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election,” was authored by Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Ananya Gupta, Tess Hemmila, Amira Jadoon, Bart Knijnenburg, and Arie Perliger.

Poland's prime minister says the next seven or eight months could decide the region's security. Donald Tusk said there are signs of serious Russian preparations to escalate tensions, both in the war against Ukraine and across the region, according to Ukrinform.
Tusk's warning follows weeks of similar alarms from the countries on NATO's eastern edge. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on 15 July that intelligence pointed to possible Russian strikes on critical infrastructure in the Baltic states or Poland, according to Defense News.
Poland is the main transit route for Western military aid to Ukraine, which makes its security inseparable from Ukraine's. Tusk himself said in July that Russia could be ready for a confrontation with Europe as early as 2027.
The CIA visit was not the whole of it
At the meeting, reporters asked Tusk about the recent visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow. Poland is in constant contact with the agency's leadership and was not caught off guard by news of Ratcliffe's activity, he said.
Some security information must stay confidential, Tusk added, but that does not mean the public should be deprived of information about the most important threats.
The signals go beyond one trip
The matter is no longer only the CIA director's visit to Moscow, Tusk said. Over recent weeks, numerous public signals have pointed to Russian preparation for escalation.
Russia is very seriously preparing to escalate tensions, both in the war with Ukraine and across the whole region, and that for Russia this fall and winter are meant to be key, he claimed.
Moscow states its aims openly
Some Russian figures have described the war's purpose in plain terms. This week, State Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said Russia views Ukraine as a "territory" that would allow Moscow to export its energy to Europe via a short route, not as a sovereign country.

One-Sixth international film festival opens in Yekaterinburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:44:36 UTC
23:44:36 KST

YEKATERINBURG, August 29. /TASS/. The 5th International Festival of Debut Films of the Eurasian Continent, One-Sixth, has opened in Yekaterinburg, with films from more than 12 countries, master classes and meetings with prominent actors on the program, a TASS correspondent reports.
"People come because this is a place where a true debutante can find a basis for a second step. This festival isn’t about showing first works, but about inspiring second ones," festival director and president Yevgeny Grigoryev said at the opening ceremony.
He said this year’s festival is dedicated to teamwork, noting that film projects often bring together people who have never worked with one another before.
"We often believe in project-based approaches, and when you gather people for a project, there’s a grinding process; no one knows each other. Economically, it’s quite simple - you get them together, make a film, and then go your separate ways," Grigoryev said.
The opening ceremony featured the first Russian screening of Sasha Gromova’s Legend Without a Number. The film follows Ivan, a former football player who becomes a television presenter and humiliates a longtime rival - a lapta (Russian baseball) coach - on live television. To save his career, Ivan is forced to assemble his own team and win the match.
The festival will also hold a memorial day dedicated to director Alexey Balabanov on September 2. Guests will be presented with Balabanov Portrait, a new book by Andrey Zakhariev and Mikhail Volodin. A public reading of the script for the upcoming film Northerners is also planned.
The program includes master classes, meetings with film stars, as well as business and educational events.
The competition features 12 feature films, 12 documentaries and 12 animated films, including six Russian and six foreign entries in each category. Animation has been added to the competition for the first time this year. The lineup includes films from Russia, Italy, the Netherlands, Croatia, Singapore, France, Poland, Japan, India, Thailand, Belgium and other countries.
About the Festival
The festival was launched in 2022 on the initiative of the Sverdlovsk Film Studio with the support of the Russian Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of Culture of the Sverdlovsk Region. The Innovative Cultural Center of the Sverdlovsk Region joined the festival’s organization in 2023.
Over its four-year history, the festival has attracted more than 28,000 spectators and hosted over 200 competition and special screenings in Yekaterinburg and across the Sverdlovsk Region.
TASS is the festival’s general information partner.

Dozens of Israeli settlers attack flashpoint West Bank village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Dozens of Israeli settlers attack flashpoint West Bank village
Qusra, Palestinian Territories - Dozens of Israeli settlers attacked the Palestinian village of Qusra in the northern occupied West Bank on Aug 29, residents and the military said, after nearly three weeks of tension in the area.
Earlier in August a group of rogue settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing domestic and international condemnation.
Weeks later, Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.
On Aug 29, Qusra resident Yussef Abdul Kareem Hassan told AFP that a handful of villagers were doing work on a house when they were approached by a small group of settlers.
The settlers then called for backup and returned with dozens more, Hassan said, adding that they had surrounded the Palestinians inside the house and began throwing stones.
Footage of Qusra on Aug 29 showed dozens of Israeli forces deployed to the site.
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police forces were dispatched “following reports that Israeli rioters had arrived in the area and that violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians.”
“Upon their arrival, the security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside,” a military statement said, adding that it was “aware of reports of Palestinian injuries”.
It said forces had worked to remove the settlers from the house, separate the groups, and confiscate vehicles “that were suspected of having been used to reach the area.”
The vehicles would be used as evidence in a police investigation that has been opened, it said, adding that forces continued to operate in the area “to prevent further disturbances and restore order”.
“The security forces strongly condemn all forms of violence,” it said.
Violence by Israeli settlers towards Palestinians in the West Bank has persisted for years, often with little or no legal consequence, but recent months have seen a surge in attacks.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the Palestinian territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed at least 1,103 Palestinians in the West Bank, including both militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.
Israeli figures show at least 48 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period. AFP

With hundreds dead and thousands missing, Nepal-Tibet flood nightmare may not be over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:39:30 UTC
23:39:30 KST

As the scale of the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet continues to emerge, countries in the region are offering assistance and officials in Kathmandu estimate that rebuilding could cost $4 billion to $5 billion.
Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday that the figure was only a preliminary estimate.
“This is just an estimate. Loss and damage is being assessed,” he said.
Nepal, meanwhile, suspended search and rescue operations Saturday because of poor weather. Authorities are continuing to monitor two lakes upstream, including one formed by the flooding that began overflowing Friday.
Nepalese officials warned that the lakes pose a continuing flood risk. A Chinese government geological hazards expert said more than 100 glacial lakes are scattered across the region and could also pose a significant threat.
Reuters reported that at least 675 people have been killed in Nepal and seven in Tibet. About 3,000 people remain missing, including roughly 2,426 in Nepal.
With rescue operations temporarily halted by the weather, Nepalese authorities are focusing largely on transporting survivors to the capital, Kathmandu.
Nepal’s foreign minister said the country does not need additional assistance with search and rescue operations but does need help extracting people trapped in tunnels, restoring transportation and communications where bridges have been destroyed, identifying bodies, conducting DNA testing and storing bodies for extended periods.
“We have already made requests for such specialised services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how,” he told Reuters overnight.
China has called for international cooperation, while India sent three flights carrying about 60 metric tons of aid, including blankets, medicine and water purification tablets.
India is also planning to send a tunnel rescue team and a medical team and has offered its disaster response force and technical teams to assist with reconstruction.
‘Our world turned upside down’
Families around the world are closely following the search for people missing in the disaster, many of whom are foreign tourists who had been traveling in the region.
“We don’t know anything,” Mukti Patel, a Virginia resident whose father, sister, brother-in-law and her brother-in-law’s mother disappeared in the flash floods, told The Associated Press.
Patel knows the hotel where her relatives were staying was badly damaged but is holding out hope that they survived.
Sanket Pandey, the head of a company that organizes tours in the region, told the AP that 40 travelers and seven tour guides who had traveled to the area were missing. The company, which has an office in Baltimore, had organized a two-week trip to the region. Families are now trying to gather any information they can.
“It’s really difficult to have nothing,” Pandey said.
Jiwan Jyoti, a 50-year-old U.S. citizen from Massachusetts, was traveling with the group and is among those missing.
“They had stopped in Timure, Nepal, before they were set to leave for a pilgrimage to Mount Kailashin Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others,” a friend said.
Jyoti called her family while eating breakfast Wednesday and preparing to cross the border into Tibet.
Her friend said the call ended “at around 8:40 a.m. local time in Nepal, and then I think around 8:45, this flash floods came, and then our world turned upside down.”
She later learned that the hotel where Jyoti had been staying — and where Apple’s Find My app last recorded her location — had been completely destroyed.
“She was essentially almost in the epicenter over there,” the friend said.
Vaasavi Unnava believed her parents had already crossed into Tibet with the same tour group when she learned of the flooding.
“I was not really that worried, but I just sent them a text like to be sure,” she said.
The WhatsApp message was never delivered.
Her parents had set out on a retirement trip and were excited about spending two months with family in India after climbing Mount Kailash. The California couple are among dozens of U.S. citizens reported missing in the floods.
“They were so, so excited. My dad was talking about finally getting to spend time with his mother,” Unava said.
Video circulated on Chinese social media over the past day appeared to capture the collapse of part of the glacier that triggered the catastrophic flooding.
The drone footage was recorded at an altitude of more than 7,200 meters (23,600 feet) above sea level. Amid clouds and snow-covered peaks, a massive cloud of dust can suddenly be seen rising as part of the glacier crashes into the valley floor roughly 1 kilometer (0.6 mile) below. An analysis by the BBC found that the location corresponded with the direction in which the floodwaters traveled down the Trishuli River.
Other dramatic footage emerged from Bidur, a town downstream along the Trishuli River, and was verified by international media outlets. The video showed several people sheltering on a balcony of a building that withstood the massive flood as waves of water and mud surged beside it.
Some of the people were later seen standing on the same balcony after the water level had fallen, surrounded by mud and debris. One woman was seen waving a red cloth from the roof in an apparent appeal for help.
Nepal’s rescue efforts have relied heavily on helicopters because the massive torrent that struck the border region with Tibet — already difficult to traverse because of its mountainous terrain — swept away dozens of bridges and blocked more than 40 kilometers (25 miles) of roads.
In some cases, rescuers have descended from helicopters on ropes before hoisting survivors to safety.
Among those rescued was Dibga Tamang, who was evacuated from Rasuwa district Thursday.
“All of our people have gone. They are dead,” he said. “I have no one left waiting for me. Everything and everyone is gone. The end.”
More than 3,200 people have been evacuated by helicopter from the disaster zone, mainly to Kathmandu, according to Nepal’s disaster management authority.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire, one of the survivors in Timure, a Nepalese village near the Chinese border, arrived at work at 8 a.m. Wednesday. He said he felt the ground shaking while he was working.
“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us. We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building,” he said. “I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”
Disaster, step by step
The collapse
At an elevation of about 5,200 meters (17,100 feet), part of the glacier broke away and collapsed. It plunged roughly 1 kilometer (0.6 mile) into the valley below, initially leading to suspicions that an earthquake had struck.
It was later determined that the seismic energy, equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, was generated directly by the avalanche of ice and rock crashing above ground rather than an earthquake triggering the collapse.
The movement
The enormous mass of ice, rock and mud crashed into the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet.
According to a Chinese government geologist, the avalanche traveled at about 50 meters per second, or roughly 180 kilometers per hour (112 mph), for more than 20 kilometers (12 miles), leaving people with little time to react.
A ‘wall’ surges downstream
The water and debris did not move like an ordinary flood but instead formed a massive wave of mud that grew higher as it advanced.
One account described it as resembling “liquid cement.” The Trishuli River rose by about 9 meters (30 feet) in half an hour.
Tibet hit first
The massive flow traveled downstream into Gyirong County in Tibet. The Tibet-Nepal border crossing was severely damaged and almost entirely buried under mud.
Some people described the area Thursday as a place where civilization had effectively disappeared. Buildings, roads and bridges were swept away as the torrent continued toward Nepal.
The flood enters Nepal
The torrent continued through the river system into Nepal, traveling about 100 kilometers (62 miles) downstream while dropping roughly 4,500 meters (14,800 feet) in elevation.
The floodwaters swept away infrastructure, destroyed villages and cut off entire communities.
The fear: Another flood
The disaster created two new lakes on opposite sides of the border. Authorities in both countries have warned that the lakes could breach, potentially unleashing another destructive wave of flooding.

Prague’s spires whisper Maharal’s hidden history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:14 UTC
23:35:14 KST

The anniversary of the passing of the Maharal of Prague falls on 18 Elul, which this year is August 31. This is an opportunity for Jewish travelers to visit the city where his name still seems to hover among the pointed rooftops.
Over four hundred years have passed since his death in 1609, yet in Prague, time is a flexible substance. It clings to the stones, becomes trapped between the vaulted ceilings of the synagogues, and hides in the cracks between the ancient tombstones.
Prague is beautiful. In the morning, it awakens from a thin mist rising from the Vltava River, bells ring above the rooftops, and red trams squeal along the tracks.
Czechia is considered one of the most Israel-friendly countries in Europe, and Prague gives Jewish travelers a relatively pleasant and safe feeling. While in various European destinations we are required to exercise greater caution in the face of antisemitism, on the streets of Prague I felt free to walk around even with my kippah and tzitzit openly visible.
But the deeper connection between Prague and the Jews cannot be measured by political declarations. You have to walk to the old Jewish Quarter, Josefov, and open a heavy door there.
The Altneuschul
The “Old-New Synagogue” is one of those places where it seems that history did not end, but merely took a short break. It is the oldest synagogue in Europe that is still active. It was built in 1270 and has served the community for more than 700 years.
Legend has it that stones from the ruins of the Temple in Jerusalem were incorporated into the foundations of the Altneuschul, giving rise to the interpretation that its name derives from the Hebrew words meaning “on condition,” referring to the condition that the stones would one day be taken to Jerusalem when the Messiah comes.
But the truth is less poetic. “Alt-neu” means “old-new.” At first, it was called “The New Synagogue.” Over the course of history, additional synagogues were built in the Jewish Quarter, and one of them proudly bore the name “New.” To distinguish between the two synagogues, the word “Old” was added to the name of the older one, hence the name “Old-New.”
The stone floor is lower than the entrance. Overhead rise six Gothic vaults, light filters sparingly through twelve windows, and the entire hall is steeped in that dignified dimness found in places where generations have whispered the same prayers.
The Holy Ark on the eastern wall is made of marble, and above it is a pointed arch with stone decorations. Next to the Holy Ark stands the “Maharal’s Chair,” and care is taken that no one sits on it.
In the center of the synagogue is a raised bimah with a table for reading the Torah, surrounded by iron railings. Above them flies the flag of the Jewish community dating from the 17th century. It is a red flag embroidered with a yellow Star of David, with a Jewish hat at its center. The flag also has an embroidered yellow border, at the top of which are the words “Shema Yisrael.”
And above it all is the attic. There, Prague whispers, lies the Golem.
Here the Maharal prayed and taught. Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel was much more than the city’s chief rabbi. Alongside his extensive knowledge of the Talmud and Midrash, he also studied philosophy and the sciences and wrote dozens of books.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook wrote that the Maharal had “redeemed” the teachings of Kabbalah from their concealment and made them accessible to the wider public. That is why most of us studied his book Netivot Olam in Yeshivot Bnei Akiva. I recommend packing it for a trip to Prague so that you can return to reading it here as well.
The Golem that never left Prague
The Maharal is probably the best-known Jewish rabbi today, even among Christians, and that is because of the story of the Golem. According to legend, when the Jews of Prague suffered from blood libels and persecution, the Maharal created a human figure out of clay and breathed life into it. Something like a modern robot. The Maharal sent the Golem into the streets of Prague “to deal” with non-Jews who harassed Jews and with those who spread blood libels.
One Friday evening, the Maharal forgot to deactivate the Golem, and it went out into the street and began to run wild and cause damage. The Maharal was informed of this in the middle of the recitation of “Mizmor Shir” of the Kabbalat Shabbat prayer.
The Maharal immediately went out into the street, brought the Golem, and deactivated it. Afterwards, the rabbi returned to the synagogue and began reciting “Mizmor Shir” once again. Since then, to this very day, the custom at the Altneuschul has been to recite “Mizmor Shir” twice during the Friday Maariv service. It is the only place in the world where this custom is observed.
The story of the Golem of Prague has no reliable historical basis. But in Prague, sometimes the legend is stronger than the footnote. Figures of the Golem peer out from the windows of souvenir shops, made of clay and wood, and the story continues to walk the streets as though someone had forgotten to erase the letter that gives it life.
A statue of the Maharal stands at the corner of Prague’s New City Hall on Mariánské námestí, near the Jewish Quarter. In the entire world, only two rabbis are commemorated as part of a city’s mythology with public statues: the Maharal in Prague and the Rambam (Maimonides) in Córdoba, Spain.
The synagogues of Prague
Several other synagogues remain in the Josefov Quarter, all within a short walking distance of one another. One of them, the Pinkas Synagogue, now serves as a Holocaust museum. Of the original synagogue, only the Holy Ark and the Torah-reading bimah remain. The names of 77,297 Jews from Bohemia who were murdered in the Holocaust are inscribed on the walls.
A walking path leads from the Pinkas Synagogue along the Old Jewish Cemetery. Here, the atmosphere changes.
Thousands of tombstones stand crowded together, leaning toward one another like old people wishing to whisper a secret. Among the graves is that of the Maharal.
Beside his tombstone, people leave notes and small stones. Some pray. Others simply stand. Perhaps this is the Maharal’s true power: not the Golem, but the fact that hundreds of years after his death, people still come to talk to him.
The Klausen Synagogue is the largest of the synagogues that remain from the old ghetto. It stands on the other side of the cemetery, in an area where houses of study established by Mordechai Maisel once operated and where the Maharal taught.
A Jewish itinerary in Prague should also include the Spanish Synagogue, built in the 19th century, whose rich Moorish design is reminiscent of the Alhambra Palace. Gold, arabesques, and geometric patterns make its interior one of the most impressive in the city.
The Maisel Synagogue was established by Mordechai Maisel, one of Prague’s wealthiest Jews and one of the community’s greatest benefactors during the Maharal’s time. Today, it houses an exhibition on the history of the Jews of Bohemia and Moravia, and among the exhibits are original writings of the Maharal.
A ticket office for admission to all the synagogues is located at Maiselova St. 38/15, opposite the Altneuschul. There is usually a long line there, so it is better to buy tickets online in advance.
Outside Josefov stands one of the most beautiful synagogues in the world, the Jerusalem Synagogue. After the gray stone and dimness of the Altneuschul, entering it feels almost like an explosion of color. The façade combines Moorish and Art Nouveau styles, with blue, red, and gold. Inside, colorful arches stretch overhead, Hebrew verses decorate the walls, and sunlight breaks through the stained-glass windows, painting the interior with color.
One Maharal against a hundred spires
Prague is a beautiful, romantic, and vibrant city with numerous opportunities for entertainment and sightseeing. Prague is also known as the “City of a Hundred Spires.” It is blessed with many tourist attractions that have no connection to Judaism. Here are a few recommendations:
Old Town Square is its beating heart. In front of the Astronomical Clock, tourists crowd together and raise their phones every hour on the hour.
From there, it is worth continuing to Charles Bridge, preferably early in the morning, when the stone is still cold, and the Vltava is silver-gray. In the first light, the statues gradually emerge from the darkness, and the spires on the far side of the river acquire edges of gold. In the center of the bridge, there is also a statue of a cross bearing the Hebrew words “Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh, Hashem Tzevaot” (“Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts”) written in gold.
Across the river rises Prague Castle, a vast complex of palaces, courtyards, and St. Vitus Cathedral.
You can cruise along the Vltava, lose yourself in the alleys of Malá Strana, or simply sit in a café and watch the trams pass by.
After a visit to Josefov, Prague looks different. Behind its Gothic and Baroque beauty lies another city, Jewish, ancient, and filled with memories, where the Maharal still seems to walk between the synagogue and the cemetery.
Perhaps that is why the Golem legend lives on: Prague itself is a little like a Golem, shaped from stone, clay, and memory, with a spirit that refuses to fade. Those who follow in the Maharal’s footsteps discover that sometimes the best way to know a city is to listen to the whispers beneath its towers.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

EPOS film fest explores fine art, literature, theater and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:11 UTC
23:35:11 KST

The 17th EPOS International Art Film Festival, which presents dozens of films from Israel and abroad exploring art, literature, architecture, music, dance, theater, and photography, will take place between September 16 and September 19 at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
This year, the festival will expand beyond Tel Aviv for the first time with EPOS in the Gilboa, a new program at the Mishkan Museum of Art at Ein Harod, created in cooperation with the Gilboa Regional Council.
Six festival films will be screened there from September 17-19, with each screening accompanied by a short lecture connected to the film’s subject.
The festival will open with Take the Money and Run, a documentary about Danish artist Jens Haaning and an incident that became one of the contemporary art world’s most provocative controversies.
A Copenhagen museum lent Haaning half a million kroner to create a work incorporating banknotes on two large canvases.
Instead, the museum received two empty frames and a work titled Take the Money and Run. The disappearance of the money sparked an international debate over whether Haaning had created a daring conceptual artwork or simply taken the museum’s cash.
Naked Ambition explores the life of famed photographer Bunny Yeager
The closing film, Naked Ambition, focuses on Bunny Yeager, a successful photographer for Playboy Magazine during the 1950s and 1960s. Decades later, Yeager was embraced by some feminist movements as an example of an independent woman who helped other women take pride in their bodies, and her photographs were exhibited in American museums.
A special tribute will also be held in memory of Israeli director Ram Loevy, featuring a screening of Bread, about a bakery worker who loses his livelihood after 20 years and begins a hunger strike. The film was among the early Israeli works to confront the economic distress of development towns.
Israeli films at the festival include Seven Tractates on the Life of Bruria, directed by Bruria Pasternak Sharvit, an autobiographical work about her life in the mainly haredi (ultra-Orthodox) city of Bnei Brak as an artist and mother of five.
Another is On Her Own, directed by Bracha Zisman-Cohen, which portrays artist Raida Adon and the idea that, wherever she lives, only art truly feels like home.
There is also Dalit Kimor’s Ida’s Dance Club, about a ballroom-dancing competition whose participants have long passed retirement age but continue to dance, sing, fall in love, and experience disappointment.
The festival will also include two competitions centered on Tel Aviv-Jaffa. The second annual Urban Diary competition, produced in cooperation with the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Museum, will present short films that examine the city through cultural, personal, and social perspectives.
Then, the films will be screened at Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Museum and added to its collection of urban stories. A separate short-film competition will focus on artists and art in Israel, aiming to promote cinematic work about the country’s cultural life and help preserve it through film.
For younger viewers, EPOS will present Louisa, an award-winning production by Jerusalem’s Train Theater, created by Iris Domany. Recommended for children aged five and up, the performance follows a video and animation artist whose tiny collections gradually come to life through the lens of a magnifying camera, creating the world of Louisa, a girl searching for a sense of belonging.
Poetry Movies will recognize poets and address films dealing with war and AI
Another program, Poetry Movies, curated by Yasmin Kaini, will include tributes to poets Israel Eliraz and Hedva Harechavi, as well as films dealing with war and artificial intelligence. The program will also feature the premiere of Taha: The Voice
Between the Lines, a short documentary about Palestinian poet Taha Muhammad Ali, who died in 2010. His poetry, translated into dozens of languages, dealt less directly with the conflict than with pain, suffering, and hope.
The festival will pay tribute to Czech-born British playwright Tom Stoppard, with a documentary, Tom Stoppard: A Charmed Life, offering a rare look at his life and work, as well as a screening of the film adaptation of Anna Karenina, for which Stoppard wrote the screenplay.
Music documentaries will include films about Gustav Mahler’s years in New York; the extraordinary career of cellist
Jacqueline du Pré, who Yo-Yo Ma recalls married Daniel Barenboim, and who battled with illness; conductor Simon Rattle; and German conductor Joana Mallwitz.
Other films examine the lives and work of artists including Caravaggio, Egon Schiele, conceptual artist Mierle Laderman
Ukeles, architects Winy Maas and Soren Pihlmann, photographer Martin Schoeller, dancer and choreographer Germaine Acogny, and theater director Robert Wilson.
EPOS is under the artistic direction of Miki Laron, joined by artistic directors Yotam David Zitter and Shani Kiniso.
For more information, visit the festival website at https://filmart.co.il/en/home-english/

Who owns Judaism? Israel must take it back from the religious establishment - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
14:35:05 UTC
23:35:05 KST

The upcoming elections will determine not only who sits in the next government but also what kind of country we want to be. Amid the debate over haredi (ultra-Orthodox) military enlistment, public funding, religious services, and Israel’s identity, a more fundamental question has been forgotten: Who actually owns our Judaism?
In Israel, a dangerous equation has taken root: Judaism is equated with religiosity, religiosity with Orthodoxy, and Orthodoxy with the rabbinical establishment and the haredi political parties.
From there, it is only a short step to sectoral demands rooted in a notion of Jewish superiority: Those who lead a religious way of life are perceived as preserving Judaism on behalf of the entire public and, as such, are entitled to special status. This ranges from exemption from the most basic civic obligation in the State of Israel – military service – to the demand that society subsidize a nonproductive way of life whose cost to the public continues to grow.
The ongoing wars, which have underscored the urgent need to integrate haredim into Israeli society and, above all, to enlist them in the IDF, cannot be separated from the struggle over the Jewish identity of the state. Nor can it be separated from the fact that haredi control of the religious establishment and religious services translates into control over the Jewish character of the state.
Kashrut, the Chief Rabbinate, religious councils, rabbinical appointments, marriage, and divorce have long since become centers of political power. They serve as instruments in reinforcing an imagined division of roles that has become embedded in the public consciousness – a division that is not only false but generates alienation from Judaism itself.
At the same time, however, the opposite phenomenon is taking place. Outside the religious establishment, official religious services, and political appointments that are handed out as spoils to haredi parties, an Israeli Judaism is flourishing: traditional, popular, cultural, and communal. It thrives in music, literature, customs, and in the Israeli way of life itself.
Israelis have not abandoned Judaism
Who decided that Judaism belongs only to those who wear a kippah? In Israel of 2026, this is no longer a philosophical or theological question. It has become a political and civic question – and even a question about our very ability to live here together.
Israelis have not abandoned Judaism. They are abandoning those who claim ownership over it.
The effort to enlist haredim in the military and integrate them into the workforce must begin by giving Judaism back to the Jews. First and foremost, we must break the notion that anyone can claim to be the “owners” of Judaism.
This is one of the great challenges facing the next government: dismantling the ideological foundation that allows one sector, on the one hand, to appropriate Judaism as its exclusive property and, on the other, to demand special privileges.
It is time to say what may have become almost taboo in Israel: Judaism does not belong to the religious establishment. It does not belong to any political party, to the rabbinate, or to any particular sector. It belongs to all of us.
In the next Knesset, this principle must be translated into action: breaking monopolies in religious services; restoring competition in kashrut services and allowing Tzohar rabbis to operate as a state-recognized authority; transforming religious services into services that truly serve the public; turning the rabbinate and religious councils from arenas of political patronage into institutions that work for the public good; giving greater power to local communities, a greater role to women, and greater freedom of choice to every citizen.
In a country increasingly divided into identities and tribes, and one that must integrate its haredi population, this is no longer merely a question of religion and state.
It is a question about our future.
The writer is a member of the Yisrael Beytenu party list.
